articles.title: What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach
articles.text:
What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach
- Date:
  November 25, 2026
- Source:
  The Hebrew University of Jerusalem
- Summary:
  A new theory suggests that the brain may chemically encode and retrieve memories rather than relying solely on electrical signals. Researchers propose that interactions between brain cells and their molecular surroundings could help explain the intimate connection between memory, emotion, and thought. Their findings challenge the assumption that increasingly powerful computers could eventually develop human-like consciousness.
- Share:
The fundamental difference between human intelligence and artificial intelligence may have less to do with computing power than with the chemistry of memory. Researchers propose that the brain not only communicates through electrical signals but may also "write" and "read" memories through chemical interactions involving neurons, astrocytes, and the molecules surrounding them. By linking memory to emotion and thought, the theory raises an increasingly relevant question: Can computational power alone give rise to the kind of consciousness experienced by living organisms?
Hearing a familiar song can transport someone back decades. A distinctive scent can bring a forgotten person or place to mind, while recalling a terrifying experience can trigger both emotional and physical reactions within moments.
Like the human brain, computers can store and retrieve information. However, the mechanisms underlying biological memory may be fundamentally different.
A new review by Dr. Gerard Marx of MX Biotech Ltd. and Professor Chaim Gilon of the Department of Chemistry at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem explores the physical and chemical mechanisms that could link memory, emotion, and thought.
In their paper, "Consciousness, Memory and Intelligence: A Mechanistic Perspective," the researchers suggest that understanding memory requires more than studying neurons and their electrical activity. They argue that other brain cells, particularly astrocytes, and the intricate molecular environment surrounding them may also play essential roles.
Building on their previous research into the molecular foundations of memory, Marx and Gilon examine whether the processes responsible for storing and retrieving experiences could also shed light on the origins of intelligence, thought, and consciousness.
The Brain's Hidden Chemical Code for Memory
Central to the researchers' proposal is a model known as the Tripartite Mechanism of Memory.
According to this theory, memories emerge from interactions between three major components: brain cells, especially astrocytes working alongside neurons; the molecular substances surrounding those cells; and various chemicals, including metal ions, neurotransmitters, and gliotransmitters.
Rather than relying exclusively on electrical communication between neurons, the brain may use chemical processes to encode and retrieve information.
Astrocytes, which are abundant throughout the brain and maintain close interactions with neurons, are particularly important to this proposed mechanism. Marx and Gilon suggest that groups of astrocytes help process cognitive information through their interactions with neurons and the extracellular environment, the space and molecular material surrounding brain cells.
The new paper expands this hypothesis to explore the nature of thought itself. If the brain can physically encode an experience as a memory, the process of recovering that information, recognizing it, and interpreting its significance might contribute to the formation of thoughts.
Why Memories Carry Emotional Meaning
One of the central arguments of the researchers' theory is that biological memories contain more than stored information. They are also closely connected to emotional experiences.
A scent associated with childhood may spark feelings of happiness. Hearing a familiar voice can provide reassurance, while remembering a frightening event may produce an immediate physical response.
Marx and Gilon contend that a physical model of memory must account for these emotional associations. Their proposed mechanism incorporates neurotransmitters and other chemical messengers that may help encode cognitive information alongside its emotional significance.
This potential biochemical connection between memory and emotion provides a starting point for investigating larger questions about how the brain generates thought, intelligence, and conscious experiences.
What Human Consciousness May Have That AI Lacks
The rapid development of artificial intelligence makes these ideas particularly relevant.
Although computers and brains can both retain and access information, the physical mechanisms behind these abilities may differ considerably. Computer memory is ultimately encoded in electronic hardware. Biological memory, the researchers propose, may instead depend on the intricate cellular and chemical machinery of living brain tissue.
This distinction becomes increasingly significant as AI systems grow more capable of performing tasks traditionally associated with human reasoning and intelligence.
Marx and Gilon challenge the assumption that simply increasing computational power and complexity will eventually produce consciousness comparable to that of a living brain. They argue that electronic systems lack the biological structures and emotional mechanisms found in living organisms.
The researchers are not suggesting that AI cannot develop increasingly advanced intellectual capabilities. Instead, they question whether demonstrating intelligent behavior is equivalent to possessing the biological mechanisms responsible for memory, emotion, and conscious experience.
How Memory May Give Rise to Thought
Marx and Gilon emphasize that their theory does not solve the enduring mystery of consciousness. They explicitly acknowledge that the nature of conscious life remains poorly understood.
However, their proposed biochemical framework offers a different way to investigate the physical processes that may underlie mental activity. By examining interactions between brain cells and their chemical environment, the Tripartite Mechanism of Memory could provide researchers with another avenue for exploring how the mind works.
While their earlier research focused on how memories might be physically encoded within the brain, their latest work addresses a much broader problem.
Understanding how living brain tissue transforms experience into memory could eventually help explain how memories become thoughts, how conscious experiences arise, and what fundamentally distinguishes biological intelligence from artificial intelligence.

Materials provided by The Hebrew University of Jerusalem. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Gerard Marx, Chaim Gilon. Consciousness, Memory and Intelligence: A Mechanistic Perspective. International Journal of Psychiatry Research, 2026; 9 (3) DOI: 10.33425/2641-4317.1251

articles.title: Here's how to stop Hisense smart TVs from spying on you
articles.text:
In brief: Like other smart TV manufacturers, Hisense tracks users' viewing habits for targeted advertising. However, a recent reverse-engineering effort revealed where Hisense's traffic goes and how it might transmit what users say. A GitHub repository also provides detailed instructions for disabling ad tracking. Experts recommend disconnecting smart TVs from the internet and streaming content via external devices.
A recent write-up from software engineer Gabriel Werneck outlines how Hisense's VIDAA TVs send user viewing data to Israeli ad firm Nexxen. Opting out of certain settings appears to stop this behavior, but other manufacturers have been caught ignoring opt-outs before.
When Werneck used DeepSeek to reverse-engineer his VIDAA smart TV's operating system, he discovered that it uses its microphone to identify viewing content for targeted ads. Most smart TVs use automatic content recognition (ACR) via intermittent screencaps.
VIDAA TVs use microphones to recognize voice commands, which requires them to listen at all times. However, Werneck discovered that Nexxen receives audio data from the microphones, including sound from the TV's speakers. Like other ACR systems, VIDAA TVs recognize content from all inputs, including HDMI ports and internally installed streaming apps.
Furthermore, privacy settings that supposedly limit or disable personalized tracking are split across two menus with five checkboxes in all. The most important appears to be "Agree to Enhanced Viewing Service," located under System > Support > Disclaimer and Privacy > Data Sharing, Privacy and EULA. However, other checkboxes also mention data sharing and advertising, so privacy-minded users should leave them unchecked as well.
Disabling these features doesn't stop ACR from identifying content. It only prevents the TV from transmitting data to Nexxen. This is likely also true if users disconnect the TV from the internet.
In September, the same behavior was discovered in LG TVs. Working with security researchers, Gamers Nexus discovered that the company's OLED TVs tracked content, scanned Wi-Fi networks without owners' consent, and recorded conversations. They also uncovered multiple severe security gaps that could allow hackers to execute remote code and steal data.
Texas sued five smart TV makers, including LG and Hisense, last year for ACR recording, and Vizio paid a $2.2 million settlement for the practice in 2017. However, research from earlier this month revealed that Vizio TVs, more than any other, ignore opt-out requests and transmit the same amount of data regardless of whether users consent to personalized ads.
Disconnecting smart TVs from the internet and using external streaming devices is likely the best way to avoid tracking. While some streaming boxes also engage in ACR, the Apple TV doesn't.

articles.title: Engineering Reliable Telematics from Smartphone Sensors
articles.text:
Key Takeaways
- Smartphone GPS, motion sensors, and vehicle interfaces can each report valid measurements that produce incorrect results when combined without accounting for timing and coordinate frames.
- Preserve raw observations and their provenance before synchronizing, transforming, or normalizing them.
- Introduce a quality gate that determines whether telemetry is suitable for a particular decision instead of forcing every observation into a definitive result.
- Design for real-world conditions, including delayed GPS updates, phone movement, background interruptions, and intermittent connectivity.
- Monitor data quality alongside conventional application and infrastructure metrics because a functioning pipeline can still produce unreliable driving events.
Why this matters: the phone is not the vehicle
A smartphone can provide a surprising amount of information about a journey, including GPS estimates location and speed, accelerometers measure motion along the device's axes, gyroscopes capture rotation, and others. A connected vehicle may expose additional signals, such as speed, engine state, or diagnostic information.
Combining these sources creates opportunities for fleet monitoring, usage-based insurance, driving-behavior analysis, trip reconstruction, and connected mobility services.
However, having more sensors does not automatically produce better telemetry.
In fact, a GPS update may arrive after a vehicle has already slowed down. A phone may rotate in its mount, changing how its accelerometer readings relate to the vehicle's movement. An application may pause collection when the operating system restricts background activity. A backend service may receive observations out of order after a device reconnects.
Each observation may look reasonable in isolation, but the problem appears when the system combines observations that do not describe the same moment, coordinate frame, or physical event.
I would approach this as an architectural problem before treating it as a sensor-processing problem. The goal is not to make every sensor perfect. It is to build a system that understands the limitations of its inputs and prevents unsuitable evidence from silently becoming a business decision.
This distinction matters because a misleading telemetry event can have consequences beyond an inaccurate chart. It may influence a driver's score, trigger a fleet alert, affect an insurance calculation, or lead an operations team to investigate an event that never happened as represented.
Who should read this, and what will they gain?
For architects, the challenge is deciding where sensor collection, normalization, quality evaluation, and event detection belong and what contracts connect those stages.
For mobile engineers, the concern is preserving useful observations despite changing device orientation, sampling gaps, intermittent connectivity, and operating-system lifecycle behavior.
For streaming and data engineers, the problem includes delayed events, out-of-order delivery, duplicate observations, and reconciling streams that operate at different sampling rates.
For product and operations teams, the question is how to distinguish a confident event from one that needs further evidence or should not be reported at all.
The practical outcome is a design approach that makes data limitations visible, keeps event logic separate from data-quality decisions, and provides evidence that can be inspected when a result is challenged.
How this architecture took shape
I arrived at this architecture by tracing the journey of a telemetry observation from the moment it is captured to the point at which an application uses it to make a decision. Rather than starting with a sensor-fusion algorithm, I considered what could go wrong at each step. A speed measurement could be delayed, two observations could represent different moments, a phone's orientation could change, or an operating system interruption could leave gaps in the collected data. Each problem affects a different part of the processing flow, but all can ultimately influence the same business decision.
This led me to identify the responsibilities that a reliable pipeline needs to address independently: preserving the original measurements, establishing their temporal relationship, interpreting them in a consistent reference frame, evaluating their quality, detecting events, and retaining the evidence behind the resulting decisions. These responsibilities form the six logical stages described below. The intent is not to prescribe a particular deployment topology, but to establish clear architectural boundaries so that uncertainty introduced at one stage does not silently propagate into the next.
Start with the architecture, not the algorithm
I prefer to separate raw measurement collection from interpretation. Requirements such as detecting harsh braking, classifying trips, or calculating a driving score should not dictate how raw observations are represented.
A practical architecture has six logical stages, as the following image shows. They do not need to be six separately deployed services, as several can run within the same mobile application. The separation into six stages matters because each stage has a distinct responsibility, failure modes, and validation requirements. In the next sections, we are going to review all these stages in detail.
Figure 1. A quality-aware mobile telematics pipeline (Source: created by the author)
1. Collect and preserve raw observations
Start by retaining the original observation before applying transformations.
A record should carry the value and its unit, source or sensor type, measurement timestamp, available arrival timestamp, and relevant metadata. Depending on the source, that metadata might include accuracy estimates, sensor sampling information, device identifiers, or the vehicle association.
Why preserve the original? Because a later transformation may be incorrect, an assumption may change, or an event may be disputed. If the system retains only its normalized output, engineers may be unable to determine whether the original observation was poor or the transformation introduced the error.
For example, suppose an application converts a GPS speed reading into a standardized unit and later combines it with vehicle speed. If an event looks implausible, the engineering team should be able to inspect the original value, its timestamp, and the conversion applied to it.
Preservation does not mean keeping every field forever, since retention, privacy, security, and storage policies still apply. It means defining which evidence is needed for diagnosis and traceability before transformations discard it.
2. Establish temporal alignment
Sensor streams do not necessarily report at the same frequency or on the same schedule. A vehicle interface may produce frequent speed updates while GPS observations arrive less often. Mobile and backend components may also introduce different buffering and delivery delays.
The first distinction I make is between measurement time and arrival time.
Measurement time describes when the observation was captured, according to its source clock. Arrival time describes when a component received it. Arrival time is useful for understanding latency, but it is not a safe substitute for measurement time when reconstructing physical events.
A stream processor that compares the latest values received from two sources can accidentally compare different moments. This becomes especially problematic during rapid acceleration, braking, or turning, when the underlying state changes quickly.
The architecture should therefore define an alignment policy. It needs to specify how observations are matched, how much temporal separation is acceptable for each use case, and what happens when the system cannot find a suitable match.
Interpolation may be appropriate for some continuous signals, but it should not be applied indiscriminately. It can create a plausible-looking value where the evidence is sparse, and it may obscure a sharp change. The system should retain whether a value was directly measured, interpolated, or otherwise estimated.
When alignment cannot be established within the required tolerance, the right result may be lower confidence or no event at all.
3. Normalize coordinate frames and measurement semantics
A measurement's value is only part of its meaning. Its unit, coordinate frame, source, and interpretation matter just as much.
A phone's accelerometer reports motion in device coordinates. Those axes are attached to the phone, not inherently to the vehicle. If the phone rotates in a mount, the relationship between the phone's axes and the vehicle's forward, lateral, and vertical directions changes.
A system that assumes the phone is always mounted in the same orientation can interpret device movement as vehicle movement. That can distort acceleration, braking, and turning estimates.
Normalization should make these assumptions explicit. It may include unit conversion, coordinate transformation, sensor calibration, and checks on the validity of orientation estimates. A transformed observation should retain enough information to identify the transformation and its assumptions.
The system must also distinguish coordinate normalization from measurement quality. A transformation can be mathematically correct but based on an uncertain orientation estimate. The result may therefore remain unsuitable for a particular event calculation.
4. Evaluate data quality before accepting a measurement
At this stage, the system asks a different question: not simply whether a value exists, but whether it is fit for the intended use.
Useful checks include freshness, timestamp alignment, missing samples, source consistency, measurement uncertainty, and the reliability of any required coordinate transformation.
These checks should not be buried inside individual event rules. A shared quality stage gives different event detectors a consistent view of the evidence and makes quality decisions easier to monitor and test.
I would use three broad outcomes:
- Accept: The observation meets the requirements for the intended calculation.
- Degrade: The observation remains useful, but the system should limit its use or communicate reduced confidence.
- Abstain: The available evidence does not support a decision that is reliable enough for the intended use.
These are not universal labels with fixed thresholds. A GPS observation might be adequate for a coarse trip map but unsuitable for calculating a short, sharp braking event. Quality must be evaluated in context.
5. Detect events using qualified evidence
Event detection should consume measurements that have already passed through the relevant quality checks.
This does not mean every event requires every sensor. A trip-start detector and a harsh-braking detector have different evidence requirements. The architecture should allow each detector to declare what it needs and how it handles missing or uncertain inputs.
Consider a braking detector that combines vehicle speed and GPS speed. If the two values refer to different moments, the detector may infer a rate of deceleration that is not supported by the underlying movement. A quality-aware design prevents the detector from treating a poor match as equivalent to aligned observations.
The detector should also distinguish the event's classification from the quality of its evidence. An event may be a candidate for further review rather than a definitive result. Keeping these concepts separate makes the system easier to tune without changing the meaning of quality checks throughout the pipeline.
6. Produce a decision with supporting evidence
The final stage produces more than an event label.
A useful event record can include the event type, event time or interval, relevant vehicle or trip association, quality status, supporting observations, and the processing-rule version. Where a confidence estimate is used, its meaning and limitations should be documented rather than treating it as a universal probability of correctness.
This information makes a decision inspectable. An engineer can trace an event to the observations that supported it, see whether any measurements were downgraded, and understand which processing logic was applied.
It also helps separate two questions that are often conflated: "What did the system decide?" and "What evidence justified that decision?"
These six stages form one continuous data path. Raw preservation protects the evidence; temporal alignment and normalization make observations comparable; the quality gate determines their suitability; event detection applies the domain logic; and the final record explains the result.
How the six stages work together
The value of this architecture comes from the boundaries between stages.
- If the phone and vehicle speed measurements disagree, temporal alignment checks whether they describe comparable moments.
- If a phone rotates, normalization identifies that the relationship between device axes and vehicle axes has changed.
- If the available evidence remains insufficient, the quality gate prevents the uncertainty from disappearing.
- The event detector uses only evidence that meets the requirements for its task.
- The final output retains enough provenance and quality information to support investigation and improvement.
This is deliberately more than a sensor-fusion algorithm. It is a contract for how imperfect physical observations become software decisions.
The principle is straightforward: preserve what was measured, establish what it means, evaluate whether it is fit for use, and only then act on it.
Real-world example 1: The phantom braking event
Imagine a fleet operator whose mobile application scores driving behavior. Drivers receive alerts for harsh braking, and fleet managers use the events to identify potentially risky patterns.
One morning, a driver approaches a traffic light and brakes normally. The smartphone collects GPS-derived speed while the vehicle interface reports speed independently. The backend later records a harsh-braking event.
The driver disputes the alert. The vehicle did slow down, but not as abruptly as the application claims.
The engineering team examines the processing flow and discovers that the phone and vehicle streams were paired by arrival order. GPS updates were less frequent, and one observation represented an earlier point in the journey. During deceleration, the system compared that older speed estimate with a more recent vehicle measurement.
The discrepancy looked like physical behavior. Part of it was actually a timing problem.
The pipeline had accepted both values because they were syntactically valid. It had no mechanism to establish whether they were temporally comparable.
Figure 2. How a timing mismatch can create a misleading event (Source: created by the author)
What changes?
The team introduces a temporal-alignment stage before event detection. Each observation retains its measurement timestamp, while arrival time is tracked separately. The pipeline evaluates the freshness of each observation and avoids comparing streams when timing uncertainty exceeds the application's defined tolerance.
The detector also stops treating every speed discrepancy as equivalent. When the measurements are not sufficiently aligned, it lowers confidence or abstains from generating a definitive event.
The team adds monitoring for timestamp offsets, stale observations, alignment failures, and event reclassification. These metrics help distinguish a change in driving behavior from a change in data quality.
This approach does not guarantee that every braking event will be classified correctly. It gives engineers a way to identify a measurement-comparison problem before treating it as driver behavior.
The same pattern applies to fleet diagnostics, trip reconstruction, usage-based insurance, and connected-vehicle analytics.
The lesson: before interpreting disagreement between sensors as physical behavior, establish whether the measurements are temporally comparable.
Coordinate frames: accurate measurements can still mean the wrong thing
Time alignment does not solve the second major problem: orientation.
An accelerometer measures along the device's axes. A vehicle-relative interpretation assumes that the system knows how those axes relate to the vehicle. If the phone rotates, that relationship changes.
The gyroscope can help estimate rotation, and sensor-fusion algorithms can estimate orientation. Neither eliminates uncertainty automatically. Estimates may drift, the initial orientation may be unknown, and the phone can move independently of the vehicle.
A field named longitudinalAcceleration can therefore be misleading if it was calculated from device-relative measurements while the phone's orientation was uncertain.
The architecture should distinguish raw device-frame measurements from transformed estimates and preserve the assumptions behind each transformation.
Real-world example 2: The phone moves, but the vehicle does not turn
Consider a mobile telematics application that detects cornering and sudden lateral movement using the phone's accelerometer and gyroscope.
A driver starts a journey with the phone secured in a horizontal dashboard mount. The application estimates orientation and interprets motion relative to the vehicle. Later, the mount loosens on a rough road, and the phone rotates. The driver continues straight.
The application detects apparent lateral movement and records an aggressive-turning event.
The sensor values changed, but the physical interpretation was wrong. The device's orientation changed, so the relationship between its axes and the vehicle's direction of travel was no longer the same.
This problem is easy to miss when testing only with a phone mounted in a fixed position. The algorithm may perform well in a controlled setup and fail when users reposition the phone, adjust the mount, or carry it during a trip.
Figure 3. The device frame is not automatically the vehicle frame (Source: created by the author)
What changes?
The team makes orientation confidence an explicit input to event detection. Raw accelerometer and gyroscope observations are preserved, while transformed measurements carry metadata describing the estimated reference frame and the confidence in that transformation.
The detector no longer assumes that one phone orientation remains valid for the entire journey. It monitors orientation changes and identifies periods when the relationship between the device and vehicle is uncertain.
When orientation is reliable, the application can use transformed measurements according to its validated detection policy. When confidence falls, it can rely on other trustworthy evidence, reduce the confidence of the event, or abstain from making a definitive classification.
The team tests deliberate phone rotations, loose mounts, different mounting positions, and periods when orientation cannot be estimated reliably. It measures false positives and false negatives against a defined reference rather than assuming that a more sophisticated algorithm automatically improves accuracy.
This also improves the user experience. Instead of penalizing a driver for an uncertain observation, the application can indicate that it could not classify the event reliably.
The lesson: sensor accuracy and interpretation accuracy are different things. A sensor can report its measurement correctly while the application assigns that measurement the wrong physical meaning.
The same principle applies to phone-based activity recognition, wearable devices, robotics, and industrial IoT.
The quality gate: a contract between sensors and business logic
The quality gate is the fourth stage in the architecture, but its responsibility extends beyond checking whether sensor values look reasonable. It determines whether the available measurements are reliable enough for the specific decision an application intends to make.
The preceding stages preserve observations, establish temporal relationships, and normalize their measurement semantics. However, even after these steps, the resulting measurements may still contain uncertainty, missing samples, or inconsistencies. Without an explicit quality evaluation, individual event detectors must handle these conditions independently, often using different assumptions and fallback rules. This can lead to inconsistent decisions across the application.
I consider the quality gate a contract between the telemetry pipeline and the business logic that consumes its output. It makes the limitations of the available evidence explicit and defines what downstream components are permitted to do with it.
This section explores three aspects of that contract: why measurement quality must be evaluated in the context of the intended decision, how the system should distinguish between accepting, degrading, and abstaining from a result, and why abstention should be treated as a legitimate outcome rather than a processing failure.
Quality depends on the decision
Suppose a fleet application supports two functions: displaying the approximate route of a trip and identifying a short, aggressive braking maneuver.
The route display may tolerate a less frequent location update. The braking detector needs evidence that is sufficiently aligned in time and suitable for estimating a rapid change in speed.
Using the same universal threshold for both functions can be unnecessarily restrictive for one and dangerously permissive for the other.
Instead, each consumer should declare its requirements. The quality gate evaluates the observation against those requirements and communicates the outcome.
This approach also makes product trade-offs explicit. If a team wants more events at the expense of accepting weaker evidence, that decision becomes a documented policy choice that can be evaluated—not an accidental consequence of a permissive fallback in a detector.
Abstention is a valid result
Engineering teams often focus on maximizing the number of events detected. But a system that always returns an answer can create a false sense of certainty.
Abstention is useful when the evidence does not support the intended decision. It should not be treated as an exception that disappears into a log file.
The system should record why it abstained, whether additional data could resolve the uncertainty, and whether the decision needs to be revisited. For some use cases, waiting briefly for a delayed observation is reasonable. For others, the system may need to return an explicit "insufficient evidence" outcome.
This is especially important when events influence human decisions, scores, or downstream automation. A clearly identified lack of evidence is often more useful than a precise-looking result that cannot be defended.
Make data quality observable
A quality-aware architecture is only as good as the team's ability to see it working. If the system records only the number of events generated, it becomes difficult to distinguish a genuine change in driving behavior from a change in sensor availability, application lifecycle, or processing logic.
I would monitor the quality pipeline alongside the business outcomes.
Useful operational signals include:
- Freshness: How old are observations when a consumer uses them?
- Temporal alignment: How far apart are measurements paired for the same calculation?
- Sampling gaps: How often do expected observations go missing, and how long do gaps last?
- Quality outcomes: What proportion of observations are accepted, degraded, or rejected, and for what reasons?
- Orientation confidence: How often does an orientation-dependent calculation lack a sufficiently reliable transformation?
- Event stability: How often are candidate events revised or reclassified after delayed observations arrive?
- Processing latency: How long does it take from measurement to event decision, separately from the measurement's age?
- Provenance completeness: Can an event be traced to its supporting observations and processing-rule version?
These measurements should be segmented where useful by device type, operating-system version, sensor source, application version, and collection conditions. Otherwise, a system-wide average may conceal a failure affecting a particular group of devices.
I would also connect quality metrics to event outcomes. If the number of harsh-braking events suddenly rises, the team should be able to investigate whether driving behavior changed, timestamp skew increased, or a new application version altered sampling behavior.
This requires a distinction between technical metrics and business metrics. Event counts and driver scores tell us what the application concluded. Freshness, alignment, and rejection metrics help explain whether the evidence behind those conclusions changed.
Observability should support investigation, not just dashboards. Logs and event records need enough structured context to reconstruct a decision while respecting data-retention and privacy requirements.
Account for the mobile operating system
A smartphone sensor pipeline does not run in a perfectly controlled environment. Applications can move into the background, devices can enter power-saving modes, connectivity can disappear, and operating systems can constrain background execution.
The architecture should not assume that a requested sampling rate guarantees a continuous stream.
On the device, collection code should handle sensor unavailability, sampling gaps, lifecycle transitions, and local buffering. When connectivity returns, queued observations may arrive in a burst or out of order. The backend should therefore apply its temporal-alignment and duplicate-handling policies even when the data originated from a single phone.
The system should preserve the distinction between the time an observation was measured and the time it was uploaded. It should also make gaps visible rather than filling them silently with fabricated continuity.
Offline operation introduces another design decision: how much data to buffer and for how long. That depends on the product's latency, privacy, storage, and battery constraints. Not every observation needs to be retained indefinitely, but the policy should be deliberate.
These concerns are not separate from sensor reliability. They determine whether the system has enough timely evidence to make a defensible decision.
Where to start: a practical implementation plan
I would not attempt to perfect every sensor or event detector at once. I would start with one high-impact event and establish a reliable path through the architecture.
- Preserve the evidence. Confirm that raw values, units, source identifiers, measurement timestamps, arrival timestamps, and relevant metadata are captured before transformation.
- Define the temporal contract. Document how observations are aligned, how stale data is handled, and what happens when a required measurement is missing or late.
- Make coordinate assumptions explicit. Identify which calculations depend on phone orientation, how transformations are established, and how uncertainty affects downstream use.
- Introduce a quality contract. Define accept, degrade, and abstain outcomes for one event type. Record reason codes so that quality failures can be distinguished from event-rule failures.
- Validate failure scenarios. Test delayed, missing, duplicated, out-of-order, and contradictory observations. Test phone rotations and changes in sensor availability, not only normal journeys.
- Instrument the pipeline. Track timestamp skew, data freshness, sampling gaps, quality outcomes, event revisions, and end-to-end latency.
- Expand incrementally. Once the chosen event has a defensible processing path, apply the same architectural contracts to other event types, adapting the quality requirements to each use case.
The goal is not to add complexity for its own sake. It is to discover where the system's assumptions are hidden and make them explicit before those assumptions affect a business decision.
What this architecture does not solve
A quality-aware architecture makes sensor limitations and processing uncertainty explicit, but it does not eliminate them. Architects and developers should consider several limitations when applying this model.
It cannot recover missing evidence
The architecture can identify missing samples, stale observations, and unreliable measurements, but it cannot reconstruct physical events when evidence was never captured. Interpolation and estimation may help, but introduce assumptions and should not be treated as direct measurements. When evidence is insufficient, the system should communicate that limitation rather than manufacture continuity.
It does not replace algorithm validation
The six stages define architectural responsibilities, not specific sensor-fusion, calibration, or event-detection algorithms. Developers must validate these techniques against appropriate reference measurements and real-world conditions. A well-structured pipeline cannot compensate for an inaccurate orientation estimate or an incorrectly designed detection algorithm.
Quality thresholds are not universal
Freshness, timestamp tolerance, measurement uncertainty, and orientation confidence must be evaluated against the intended decision. Requirements for displaying a trip route differ from those for detecting harsh braking. Thresholds should be validated for each use case, and confidence scores should not be treated as universal probabilities of correctness.
Operational trade-offs remain
Background execution restrictions, battery consumption, connectivity, device diversity, and privacy influence what can be collected and processed. Teams must balance these constraints with evidence requirements and processing latency. They must also define how uncertain outcomes and abstentions are communicated and when additional data or manual review is appropriate.
Ultimately, this architecture is a framework for managing uncertainty, not a guarantee of perfect telemetry. Its effectiveness depends on sensor quality, validated algorithms, appropriate quality requirements, and continuous testing under real-world conditions.
Conclusion: reliability belongs to the pipeline
Smartphones make telematics more accessible by combining location, motion sensors, computing power, and connectivity in a single device. But the convenience comes with a trade-off: device placement varies, sampling behavior is managed by the mobile platform, and measurements have different timing and coordinate semantics.
The architectural response is to separate observation from interpretation. Preserve what the phone measured. Establish when and in what frame it was measured. Evaluate whether the evidence is suitable for the decision. Only then should business logic act on the result.
The phantom braking scenario shows why measurements from different sources must be temporally comparable. The rotated-phone scenario shows why device orientation must be treated as a variable rather than an assumption. Both demonstrate why a technically healthy pipeline can still produce an unreliable conclusion.
The distinction is simple: collecting telemetry produces data. Engineering reliable telemetry produces evidence that downstream systems can evaluate, qualify, and use responsibly.

articles.title: IA recria voz de comentarista morto em 2023
articles.text:
IA recria voz de comentarista morto em 2023
Novidade faz parte do EA Sports FC 27. EA teve autorização da família de John Motson.
O EA Sports FC 27 terá um comentarista já falecido pela primeira vez a partir desta quinta-feira (26/11). John Motson era uma das principais vozes da BBC Sports e fez parte do FIFA 96 ao FIFA 2005. Sua voz será recriada pela EA utilizando inteligência artificial, com aprovação da família dele.
Motson faleceu em 2023, aos 77 anos, pouco depois da chegada das IAs generativas. Os comentários serão realizados utilizando gravações antigas e conteúdo gerado com a tecnologia. Seu filho, Fred Motson, afirmou à BBC que a novidade significa muito para ele, já que cresceu jogando o game e mostrando ao pai o resultado do seu trabalho. A viúva de Motson também concedeu a autorização.
Segundo o diretor sênior de game design do EA FC, Mat Prior, isso só foi possível por conta da aprovação da família. A ideia teria partido da própria empresa, numa espécie de homenagem a uma das primeiras vozes do simulador de futebol.
Apesar de ser uma homenagem um tanto controversa, a inclusão da voz de Motson no game foi elogiada por Guy Mowbray, atual comentarista do game. Ele enxerga o movimento como um uso “legal” e “não-assustador” da IA. De acordo com Guy, é interessante que seu “legado” possa continuar dessa maneira.
Outro nome conhecido da franquia, Derek Rae também viu com bons olhos a homenagem, e destacou as facilidades que o uso de IA poderia trazer ao trabalho de gravação. Uma possibilidade apontada pelo narrador envolve a geração de nomes mais simples, como “Smith” e “Jones, por exemplo, o que salvaria bastante tempo de trabalho.
Para o filho de Motson, o pai teria adorado a ideia de fazer parte do game mesmo após sua morte, mesmo tendo pouca afinidade com tecnologia em geral. Segundo ele, apesar de não entender o que a IA estaria fazendo ali, Motson “sempre gostou de se envolver em projetos do tipo”.
Além dos envolvidos no jogo, outro personagem comentou a novidade. O fundador do movimento Save Our Voices Now, que milita contra a prática, não vê com bons olhos o uso da voz de Motson sem a possibilidade de consentimento. Ele afirma que a aprovação da família não deveria ser suficiente, e a clonagem seria correta apenas se uma pessoa já falecida houvesse concordado com esse tipo de uso antes de morrer.
De fato, é uma homenagem que chama atenção, e lembra o comercial da Volkswagen feito em 2023 que trazia uma recriação da cantora Elis Regina utilizando deepfake. Também houve consentimento da família e a própria filha Maria Rita “contracenou” com a mãe na propaganda. Na época, o Conar, Conselho Nacional de Autorregulamentação Publicitária, chegou a abrir um processo ético contra a montadora, mas acabou arquivando o caso.

articles.title: Feds still regularly meeting with Starlink despite calls for digital sovereignty: report
articles.text:
Government officials are still holding frequent meetings with SpaceX’s Starlink even as they’re publicly touting the need for Canada to have digital sovereignty, according to journalist Peter Nowak.
On his Do Not Pass Go Substack, Nowak reported that lobbyists from the Texas-based satellite internet company have met with Canadian government officials at least 56 times this year. In one of these meetings, Starlink representatives gave Innovation, Science and Economic Development (ISED) a 10-page report on the potential impact of its tech in Janet, Alta. and Saint Laurent, Que. ISED then granted SpaceX temporary use of some of its E-band frequencies in the two areas.
Nowak noted that Rogers supported the agreement due to its ongoing business with Starlink to power its own satellite service. However, New Brunswick-based satellite company Xplore opposed the request by arguing that international technical rules related to E-band service haven’t yet been established. The Canadian Association of Wireless Internet Service Providers has also called for greater transparency and spectrum sharing.
Nowak added that he obtained the impact report from the April meeting through an access-to-information request, but it was entirely redacted. He said neither ISED nor Starlink have provided an unredacted version, so it’s unclear exactly what these agreements entail.
All of this comes as the Canadian government has talked about the need to invest in Canadian tech platforms to pursue digital sovereignty.
While some Canadian companies like Terrestar and Telesat are working on their own satellite options, they’re naturally not on the level of Starlink. Looking ahead, Prime Minister Mark Carney said in September that there’s “no question” that Canada will diversify from Starlink. The statement came after SpaceX owner Elon Musk admitted that he throttled Starlink service in Ukraine amid its war with Russia.
Last month, the Investigative Journalism Foundation (IJF) also examined just how many provinces rely on Starlink, especially in rural areas. While Ontario ended its $100 million deal with Starlink last year amid the wider trade war with the U.S., jurisdictions in pretty much every province and territory were found to have deals of varying sizes with Starlink. It was a stark reminder of the challenges Canada will face when diversifying from the U.S. technology that has become ingrained in many parts of the country.
And of course, those are just existing deals which would carry big — and potentially unseen — costs to break, as we saw with Ontario and Starlink. Nowak’s latest reporting on Starlink’s lobbying efforts shows that Canada is continuing to meet with the company, which certainly runs counter to the idea of diversification.
At the end of his report, Nowak notes that he asked ISED why officials keep meeting with Starlink amid calls for Canadian-owned tech infrastructure. In response, ISED argued that such engagement doesn’t constitute endorsement and that it has a responsibility to meet with a wider range of companies.
“Decisions related to spectrum use and licensing are made in accordance with Canadian laws, policies and technical requirements, and in the interests of Canadians,” the representative said.
Image credit: SpaceX
Source: Do Not Pass Go

articles.title: Black Friday Australia laptop deals for 2026: score up to 52% off Lenovo, Apple, Dell, HP and more
articles.text:
Black Friday Australia laptop deals for 2026: score up to 52% off Lenovo, Apple, Dell, HP and more
I'm tracking the best Australian discounts and you can save a bundle on a new notebook for home, work or gaming
Black Friday is here! The sale fell on 27 November this year, and runs through to Cyber Monday on November 30, and Australian retailers are offering excellent discounts on a huge range of laptops.
You can get a Lenovo machine with 16GB of RAM for under AU$900, and there are also deals on lightweight 2-in-1s through to high-end gaming laptops.
Apple deals are also better than usual, with some great prices on refurbished MacBook Neos, or new models from Amazon.
As TechRadar Australia's resident laptop expert, I'm here to help. I've been keeping tabs on price changes across the entire year, so I can confidently tell you what's an actual good buy and filter out all the bad deals. I've been hunting Black Friday deals since the start of the month, as many device-makers started their sales early, and will be here till at least December 3.
If you’re still deciding what to buy, our guides to the best laptops in Australia and the best gaming laptops explain what to look for. It’s also worth checking our HP coupon codes and Lenovo coupon codes if you’re buying direct.
Top retailers for Black Friday laptop deals
- Lenovo: great deals on a wide range of everyday and gaming laptops
- Amazon: sparse but solid laptop deals
- JB Hi-Fi: big discounts on Apple laptops
- HP: take an extra 5% off with code FUTURE5
- Mwave: deals on major PC brands
- The Good Guys: great for MacBooks and Microsoft deals
- Apple: much loved laptops but few discounts when buying direct
After something else entirely? Check out our full coverage of Black Friday deals and get your Christmas shopping done before the rush.
Everyday laptop deals
The CM14 is an affordable Chromebook with a pretty good for the price 14-inch, 1920 x 1080 display. The Kompanio 540 CPU and 4GB of RAM are fine for light browsing and streaming, and the 64GB of storage is enough if you mostly use web apps and keep your files online.
The Aspire Lite is a budget Windows laptop with a 14-inch, 1920 x 1200 anti-glare screen and a weight of just 1.3kg. The Ryzen 3 and 8GB of RAM are fine for browsing and streaming, and the 256GB SSD is reasonable for the price.
The Core Ultra 5 322 and 16GB of RAM make this a well-equipped everyday laptop for the money. Its roomy 15.3-inch, 1920 x 1200 IPS display is rated at 400 nits, brighter than many screens on machines in this price range.
The IdeaPad Slim 3x gives you a roomy 15.3-inch, 1920 x 1200 IPS display and 16GB of RAM at an affordable price. Its eight-core Snapdragon X is well suited to everyday multitasking, though it’s worth checking that any specialist apps or peripherals you rely on support Windows on Arm.
The Dell 15 is well equipped for the money, with a 10-core Intel Core i5-1334U and 16GB of RAM to handle everyday tasks and multitasking. Its 15.6-inch display pairs a 1920 x 1080 resolution with a 120Hz refresh rate for a smooth experience.
The OmniBook 5’s 14-inch, 1920 x 1200 OLED display covers the full DCI-P3 colour gamut, so it’s a good pick for editing photos as well as watching movies. At 1.33kg it’s easy to carry, and the Intel Core 5 320 and 16GB of RAM are well suited to everyday use. Use the code BF10 to get the full discount here.
The OmniBook 5 gives you a large 16-inch, 1920 x 1200 OLED display without spending premium laptop money. The Core Ultra 5 225U and 16GB of RAM are a good fit for everyday multitasking. Use BF10 at checkout for the full discount.
At just 1kg, the XPS 13 is an easy laptop to travel with, and its sharp 13.4-inch, 2560 x 1600 touchscreen has an above average 120Hz refresh rate. The Core 5 320 and 16GB of RAM are also a capable everyday combination for a laptop this compact.
MacBook deals
This Apple Certified Refurbished MacBook Neo is an affordable way into macOS and comes with a one-year Apple warranty. The A18 Pro and 8GB of memory suit everyday use, and the 13-inch, 2408 x 1506 display is sharp for a laptop in this price range. Buying refurbished gives a decent discount compared to buying it new for AU$1,049 from Apple.
This Apple Certified Refurbished Neo has a 512GB SSD for keeping photos and apps on the laptop, plus Touch ID for signing in and approving purchases. The A18 Pro and 8GB of memory make it a good everyday Mac, and Apple includes a one-year warranty. Buying refurbished gives a decent discount compared to buying it new for AU$1,249 from Apple.
This is the cheapest option going if you want the M5 Air and with the 512GB SSD. Want to know more? Check out our MacBook Air M5 review.
Apple has raised prices, and we have seen very few discounts so far, making this minor drop worth considering. This is the upgraded Air with the 1TB SSD and M5 CPU with a 10-core GPU (rather than the base spec 8-core) that costs AU$2549 from Apple. Want to know more? Check out our MacBook Air M5 review.
Also consider the 15-inch Air with 1TB SSD for AU$2,597 — now 12% off compared to buying from Apple.
The last-gen M5 16GB MacBook Pro currently has a small discount from Amazon compared to buying the newer M6 model for AU$3,199 from Apple. Read our Apple MacBook Pro M5 review for the full scoop.
Thin and light laptop deals
The Yoga Slim 7 weighs just 1.16kg, yet its 14-inch, 1920 x 1200 OLED display gives movies deep blacks and rich colours. The Core Ultra 5 226V and 16GB of RAM make it a capable everyday laptop for travel.
This Snapdragon-powered laptop has an impressive spec for the price, with an X Elite X1E78100 CPU, 32GB of RAM and a 1TB SSD. It also has a very nice 2944 x 1840 OLED touchscreen display that outputs 100% of the sRGB gamut. We have seen this machine slightly cheaper, but it's still a good deal if its Windows on Arm compatibility suits the apps you use.
The Zenbook 14 has a 1920 x 1200 OLED display, 32GB of RAM and a 1TB SSD into a compact 14-inch laptop. The Ryzen AI 7 445 is well suited to everyday multitasking, and the extra memory gives you headroom for heavier work on the go, such as editing a large photo library — though we which there was a higher resultion screen option.
2-in-1 laptop deals
The 14-inch OLED touchscreen folds back for tablet use, and the included pen is handy for handwritten notes or sketches. At 1.38kg it’s light enough to carry to class, and the Core Ultra 5 226V and 16GB of RAM give it the performance to be a capable everyday laptop.
This large-screen 2-in-1 from HP uses the Intel Series 2 Core Ultra 7 258V CPU, giving it a good mix of performance and battery life. The 16-inch laptop also has a 2880 x 1800 OLED touchscreen, 32GB of RAM, 1TB of storage, Wi-Fi 7, Thunderbolt 4 and a facial recognition webcam. We have seen it for slightly less, but this is still a pretty good price if you want a big premium 2-in-1. Use code BF10 at the checkout for the full discount.
Gaming laptop deals
The Victus is an entry-level gaming laptop with an RTX 4050 that’s well matched to its 15.6-inch, 1920 x 1080 display. The 144Hz refresh rate suits competitive games. Use BFDEAL at checkout to get the full discount.
The Cyborg 15 is an affordable option for 1080p gaming, with an RTX 5060 and a 15.6-inch, 144Hz display that suits fast-paced multiplayer games. The 16GB of RAM is a decent starting point, though be aware the GPU is limited to 55W so the 5060 will give slower frame rates than models with higher graphics power levels.
The Lenovo LOQ Essential 15 is an affordable way to get RTX 5060 graphics, with a 15.6-inch, 1920 x 1080 display that refreshes at 144Hz for smooth play in fast-paced games. The main trade-off is the GPU’s 65W power limit, so expect lower frame rates in demanding games than you’d get from a higher-powered RTX 5060 laptop.
The Legion 5i gives its RTX 5060 up to 115W, a good match for playing demanding games at the 15.3-inch screen’s native 1920 x 1200 resolution. The 1TB SSD is a welcome inclusion at this price, especially if you keep several big games installed.
The Gaming A16 is a relatively affordable way to get an RTX 5070 and a 16-inch IPS screen in the same laptop. The 165Hz refresh rate suits competitive games, while the 1TB SSD gives you room for a mix of multiplayer favourites and larger single-player titles.
Intel’s 24-core i9-14900HX and 32GB of RAM make this Legion a good fit for heavier workloads beyond gaming, including video editing and 3D rendering. Its RTX 5070 drives a 15.1-inch, 2560 x 1600 OLED display with a 165Hz refresh rate.
The RTX 5070 Ti and its 12GB of video memory are a good match for high-detail gaming on the W16’s 16-inch, 2560 x 1600 display. The 300Hz refresh rate is most useful in competitive games, while the single 16GB RAM stick is the main compromise for a gaming laptop in this class.
The Pro model of one of our favourite Lenovo laptops has a reasonable discount on the RTX 5070 Ti variant. The pre-discount web price is beyond steep, but at this sale price it's decent enough value for a premium gaming machine with an OLED, 2560 x 1600, 165Hz display.
The Legion Pro 7i pairs a 175W RTX 5080 with a 16-inch, 2560 x 1600 OLED display, giving demanding games plenty of graphics power and the deep blacks that make dark scenes stand out. The 240Hz refresh rate also makes good use of the higher frame rates you can reach in competitive games.
For those who want mighty gaming power, the Legion Pro 7i with an Intel Ultra 9 275HX processor and RTX 5090 GPU is one of the better options going, despite the painfully high cost compared to last year. There are very few comparable machines at this price, making it an excellent deal if you are willing to spend big. Read our review to learn more.
The MacBook Air I’d start with
If you want a MacBook for everyday use and some photo editing, the 13-inch M5 Air with 512GB of storage is the configuration I’d start with. The AU$1,797 pricegets you the M5 chip and 16GB of memory in a very compact laptop with excellent battery life.
The 1TB version is also worth considering if you like to keep a lot of data on your device, and it's currently reduced by 12% for Black Friday.
Want to know more? Our 13-inch M5 Air review has the full rundown.
- Apple MacBook Air 13-inch | M5 / 16GB / 512GB SSD: AU$1,797 at Amazon
A 1.16kg Yoga for the daily commute
The Lenovo Yoga Slim 7 weighs just 1.16kg, which is a good reason to consider it if you take your laptop on the road a lot. It also has a 14-inch, 1920 x 1200 OLED display, for those deep blacks that make a difference when you put a movie on at the end of the day.
The Good Guys has the Core Ultra 5 model with 16GB of RAM and a 512GB SSD for AU$1,299, which is a pretty good price.
- Lenovo Yoga Slim 7 14-inch OLED | Core Ultra 5 226V / 16GB RAM / 512GB SSD: AU$1,299 at The Good Guys
Which refurbished MacBook Neo would I buy?
Apple’s two refurbished Neos have the same A18 Pro chip and 8GB of memory. The AU$899 Indigo model makes sense if you mostly browse, stream and keep your files online. It saves AU$150 over buying the same 256GB model new from Apple.
The AU$1,059 Silver model doubles the storage to 512GB and adds Touch ID for signing in and approving purchases. That refurb saves AU$190 over Apple’s new price. Of the two upgrades, the extra space is the one I’d want, especially if I kept my photos on the laptop.
- Apple MacBook Neo 13-inch (Certified Refurbished, Indigo) | A18 Pro / 8GB RAM / 256GB SSD: AU$899 at Apple
- Apple MacBook Neo 13-inch (Certified Refurbished, Silver) | A18 Pro / 8GB RAM / 512GB SSD: AU$1,059 at Apple
How much more is the 512GB Neo?
Amazon’s deal on the 256GB MacBook Neo is AU$997 and the 512GB Neo is AU$1,197. Both have 8GB of memory and the same A18 Pro chip, so the extra AU$200 buys you twice the storage and Touch ID.
Check how much storage space you’re using on your current laptop. If it’s already close to 256GB and you’d rather keep your files locally, the larger drive is the upgrade that will matter most long term.
- Apple MacBook Neo 13-inch | A18 Pro / 8GB RAM / 256GB SSD: AU$997 at Amazon
- Apple MacBook Neo 13-inch | A18 Pro / 8GB RAM / 512GB SSD: AU$1,197 at Amazon
HP OmniBook names, explained
If you’re looking through HP’s OmniBook deals, pay attention to the word “Flip”. The OmniBook 5 14 is a conventional laptop with a 14-inch OLED display. The OmniBook 5 Flip 14 has a touchscreen and a hinge that folds all the way back for tablet use.
The number doesn’t tell you the screen size either the OmniBook 3 we have been impressed with this Black Friday is a 17.3-inch model. So always make sure to check the full name and model number when comparing deals.
A 15-inch Dell for everyday use
If you want a straightforward Windows laptop with a roomy screen, JB Hi-Fi is selling a Dell 15 that's well equipped for the AU$893 asking price. The 10-core Core i5 and 16GB of RAM can comfortably handle everyday multitasking, and the 512GB SSD gives you a decent amount of local storage.
The 15.6-inch, 1920 x 1080 screen is a little nicer than I’d expect at this price too. It refreshes at 120Hz, so even scrolling a long webpage looks smoother than it does on a standard 60Hz display.
- Dell 15 DC15250 | Core i5-1334U / 16GB RAM / 512GB SSD: AU$893 at JB Hi-Fi
Affordable RTX 5060 gaming
If you’re after a gaming laptop for under AU$1,600, the Lenovo LOQ Essential 15 puts its money in the right places for 1080p play. The RTX 5060 pairs nicely with the 15.6-inch, 144Hz screen, especially if you spend more time in multiplayer matches than chasing ultra high settings.
There’s one spec worth knowing before you buy. Lenovo gives the GPU 65W in this model, so a bigger laptop with the same RTX 5060 can deliver higher frame rates.
- Lenovo LOQ Essential 15 | Core i5-13450HX / RTX 5060 / 16GB RAM / 512GB SSD: AU$1,597 at The Good Guys

articles.title: Passe Navigo non validé : l’amende tombe à 15 €, mais pas pour tout le monde
articles.text:
Dans le métro parisien, payer son forfait ne suffit pas : il faut aussi passer son passe sur le valideur. Un abonné qui oublie risque 70 € d’amende, soit autant qu’un voyageur sans aucun titre, depuis que la RATP a doublé l’amende pour passe Navigo non validé en juin 2025.
Xavier Piechaczyk, PDG de la RATP, a annoncé au Parisien ce jeudi 26 novembre 2026 que ce montant tombera à 15 € le 1er janvier 2027, comme dans les bus et les tramways. D’après la régie, interrogée par ICI Paris Île-de-France, la baisse s’applique aussi sur les tronçons des RER A et B qu’elle exploite.
Pourquoi sanctionner un trajet déjà payé ?
Une sanction est conservée, Xavier Piechaczyk estimant qu’il « reste important de valider son titre ». Il assure quand même faire la différence entre « un abonné qui paie son forfait et n’a pas correctement validé » et « une personne qui voyage délibérément sans titre ». Un abonné mensuel ou annuel ne gagne en effet rien à ne pas valider, puisque son trajet est payé d’avance, et de plus en plus cher.
Le passe mensuel coûte 90,80 € en 2026, contre 70 € lors du passage au tarif unique en 2015. En 2027, Île-de-France Mobilités envisage de porter le passe Navigo à 93,40 €.
Navigo Liberté+ : l’amende pour non validation reste à 70 €
À l’inverse, le forfait Navigo Liberté+ facture chaque trajet à la fin du mois. Un passage non validé n’y est donc jamais payé, et l’amende reste à 70 €.
Pour les valideurs en panne, en revanche, rien ne semble prévu. Pourtant, des abonnés ont déjà reçu une amende alors que les appareils de leur station ne marchaient pas, ce qui a nourri une bonne partie de la polémique.
Sur le site de la RATP, la page des montants des amendes n’a pas encore été mise à jour, ce vendredi 27 novembre au matin.

articles.title: Sauvetage en vue pour Böttcher : ce fabricant de vélos vieux de 175 ans attire déjà six repreneurs
articles.text:
Böttcher Fahrräder a été fondé il y a 175 ans à Wesseln, près de Heide, dans le nord de l’Allemagne. C’est l’un des plus vieux fabricants de vélos du pays. L’entreprise assemble des vélos électriques mécaniques, et fait aussi du commerce de gros, surtout auprès de clients professionnels.
Böttcher a réalisé environ 18,1 millions d’euros de chiffre d’affaires en 2025. L’entreprise venait aussi de repositionner sa marque en 2026, avec des vélos configurables à la carte ou livrés tout équipés.
Votre production solaire dépasse votre consommation ? Stockez le surplus au lieu de le revendre à bas prix. Le SolarFlow 2400 AC+ se branche sur votre installation existante, 100 % plug-and-play, et s’amortit plus vite grâce au Black Friday.
Sauf que le fabricant a demandé l’ouverture d’une procédure d’insolvabilité début octobre 2026, sans expliquer ses difficultés. Depuis, une question reste se pose : quelqu’un va-t-il la racheter ? Vanja Alexander Kovacev, l’administrateur provisoire nommé par le tribunal de Meldorf, a donné un début de réponse mercredi 25 novembre au média spécialisé SAZBike : cinq candidats ont déjà déposé une offre indicative pour reprendre l’activité. Pour la centaine de salariés du site, c’est le premier signe concret qu’une reprise est possible.
L’administrateur, associé au cabinet d’avocats CMS, a trouvé ces cinq candidats en relançant les acheteurs potentiels, et une sixième offre est encore attendue. Une offre indicative montre un intérêt et donne un ordre de prix, sans engagement. Vanja Alexander Kovacev mène donc maintenant des négociations plus poussées avec chaque candidat. En attendant, les salaires sont couverts pendant trois mois par l’Insolvenzgeld, une indemnité publique que l’Allemagne verse aux salariés des entreprises en faillite.
Début décembre, l’heure des offres fermes
Les candidats doivent remettre une offre ferme, c’est-à-dire qui les engage vraiment, d’ici début décembre 2026. Ces offres diront si l’un des candidats va jusqu’au rachat, et donc si l’activité peut continuer. Vanja Alexander Kovacev se dit « prudemment optimiste ». Il espère trouver une solution de reprise avant Noël, pour qu’elle s’applique au 1er janvier 2027, tout en précisant que ce calendrier peut encore bouger selon la suite des négociations.
Ghost, Simplon : le vélo germanophone traverse une année noire
Böttcher n’est pas le seul industriel du vélo germanophone en difficulté cette année. Ghost, marque de VTT installée à Waldsassen, en Bavière, et filiale du groupe néerlandais Accell, lui-même en faillite, n’a trouvé aucun repreneur prêt à payer plus que ce que rapporterait la vente de son stock. Elle a donc annoncé l’arrêt de ses activités début novembre 2026. Quelques jours plus tard, Bike Tree a racheté la marque.
Cette société, qui appartient au groupe singapourien DuTech, venait de reprendre Winora et Haibike. Elle a toutefois acheté le nom et les droits de propriété intellectuelle, sans les 53 salariés. En Autriche, la société qui fabrique les vélos Simplon a demandé une nouvelle procédure de redressement le 2 septembre 2026, la deuxième en deux ans, avec 33,4 millions d’euros de dettes et 54 salariés concernés.
Chez Böttcher, la production et le commerce de gros continuent à Wesseln, et l’entreprise prend toujours des commandes. Les offres fermes attendues début décembre doivent permettre de trancher avant Noël ; l’administrateur n’a dévoilé pour l’instant ni l’identité des candidats ni le montant de leurs offres.

articles.title: Le Black Friday baisse le prix et monte le son : l’enceinte JBL Flip Essential 3 SE passe à 64,22 € chez Amazon
articles.text:
L’enceinte portable JBL Flip Essential 3 SE vous permet d’emporter de quoi écouter votre musique partout avec vous. Durant le Black Friday, Amazon la propose à 64,22 € au lieu de 129,99 €, ce qui représente 51 % de réduction.
Écouter de la musique depuis le haut-parleur d’un smartphone n’est pas toujours l’idéal pour en faire profiter votre entourage. Dans ce cas, vous doter d’une enceinte Bluetooth portable peut s’avérer utile. La JBL Flip Essential 3 SE est un modèle qui répond à ce besoin, et même à d’autres grâce à sa protection contre l’eau et la poussière. Elle est actuellement disponible pour 64,22 € chez Amazon dans le cadre des offres du Black Friday.
La JBL Flip Essential 3 SE est disponible à 64,22 € au lieu de 129,99 € chez Amazon à l’occasion du Black Friday.
Pourquoi choisir la JBL Flip Essential 3 SE ?
- Pour son format transportable : avec ses 18 cm de longueur et son poids de 550 g, elle se glisse facilement dans un sac.
- Pour sa résistance IP67 : sa protection contre l’eau et la poussière facilite son utilisation à l’extérieur, y compris sur la plage.
- Pour sa connexion Auracast : vous pouvez former une paire stéréo avec deux Flip Essential 3 SE, ou diffuser votre playlist sur plusieurs enceintes JBL compatibles.
Une enceinte compacte et paramétrable
L’enceinte Flip Essential 3 SE embarque un haut-parleur pour les graves et les médiums, un tweeter dédié aux aigus et deux radiateurs passifs. L’ensemble délivre une puissance totale de 30 W RMS en mono. En utilisant l’application JBL Portable, vous pouvez ajuster différents paramètres sonores, notamment le niveau des basses.
L’indice de résistance IP67 rend ce modèle adapté à une utilisation au bord de l’eau et même dans le sable d’une plage. Quant à l’autonomie de l’enceinte, elle monte jusqu’à 12 heures, et il faut compter environ trois heures pour une recharge complète avec un chargeur adapté.
Un format pratique pour une écoute de proximité
Pour mettre en place une ambiance sonore dans une garden party, autour de la piscine ou dans une pièce, cette enceinte JBL convient bien. Néanmoins, pour une grande fête, sa puissance risque de montrer ses limites très rapidement. L’utilisation d’Auracast peut améliorer la situation, mais cela implique de disposer de plusieurs enceintes compatibles.
✅ Les points forts
- Protection contre l’eau et la poussière IP67.
- Jusqu’à 12 heures d’autonomie annoncée.
- Connexion Auracast et réglages via JBL Portable.
❌ Les limites
- Câble de recharge et adaptateur secteur non fournis.
- Association multi-enceintes limitée aux modèles compatibles Auracast.
Disponible pour 64,22 € sur Amazon, cette JBL Flip Essential 3 SE peut vous permettre d’ambiancer vos soirées à la maison.
La JBL Flip Essential 3 SE est idéale si vous cherchez une enceinte facile à emporter partout avec vous pour écouter de la musique quand vous le désirez. Sa protection IP67 est un vrai atout pour sa durée de vie.
En revanche, si vous aimez écouter de la musique dans de grands espaces et que vous appréciez les basses puissantes, ce modèle pourrait s’avérer trop limité. Mieux vaut, dans ce cas, vous tourner vers un modèle plus imposant.
