articles.title: Nigeria’s Payaza acquires Ghana’s Seesail to bring commerce tools, finance to Africa's small businesses
articles.text:
Nigerian payments infrastructure company Payaza has acquired Seesail Technologies, the Ghana-founded commerce platform for small businesses.
Payaza offers payment collection, payout and merchant tools to businesses in Africa and international markets. It handles card, mobile money and bank payments in more than 40 currencies and operates in more than 27 countries.
Disrupt Africa reported recently Payaza had been authorised by the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) to provide payment gateway services, just weeks after getting regulatory approval in Zambia.
The deal to acquire Seesail will see the entire team join Shopaza, a Payaza product, and co-founder and CEO Victor Blavo becomes general manager for Africa.
“We watched Seesail from the inside through the payments they ran on Payaza. They built real traction with very little. We believe in the dream, and we are bringing the jet fuel so they can move as fast as they can,” said Seyi Ebenezer, CEO of Payaza.

articles.title: SaaS Sprawl Is Becoming a Project Delivery Problem: How Distributed Teams Keep Work Connected
articles.text:
For many organisations, adopting another cloud application no longer feels like a technology decision. A new communication platform solves one problem, a specialist tool improves another workflow, a shared drive handles documents, spreadsheets fill reporting gaps and a separate system tracks resources or budgets.
Each addition can be perfectly rational. The difficulty appears later, when the work itself has to move across all of them. A project manager may receive an important decision in chat, update a deadline in a task tool, confirm resource availability in a spreadsheet and then recreate the same situation in a management report. Nothing is necessarily missing, yet the overall picture becomes harder to trust.
This is the operational side of SaaS sprawl. The issue is not simply that a business pays for too many subscriptions. It is that project context becomes distributed across tools at the same time as the teams doing the work become distributed across locations. Hybrid and international teams are particularly exposed because informal coordination is already more difficult. When colleagues cannot resolve an ambiguity by turning to the person sitting next to them, every missing decision, outdated status or unclear handoff has more opportunity to become a delay.
More tools can create less visibility
Modern work encourages specialised software. Communication tools are designed for fast conversation, document platforms for collaboration, CRM systems for customer activity and finance systems for commercial control. Trying to replace every specialist application with one platform would rarely make sense. The problem begins when the organisation has no clear answer to a different question: where does the authoritative project context live? If the deadline exists in one place, the scope decision in another and the reason for a delay somewhere else, people spend increasing amounts of time reconstructing the state of work rather than progressing it.
That reconstruction has a cost. A task can be marked as complete while the approval required for the next stage remains buried in email. A project manager may believe a specialist is available because the schedule does not reflect work assigned elsewhere. Leadership may receive a green status even though the delivery team already knows that an important dependency is slipping. These are rarely dramatic failures of technology. They are small gaps between systems that accumulate until somebody has to reconcile them manually.
The more distributed the team, the less forgiving those gaps become. A clarification missed at 4pm in Sydney may not be answered by a colleague in Europe until the next working cycle. A file linked in the wrong channel can hold up somebody who has only a short overlap window with the rest of the team. What would have been ten minutes of friction in one office can become half a day of waiting.
Teams need a project layer above the app layer
The answer is not necessarily fewer applications. It is clearer separation between tools that help people perform specific activities and the environment used to manage the project as a whole. Communication can still happen in chat and files can remain in specialist repositories, but the project needs a dependable management layer where responsibilities, current dates, risks, milestones, budgets and important decisions remain connected.
This is where integrated project management software can reduce the cost of coordination. FlexiProject, for example, brings project schedules, tasks, risks, budgets, deliverables and reporting into the same management environment. The practical value is not that every piece of work has to happen inside one application. It is that managers and teams have a consistent place to understand what has been agreed, what is changing and what those changes mean for delivery.
That distinction matters. A shared system should not become another destination employees have to update simply because management wants an additional dashboard. If teams still need to maintain the same status in four different places, consolidation has failed. The useful model is one in which information is captured close to the work but the important project relationships remain visible together: who owns the activity, which milestone it supports, what it depends on, whether there is a risk attached to it and what happens if the date moves.
Schedules reveal where fragmentation becomes delay
SaaS fragmentation becomes particularly visible in the schedule because dates depend on information from several parts of the organisation. A project may have a list of tasks, yet the sequence can still fail if dependencies are not maintained consistently. Marketing is waiting for legal approval, development is waiting for design, implementation depends on procurement and the customer has moved an acceptance date. If those changes are recorded in different tools, the schedule can remain technically up to date while no longer representing how the work will actually flow.
Distributed teams need more than a calendar of deadlines. They need to see relationships between activities and understand the downstream effect of change. A good schedule shows which tasks can move independently and which ones cannot, where milestones sit, who is responsible for the next step and whether a delay has started to affect work elsewhere. This is one reason dedicated project schedule software becomes more useful as delivery complexity grows. Dependencies, milestones, baselines and changing dates can be maintained as part of one schedule rather than recreated manually every time information moves between applications.
The baseline is especially important in fragmented environments. When teams continually replace old dates with new ones, the project may always look current while gradually moving away from what was originally agreed. Keeping both the approved plan and the latest forecast makes that movement visible. A three-day change can then be assessed for what it actually means: whether it is isolated, whether another team is affected and whether the same cause is likely to reappear later in the project.
SaaS sprawl also hides resource conflicts
Fragmentation does not only affect information. It can hide demand on people. A product team may assign a specialist in one application while a transformation programme reserves the same person somewhere else. Both plans look viable until the work reaches the same week. Resource conflicts become even harder to detect when departments use different project tools or when utilisation is managed in a spreadsheet that is disconnected from current schedules.
This is one of the reasons adding people does not automatically solve delivery bottlenecks. TechGuide has recently highlighted the same wider problem in software development: coordination overhead, unclear ownership and dependency chains can consume much of the extra capacity that organisations expect to gain when teams expand. The same principle applies outside engineering. If shared specialists are already committed across several projects, adding another initiative creates competition for capacity even when each project manager believes the plan is achievable.
Better visibility changes the conversation. Instead of discovering a conflict when two teams simultaneously need the same person, managers can decide earlier whether one activity should move, whether another resource can be used or whether the new commitment should wait. This does not eliminate trade-offs. It makes them deliberate rather than accidental.
The problem grows from projects into portfolios
At a certain scale, connecting information within individual projects is no longer sufficient. A business may have good schedules and disciplined project managers yet still struggle because too many initiatives compete for the same people, budgets and leadership attention. One project can be healthy on its own while weakening another project that has greater strategic value. A new priority can enter the organisation without an explicit decision about which existing work will give up capacity.
This is where the question moves from project execution to portfolio management. PPM software provides a broader view across initiatives, making it easier to compare priorities, resources, progress, risks and investment decisions instead of evaluating every project separately. That portfolio perspective is particularly useful in organisations with several business units or distributed teams, where the same specialist capacity may be allocated through different management structures.
The important point is that portfolio visibility should lead to choices. A dashboard showing twenty active projects is not inherently valuable. Leadership needs to know which of those projects still supports current priorities, where capacity is constrained and what will be displaced if another initiative is accelerated. In this sense, SaaS sprawl can expose a deeper organisational problem: the company may have digitised individual workflows without creating an equally coherent way to decide how all of that work fits together.
Connected work does not mean one tool for everything
The realistic goal for a modern technology stack is not radical consolidation. Specialist systems will continue to exist because different functions genuinely need different capabilities. A distributed organisation may rely on dozens of cloud services and still operate efficiently if the boundaries between them are understood and the project context does not disappear as work moves from one environment to another.
That requires discipline as much as technology. Teams need clear ownership, defined handoffs and an agreed place for important project decisions. Schedules have to reflect actual dependencies rather than simply collect dates. Resource commitments need to be visible before they become conflicts, while leadership needs enough portfolio context to understand when a decision in one project affects priorities elsewhere. Integrations can reduce manual copying between systems, but they cannot decide which information matters or where accountability sits.
This is particularly relevant for hybrid and international teams. The modern employee may move between collaboration platforms, cloud applications, business systems and different locations during the same day – a working model TechGuide has recently described as increasingly geographically fluid and technologically interconnected. When the workplace no longer has one obvious physical centre, the project cannot depend on information travelling informally either.
The real risk of SaaS sprawl is therefore not the number of applications on an invoice. It is the number of gaps through which project context can disappear. Organisations do not need every activity to happen inside the same tool, but they do need schedules, responsibilities, risks and priorities to remain connected closely enough that work can move without managers repeatedly reconstructing the truth. For distributed teams, that connection is what turns a collection of useful applications into a workable delivery system.

articles.title: Samsung QS90H : 13 haut-parleurs pour une immersion sans caisson
articles.text:
Vous ressentez comme une envie de donner une nouvelle dimension au son de votre téléviseur, sans transformer votre salon en installation home cinéma ? Bonne nouvelle, Samsung profite du Black Friday pour proposer sa nouvelle barre de son QS90H à 599 € seulement au lieu de 849 €.
Afin de pallier la relative faiblesse audio de nos Smart TV modernes, une barre de son permet de retrouver davantage d’ampleur dans les films, les séries ou les jeux vidéo, sans avoir pour cela à multiplier les enceintes dans la pièce et dénaturer le salon.
Avec sa QS90H, Samsung entend pousser le concept un peu plus loin. Cette barre de son tout-en-un rassemble pas moins de 13 haut-parleurs dans un seul et même boîtier, et promet une expérience sonore immersive en 7.1.2. Et à l’occasion du Black Friday, elle profite d’une remise de 250 €, faisant dégringoler son prix de 849 à 599 €. L’offre est annoncée du 26 novembre 2026 au 5 janvier 2027.
Samsung QS90H : 13 haut-parleurs pour retrouver une véritable immersion sonore
La QS90H adopte une configuration de type 7.1.2, avec des haut-parleurs orientés vers l’avant, les côtés, mais aussi les coins et le plafond. Cette disposition permet de diffuser le son dans plusieurs directions, afin de mieux envelopper les spectateurs. Au total, Samsung intègre 13 haut-parleurs donc, dont quatre woofers chargés de restituer les basses.
L’intérêt de cette conception tout-en-un ? Inutile d’installer un quelconque caisson de basses séparé pour profiter d’un rendu plus ample, puisque malgré son absence, la QS90H parvient à descendre jusqu’à 35 Hz dans les basses fréquences. La barre concentre l’ensemble des composants dans un seul appareil, ce qui permet de conserver une installation très sobre, très discrète, directement sous le téléviseur.
La compatibilité Dolby Atmos vient compléter cette configuration, et les bandes-son compatibles peuvent ainsi profiter d’une spatialisation en trois dimensions, avec des effets qui semblent provenir de différentes directions, y compris du dessus.
Avec les téléviseurs Samsung compatibles uniquement, la barre prend même en charge le Dolby Atmos sans fil via Wi-Fi, pour profiter des contenus compatibles sans avoir à la relier au téléviseur avec un câble HDMI.
Une barre de son qui adapte automatiquement son installation
C’est l’une des particularités les plus intéressantes de cette nouvelle QS90H : son étonnant design convertible. Grâce à un capteur gyroscopique intégré, la barre détecte automatiquement sa position et adapte le fonctionnement de ses haut-parleurs.
En d’autres termes, que vous choisissiez de la poser sur un meuble TV ou de la fixer au mur, elle reconnaît son agencement et se charge alors d’ajuster automatiquement la diffusion sonore. Une fonctionnalité particulièrement bienvenue, l’emplacement d’une barre de son ayant une influence directe sur le rendu audio ressenti.
Samsung ajoute également plusieurs technologies destinées à améliorer l’écoute au quotidien. SpaceFit Sound Pro ajuste notamment le son en fonction de la pièce, tandis que l’amplificateur vocal AVA Pro aide à conserver des dialogues audibles, même lorsque l’environnement est bruyant.
De quoi profiter plus confortablement d’un film ou d’une série, sans avoir à jongler constamment avec le volume.
Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, AirPlay, Chromecast… Une barre de son bien connectée
La Samsung QS90H ne se limite pas à la seule restitution sonore du téléviseur. Elle peut également servir à diffuser de la musique directement depuis un smartphone ou une tablette, pour animer une soirée par exemple. Pour cela, Samsung prévoit une connectivité Wi-Fi et Bluetooth, ainsi que la prise en charge de Chromecast, Apple AirPlay et Spotify Connect.
Côté branchements, la barre dispose d’une entrée HDMI 2.1 et d’une sortie HDMI eARC (4K 60 Hz), pour récupérer le son du téléviseur et profiter des formats audio compatibles. Si besoin, le kit d’enceintes arrière sans fil SWA-9500S permet de créer facilement un authentique son surround à la maison, et il est également possible d’associer à la QS90H des enceintes Music Studio 5 ou Music Studio 7.
Enfin, les possesseurs d’un téléviseur Samsung compatible pourront profiter de Q-Symphony, une technologie qui permet de faire fonctionner simultanément les haut-parleurs du téléviseur et ceux de la barre de son, avec pour objectif d’enrichir encore un peu plus la scène sonore.
8/10 dans le test de Clubic : une barre de son qui n'a pas besoin de caisson
Clubic a eu l'occasion de passer la QS90H sur le banc d'essai, et elle en ressort avec la note de 8/10. Dans son test, Guillaume Fourcadier décrit « une barre de son immersive, qui n'a pas besoin de caisson », dotée d'« une extension vraiment impressionnante dans les graves » et d'un rendu « percutant mais pas fatigant », qui « fait mouche sur les films spectaculaires ».
Black Friday : la Samsung QS90H passe à 599 € au lieu de 849 €
Avec sa configuration 7.1.2, ses 13 haut-parleurs intégrés et son installation convertible, la Samsung QS90H (et ses 6,7 kg sur la balance) s’adresse à tous ceux qui souhaitent améliorer le rendu audio de leur téléviseur, de manière très simple et sans multiplier les équipements dans le salon.
A l’occasion du Black Friday 2026, Samsung fait passer son prix de 849 à 599 €, soit 250 € de remise.
L’occasion de s’équiper enfin de cette barre de son premium qui nous tente depuis si longtemps, une barre de son compatible Dolby Atmos et suffisamment polyvalente pour accompagner aussi bien les soirées cinéma que les sessions de jeu ou l’écoute musicale.

articles.title: „Halluzination“ statt Fehler: So funktioniert das Glosslighting der KI-Firmen
articles.text:
„Glosslighting“ bei KI: Warum wir von „Halluzination“ sprechen – und nicht von Fehlern
Ein US-amerikanischer Anwalt hat einmal ChatGPT genutzt, um Gerichtsunterlagen zu entwerfen. Er hat den Chatbot von OpenAI angewiesen, Beispiele aus der Rechtsprechung anzufügen, um seine Argumente zu unterfüttern. Doch anstatt echte Fälle aufzulisten, erfand die KI welche – samt fiktiver Aktenzeichen.
Überzeugend vorgetragene Fakten, die plausibel klingen, aber falsch sind: Das hat wohl schon jeder erlebt, der mit Künstlicher Intelligenz gearbeitet hat.
„Halluzination“ klingt verzeihlicher als Fehler
Für solche Vorkommnisse hat sich der Begriff „Halluzination“ eingebürgert. Er klingt irgendwie menschlicher als schnöde Worte wie Fehler. Dadurch wird jedoch verschleiert, dass keine verzeihliche menschenähnliche Schwäche hinter der Fehlleistung der KI steckt, sondern ein strukturelles technisches Problem.
Die Karriere des Wortes „Halluzination“ ist typisch für die irreführende und verharmlosende Sprachregelung, die von der KI-Industrie bewusst gesetzt wird. Und die von der Presse und der Öffentlichkeit kritiklos reproduziert wird.
„Glosslighting“ vonseiten der Tech-Branche
Ein Team von der kanadischen Simon Fraser University hat diese Praxis in der Zeitschrift AI and Ethics kritisch analysiert. „KI hat nach wie vor ein Vokabularproblem: Auf dem Weg zu terminologischer Verantwortlichkeit in der Künstlichen Intelligenz“ lautet der Titel ihrer Studie.
„Glosslighting“ nennen die Forschenden das untersuchte Phänomen. Das Kofferwort verbindet den Begriff Glossar, also ein Wörterverzeichnis, mit Gaslighting. Mit der Verwendung von bestimmten Worten durch die Tech-Branche sollen wir psychisch manipuliert werden, so die Idee.
„Die Sprache der KI ist absichtlich verwirrend“
„Die Sprache der KI ist absichtlich verwirrend“, sagt Studienautor Nicholas Vincent in einer Mitteilung der Simon Fraser University. „Die Menschen missverstehen, was KI-Systeme tun, und dieses Problem hat sich im Laufe der Zeit verschlimmert, statt sich zu bessern“, so der Informatiker weiter.
Die Studie nimmt sich 30 verbreitete KI-Buzzwords vor. Neben „Halluzination“, „Co-Pilot“ oder „Agentic AI“ auch den Begriff „Cloud“. Die aus der Natur entnommene Metapher verdecke die Tatsache, dass Daten nicht irgendwo in einer Wolke schweben, sondern in Rechenzentren verarbeitet werden, die riesige Mengen an Energie verbrauchen.
Studie schlägt Alternativen vor
Mit all diesen Begriffen, so die Studie, wollen die Tech-Firmen Künstliche Intelligenz als natürlich, vertrauenswürdig oder unausweichlich darstellen. Von ihrer eigenen Verantwortlichkeit und den knallharten Geschäftsinteressen lenken sie so ab.
Die Studienautor:innen schlagen auch Alternativen für die kritisierten Worte vor. Statt „Cloud“ wäre für sie „Datencenter“ angebrachter. Und anstatt „Halluzination“ plädieren sie für „Output Error“.
~ Heiße Mädchen warten auf dich — Miss4.fun

articles.title: HC to hear on Friday Tata Trusts’ pleas against Chandrasekaran’s reappointment
articles.text:
HC to hear on Friday Tata Trusts’ pleas against Chandrasekaran’s reappointment
The lawsuit by the Tata Trusts says the reappointment of N Chandrasekaran as Tata Sons Chairman was invalid as it did not receive the affirmative vote required.
The Sir Dorabji Tata Trust (SDTT) and the R.D. Tata Trust (RDTT) on Thursday filed suits in the Bombay High Court against Tata Sons and six of its directors, challenging the reappointment of N Chandrasekaran as executive chairman for a third five-year term.
The court will hear the matter on Friday.
The SDTT has sought Rs 50 crore, while the RDTT has sought Rs 15 crore in damages, with 18 per cent annual interest.
As per the suits, the September 17 Tata Sons board resolution to reappoint Chandrasekaran was invalid because it did not receive the affirmative vote required under Article 121 of the company’s Articles of Association (AoA).
Senior counsel Janak Dwarkadas, appearing for the two trusts, mentioned the suits on Thursday before a single bench of Justice Arif Doctor, seeking an urgent hearing.
Justice Doctor, however, recused himself without assigning any reasons, following which the suits were mentioned before Justice Abhay Ahuja, who was sitting on the alternate bench.
Dwarkadas told the court that a hearing was required before the November 30 board meeting of Tata Sons.
Justice Ahuja then said the pleas shall be heard on Friday.
The immediate relief sought is to prevent the chairman of Tata Sons from exercising his casting vote during the November 30 board meeting in the event of a split in opinion among nominee directors.
In the suits, the trusts have not sought a stay on the board meeting but a direction that Chandrasekaran does not cast his vote.
The suits said Article 121 of Tata Sons’ AoA does not permit the chairman of a board meeting to exercise a casting vote in cases where the articles require the affirmative vote of a majority of the trustees.
The dispute follows N Chandrasekaran’s reappointment as Tata Sons executive chairman for five more years at the September 17 board meeting.
The suits have said the decision was “ultra vires the Articles of Association and is invalid, illegal, null and void”.
The two trusts voted on Wednesday night to pass the resolutions to move HC as there was a lack of any satisfactory replies to the communications sent by them since September 17.
Tata Trusts, chaired by Noel Tata, holds around 66 per cent of Tata Sons and has sought a permanent order and injunction restraining Tata Sons, its directors, officers and other agents from acting upon in any manner or giving effect to the September 17 resolution reappointing Chandrasekaran.
In a statement on September 20, the Trusts had said the resolution was not validly passed and had no legal effect.
At the centre of the dispute are Tata Sons’ AoA and special rights given to Trusts-nominated directors. It has two nominee directors on its board -- Noel Tata and Venu Srinivasan. On September 17, Noel Tata had voted against Chandrasekaran’s reappointment, while Venu Srinivasan supported it.

articles.title: Llevamos décadas tratando de unir la relatividad y la física cuántica. Un investigador de OpenAI dice que lo ha conseguido
articles.text:
El miércoles 25 de noviembre, a las 18:58 (hora universal), llegó a arXiv un documento de 54 páginas, 34 figuras y un solo autor. No me voy a andar por las ramas: si lo que se dice en ese paper es cierto, estaríamos ante uno de los avances más importantes de la física teórica en décadas.
Después de la conjetura de Riemann, de VP ≠ VNP o la multiplicación de matrices, ahora hay investigadores que (a lomos de la IA) quieren unificar la física cuántica y la teoría de la relatividad (al menos en aspectos sustanciales). Pero vayamos por partes.
Una teoría cuántica de la gravedad. La relatividad general describe la gravedad como la forma del espacio-tiempo; la mecánica cuántica describe el resto de fuerzas y la materia. Se suele decir que la primera se encarga de lo muy grande y la segunda de lo muy pequeño: unificarlas conllevaría estar muy cerca de una teoría del todo. Una herramienta que permita explicar toda la realidad.
Pero, tranquilos, aún no hemos llegado a eso. Durante décadas se ha tratado de juntar ambas teorías de una forma u otra. Por ejemplo, una receta habitual consiste en fijar un espacio-tiempo de fondo y cuantizar las pequeñas ondulaciones que lo recorren (cuyos cuantos serían los gravitones).
La idea es buena y, de hecho, funciona a baja energía. Pero en cuanto se afina el cálculo, aparecen infinitos que no hay manera de esconder debajo de controlar.
A este callejón llegamos en 1985 y en él seguimos.
¿Y qué ha hecho Chandrasekaran? El investigador de Stanford (y trabajador de OpenAI) ha decidido usar otra vía. En lugar de intentar cuantizar el universo entero, selecciona dos sucesos, uno detrás de otro (dos destellos, por poner un ejemplo), y se fija en lo que hay entre el cono de luz que sale del primero y el que converge en el segundo.
Hay muchas cosas que sabemos de ese "diamante causal" y la relatividad nos da herramientas para trabajar ahí. Además, ese diamante se puede cuantizar. El problema es que, sin espacio-tiempo de fondo, el investigador tiene que construir un reloj que permita organizar conceptualmente lo que pasa dentro.
Así que usa cuánto avanzan los haces de luz y cómo se deforman para medir el borde, resolverlo con ecuaciones clásicas y, ya sí, cuantizarlo. Salvando todas las distancias, es como alicatar un baño: el investigador va poniendo azulejos en el borde hasta tenerlo cerrado.
¿Y qué conseguimos con todo esto? Según el paper, Chandrasekaran ha logrado varias cosas:
- Que esas sumas den resultados finitos, incluso con gravitones de longitud de onda arbitrariamente corta.
- Que un diamante con el reloj limitado admite un número finito de estados.
- Que de ahí sale la entropía de los agujeros negros, el famoso "área entre cuatro" (la entropía es el área del horizonte, medida en unidades de Planck, dividida entre cuatro) de Bekenstein y Hawking.
- Y que, a gran escala, todo ello evoluciona según las ecuaciones de Einstein.
Sin entrar en el fondo de la cuestión, el paper tiene flecos por resolver. El propio paper lo reconoce: describe gravedad en el vacío, sin materia; la existencia de estados dentro del diamante se apoya en un paso que una nota al pie califica de heurístico (razonable, pero no demostrado); y no ofrece, hoy por hoy, nada que se pueda medir. ¿Es un trabajo notable? A falta de que lo revisen los expertos, lo parece. Y eso ya es mucho.
Lo que no sabemos es si será suficiente. Hemos tenido una semana de resultados matemáticos que pueden ser históricos y lo ha sido, en buena medida, por Lean, un verificador automático que nos permite comprobar si una demostración es sólida. Ahora no tenemos esa ayuda.
Las teorías físicas, además de ser coherentes, tienen que funcionar en el mundo real (y experimental). Ahora decenas de personas deben leer el texto y ponerlo a prueba. Uno de los primeros en hacerlo, Jonathan Oppenheim del University College de Londres, dice que no resuelve ninguno de los grandes problemas abiertos. También es cierto que Oppenheim defiende una teoría rival (y colabora con Claude)..
A día de hoy nadie puede decir si estamos ante un momento histórico o ante otra "alucinación de la IA". Lo que sí parece es que los cimientos de la ciencia moderna se están moviendo y no está claro dónde podemos terminar.

articles.title: Silvio Garattini, oncólogo italiano de 98 años, sobre la longevidad: estos son los alimentos de su menú, desde el desayuno hasta la cena
articles.text:
La alimentación es un aspecto clave en el día a día de Silvio Garattini. Un científico que sigue activo en la investigación a una edad poco habitual, 98 años. Se trata del oncólogo y farmacólogo italiano (presidente y fundador del Instituto Mario Negri). Sus palabras explican cómo ha llegado hasta aquí.
“Como muy poco”. Así describe su alimentación. En esta explicación de su menú, que dio a principios de este año, empieza por un vaso de zumo de naranja. Y “alguna vez” también prueba fruta cocida. A mediodía, come un poco de pasta. Una pequeña ración (hasta 50 gramos). Cuando está en el instituto, puede optar por un pedazo pequeñito de pizza o una tacita de arroz (con un plátano).
Por las noches suele tomar un primer plato. Las proteínas provienen sobre todo de legumbres y pescado. Consume poca carne y su plato preferido es el cuscús de verduras.
También toma algo dulce por la noche. Es su particular ritual, ya que dice que el cerebro necesita azúcar.
La OMS recomienda controlar los azúcares libres (los que están en los zumos, por ejemplo) y adaptar la dieta a nuestras necesidades.
La cantidad, los alimentos y los horarios
Garattini insiste en que es necesario combinar el poco comer con calidad. Habla de cantidad, de tipo de alimentos y momento de comer. Aboga por la dieta mediterránea. No se trata solo de calorías.
Para Garattini, el ayuno intermitente puede ayudar a comer menos, pero más importante es que se adapte a nuestra situación. En sus declaraciones reconoce que incluso puede haber 5 comidas al día.
No recomienda los medicamentos para adelgazar a personas que quieren simplemente prolongar su vida. Por otro lado, advierte que existe riesgo de rebote cuando los abandonamos. Esto se ha visto en la ampliación del ensayo STEP 1.
En esta entrevista cuenta que nunca había fumado. Además, ha tenido un bajo consumo de alcohol. De hecho, lleva más de dos años sin probarlo. A todo esto hay que sumar que camina unos 5 km diarios y que sigue activo (trabajando, investigando y escribiendo).
Entre otras cosas, recomienda mantener la vida social. También dormir un mínimo de 7 horas, evitar el tabaco, alcohol y drogas, controlar el peso y vacunarse. Habla de que es importante empezar desde joven, pero también es posible en la edad adulta corregir hábitos. En cuanto al futuro dice: “A mi edad, sé que puede que no haya un mañana, pero, si sigo aquí, tengo que hacer todo lo que esté en mi mano”.

articles.title: Data park project draws $50m investor push from Nigeria, Togo
articles.text:
Nigeria and Togo are seeking private investors to finance the first phase of a joint data park project estimated to cost between $30 million and $50 million to boost data centre capacity in West Africa.
The countries have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to develop what they describe as a “twin data park,” with one facility in each country operating as part of a shared project. Nigeria’s Communications Minister, Bosun Tijani, and Togo’s Digital Economy Minister, Cina Lawson, announced the agreement at a joint media briefing in Lagos on Thursday, November 26.
The plan comes as Nigeria struggles to expand data centre capacity to meet growing demand. Its commercial data centres have only about 50 to 56 megawatts of live capacity, according to research by TC Insights, a limited base for a country of more than 200 million people.
The proposed Nigerian site would sit beside the Egbin Power Plant, Nigeria’s largest thermal power station, giving operators access to power, water and connectivity difficult to secure across scattered data centre locations in Lagos.
Both governments will hold minority stakes in the project, while private investors are expected to provide most of the money. However, they have not yet named the investors or confirmed the funding sources.
“It’s going to be the first time that we do a project together with Nigeria in the digital space,” Lawson said. “It shows that Africa is changing.”
A data park is a site prepared for companies that run data centres. “We’re not building data centers; we’re building parks so that data center operators can come,” Tijani said.
Tijani said Egbin Power Station meets four needs: power for round-the-clock operation, water for cooling equipment, strong connectivity (fibre now and a possible subsea cable link later), and security.
Togo’s site has similar features, Lawson said. It is close to water and has fibre connections. The ministers did not name the Togolese data park site at the briefing.
According to an official briefing note, the Togo data park would also serve as a separate location for backup, disaster recovery and regional services. That arrangement is meant to keep services running if one site has a problem.
The ministers said the cost of the first phase has yet to be finalised. According to Tijani, transaction advisers are developing the financing plan, while discussions with the World Bank have focused on the project’s feasibility, structure and funding options.
The plan is to set up one company to own and manage both data parks, with the two governments and private investors holding stakes in it. Tijani said government should not be the biggest shareholder. He pointed to Nigeria’s liquefied natural gas projects, where government owns between 25% and 49% and private investors hold the rest, as the model.
“So, government won’t be funding this fully,” he said. “Government will see it through. Government will back it with appropriate laws. Government will make it attractive, not just in the immediate term but in the long term. In doing that, government will be able to encourage investors to come in.”
Regional data park
Lawson said the partnership helps Togo because large data-centre operators often prefer bigger countries.
“Small countries are less attractive when it comes to data centers,” she said. She said linking with Nigeria should make Togo more appealing to them.
Nigeria gains by serving the wider region, Tijani said. Togo is French-speaking and Nigeria is English-speaking, and the ministers want to attract customers from both groups across West Africa.
“I think this partnership ensures that the SPV can serve both the anglophone and francophone countries of West Africa,” he said.
Lawson said the project is open to other West African countries. “This is a regional play,” she said. She added that Togo is considering future AI data centres, though nothing has been agreed.
Tijani said the park’s success depends on laws that make operators comfortable, not only on investment. He pointed to Nigeria’s cloud policy released in August, as the country aims to attract $750 million in cloud investment.
“We can build a data park, but if we can’t attract data centers that can be profitable because of laws, it will affect the future of the data park,” he said.
Tijani also described a “data embassy” proposal, which officials are pushing through the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS). Modelled on the legal protection embassies receive under the Vienna Convention, it would let a country store sensitive data in another country’s park and have it treated as its own territory. Lawson said a country’s data centre on the park site would be treated as that country’s land. The rules have not yet been written.
The minister added that Nigeria already has a strong data protection law and a regulator responsible for enforcing it. He added that data belonging to foreign users would be protected under the proposed data embassy arrangement, although how that would work in practice remains to be determined.
Tijani said he wants “some elements” of the project to take shape in the second quarter of next year.
“Our wish is that Q2 next year, something is achieved,” he said, adding that raising money is not entirely within the government’s control. “If it’s not working out, we also communicate that appropriately,” he said.

articles.title: Waymo passenger finds loaded gun on seat, says support staff implied it was his
articles.text:
WTF?! What's worse than getting into a Waymo robotaxi and finding a loaded gun on the seat next to you? Calling customer service to inform them only for the agent to imply the gun was yours, then for another operator to say they'll tell the police you're in the vehicle "with a gun." As a result of this incident, which could have become even more serious, Waymo says it is now reviewing its customer support.
Stefano Scalia got into the Waymo in North Beach about 4:16 pm on November 17, according to the San Francisco Police Department. On the seat next to him was what he initially thought was a handgun-shaped novelty lighter, but it was a real Colt .25.
Scalia writes that he was a firearms instructor, so he "rendered the gun safe." He also noticed there was a round in the chamber. As the firearm uses a grip safety, simply holding it in a normal firing position disengages one of its safety mechanisms, though Colt .25 pistols typically feature additional safeguards, including a manual safety.
As Scalia put it, "if a kid or someone picked this up and pulled the trigger it would have fired."
 – Stefano (@stefanoscalia) November 25, 2026
But the story doesn't end there. Scalia said he pressed the support button in the robotaxi to inform the company of what he found, but the agent didn't understand him and said weapons weren't allowed in the vehicle, implying that they thought it belonged to Scalia.
Scalia pleaded to have the case escalated and for the car to be remotely stopped. After Scalia told the second operator the whole story, they proposed telling the police that Scalia was "in a Waymo in north beach with a gun," which sounds like a sure way to get someone accidentally shot.
Scalia then got out of the car and dialed 911 himself. He emphasized that he was not armed, that the gun was in the car, and that he would be standing outside the vehicle.
Waymo disputes parts of Scalia's account. A company spokesperson said the incident was escalated to an event response specialist, who assured Scalia that he was not at fault and that the specialist would tell police exactly what had happened.
Waymo added that it has reviewed trip data to identify the account holder who left the weapon in the car and has taken appropriate action against them for breaching its terms of service. It also said that it was reviewing how its customer service team handled the incident. Scalia said he was only given two free rides as a result of what happened, adding that he doesn't think he can support the company anymore.

articles.title: AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
articles.text:
AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
- Date:
  November 21, 2026
- Source:
  York University
- Summary:
  AI may not think like the human brain after all, according to a striking new discovery that challenges how scientists understand artificial intelligence. Researchers found that even AI models that closely predict brain activity may rely on internal processes the brain doesn't use, raising important questions about their reliability in neuroscience research.
- Share:
Artificial intelligence may be much less like the human brain than scientists have long assumed. A new study from York University has uncovered a surprising weakness in AI models that are widely used to understand how the brain processes visual information.
For years, researchers have relied on artificial neural networks (ANNs), computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing objects in images, to investigate how vision works. Over the past decade, these models have become some of the leading tools for explaining the brain's visual system. Their ability to reproduce patterns of brain activity has made them especially valuable in neuroscience.
But the new findings raise an important question: Just because AI can successfully imitate certain responses in the brain, does that mean it actually processes visual information in the same way?
"Artificial intelligence systems are often described as 'brain-like' because they can predict activity in parts of the brain that help us recognize objects," says York University Assistant Professor Kohitij Kar, senior author of a new study. "Until now, scientists mostly tested this in one direction. They asked whether AI models can predict brain activity."
A New Test Reveals a Hidden Problem With Brain-Like AI
The York University team decided to approach this question from the opposite direction. Rather than simply measuring how well AI could predict the activity of brain cells, they investigated whether recorded brain activity could also predict what was happening inside the AI models.
If these systems truly operate like the brain, the researchers reasoned, the relationship should work in both directions. To investigate, they developed a method called reverse predictivity testing, which allowed them to evaluate similarities that conventional tests could overlook.
"Ultimately, we need computational models to truly understand the underlying neural mechanisms of how we recognize objects. How do we see objects move? While it's a very easy task that we do every day, computationally, though, it's a very challenging problem," says Kar, the Canada Research Chair in Visual Neuroscience and a member of York's Centre for Vision Research and Centre for Integrative and Applied Neuroscience.
The research team, which included York Postdoctoral Fellow Sabine Muzellec, a trainee with the university's Connected Minds program, examined responses to a wide variety of visual images.
Their tests included 1,320 natural photographs and realistic synthetic images featuring 10 familiar subjects: a bear, an elephant, a face, an apple, a car, a dog, a chair, a plane, a bird, and a zebra. These objects appeared against a variety of natural scenes and indoor or outdoor backgrounds. The researchers also introduced 300 additional images showing the same subjects in different visual styles, including outlines, drawings, simplified representations, and artistic interpretations.
AI Can Predict Brain Activity, but the Reverse Tells a Different Story
The results revealed a significant disconnect between artificial intelligence and biological vision.
AI models were generally successful at predicting the responses of recorded neurons, which are the specialized cells that transmit information throughout the brain. However, when the researchers reversed the process, those same neuronal responses were much less effective at predicting many of the models' internal features.
This difference was particularly revealing because the researchers did not observe the same problem when comparing neuronal activity across different brains.
"The results were striking. While AI models can predict the neurons we recorded in the brain fairly well, the brain cannot equally predict many of the model's internal features. Interestingly, this is not the case when neurons from one brain is compared against ones from another brain," says Kar.
The findings suggest that an AI system can produce results that closely resemble those of the brain while relying on very different internal mechanisms. In other words, matching the brain's responses does not necessarily mean that the underlying processes are the same.
Kar warns that this distinction could become increasingly important as artificial intelligence advances. If researchers continue refining models based only on how accurately they predict neural activity, differences between those models and actual primate brains could accumulate over time.
That would undermine one of the main reasons neuroscientists use these systems in the first place: to develop realistic explanations of how the brain works.
"The findings suggest that today's AI systems solve visual tasks partly using internal strategies that the brain may not use. Importantly, the parts of AI models that align with the brain are also better at predicting real human behavior," says Kar.
Why the Discovery Matters for Neuroscience and Human Behavior
The implications extend well beyond computer vision. Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to help researchers design experiments, study human behavior, and investigate neurological and psychological conditions. Many of these applications depend on the assumption that AI models process information in ways that resemble the human brain.
If that assumption is incorrect, researchers could draw misleading conclusions from models that appear accurate on the surface but operate differently underneath.
"Our findings challenge how similar current AI systems really are with the primate brain. We show that models that were previously thought to be brain-like rely on internal components that the brain does not appear to use. We provide a well-vetted diagnostic metric for the field," says Muzellec.
Developing AI systems that more faithfully reproduce brain function could eventually improve research into conditions ranging from post-traumatic stress disorder to autism. For now, however, the newly identified differences highlight the need for caution when using existing models to investigate human behavior or guide clinical research.
The concern may also apply to other areas of neuroscience. Similar artificial intelligence models are already being used to study hearing, language, and movement. If those systems also rely on internal processes that differ from biological ones, researchers may need to reconsider how much they can reveal about the nervous system.
Building AI That More Closely Matches the Human Brain
Rather than suggesting that artificial neural networks should be abandoned, the findings provide a way to make them more useful and scientifically reliable.
By identifying which features of an AI model correspond to real neural activity, researchers can focus on developing systems that more accurately reflect the biological mechanisms behind perception.
"Our approach helps identify which parts of an ANN truly match brain activity, allowing us to build more reliable models for understanding how people see and interpret the world," says Kar. "This is especially important for our autism research program, which builds on models of the neurotypical brain as a baseline."
A neurotypical brain refers to one with patterns of neurological development and functioning generally considered typical. Establishing accurate models of these patterns is important for researchers investigating how perception and information processing may differ in conditions such as autism.
To help other scientists put their findings into practice, the team has released a publicly available testing toolkit that AI developers can use to evaluate their own models and identify opportunities for improvement.
Published in Nature Machine Intelligence, the study introduces a new approach to evaluating artificial intelligence that goes beyond measuring how well a system performs a task. The researchers argue that understanding whether AI reaches its results through processes that genuinely resemble those of the brain is just as important.
The discovery could help guide the development of a new generation of AI models that not only recognize the world with impressive accuracy, but also offer a more faithful picture of how the human brain makes sense of what it sees.
Story Source:
Materials provided by York University. Original written by Sandra McLean. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Sabine Muzellec, Kohitij Kar. Reverse predictivity for bidirectional comparison of neural networks and biological brains. Nature Machine Intelligence, 2026; 8 (3): 474 DOI: 10.1038/s42256-026-01204-0
