articles.title: Finetuning Your Embedding Model for Better Search: Learning from Agentic Search at Dell
articles.text:
Transcript
Rachel Shalom: I'm Rachel. I work for Dell. I'm part of a team that develops internal AI solutions for Dell. We develop solutions that basically Dell employees are using. I'm going to talk about some of the work we are doing inside Dell today. I'm actually going to start with the motivation of this talk. I'm leading an agentic search within Dell, a search system that searches for your information in internal sources like GitHub, Jira, Confluence, and other sources. Part of it is using semantic search, which is using also an embedding model. What we have noticed is that we keep failing in certain type of questions. Questions that have to do with internal terminology or questions that have to do with internal products of Dell. Here are some examples like PowerScale or CloudIQ or PowerProtect. These are the type of questions that are using internal terminology, or you can call it even internal language of Dell, that the system kept failing with retrieving the right answer. The motivation was, does the embedding model that is supposed to capture the meaning of those really understand the questions or the answers?
Outline
This is what we are going to talk about today. We'll discuss why embedding models are important and common training methodologies. We'll discuss also the common use cases for embeddings. I will talk about fine-tuning and a common loss function that is used today for training majority of the embedding models. We will talk about the use case at Dell more in depth and why we trained our own embedding model, discuss the data collection, and how did we evaluate and monitor the performance.
Why Embedding Models Are Important
Humans understand words, machines understand numbers. Embeddings is the bridge between them. Embedding is capturing the meaning of words and sentences. For example, you can see in that lane that in the embedding space, expressions that have to do with password or forgot my login or can't access account should be closer in the embedding space, while cities and countries will be in a different area in the embedding space, but closer to each other, and that's the meaning of representations. What are the common use cases for using embedding models? I think the most common one is information retrieval. Most of the companies or at least in the enterprise, you use RAG, Retrieval-Augmented Generation to retrieve information from a vector database. Classification is one more. For example, if you want to assign categories to your text, like you have incoming emails, the most trivial example is you want to target spam or not spam. Clustering is another very common use case for embedding models. If you want to make sense of your unstructured data, like you have incoming queries by customers and you want to group them together into clusters and recommendation systems to make personalized recommendations. There are probably others, but these are the most common ones.
How Are Embedding Models Trained?
Now I want to talk briefly on the general training procedures for embedding models. Usually when you train embedding models, you start with the first phase, which is the pre-training. Pre-training is done on what we call the chunk of the internet. You take everything that is available online, Wikipedia, books, public GitHub repository, anything you can imagine, and it's a lot of data, and it can be also junk data, but it's a lot of data that you put in. The way you train is by Masked Language Modeling, which means, as you see in the example, is that you give the model a sentence, each time you mask a different word, and then you let the model guess the word, and this is how you teach the model a general understanding of the language. A little bit of grammar, a little bit of word connections, but a very general understanding, not the fine-grained understanding of semantic meaning of each word, and for that, you have stage number two, which is a fine-tuning stage.
At this stage, you really have to collect high-quality data. Usually it takes a long time, and it costs a lot of money normally. I'm going to talk about the preparation of what we call contrastive learning, which is a very common way to train or fine-tune embedding models nowadays. What you do normally is you prepare pairs or triplets of examples. For example, here, you have a question. Let's call it an anchor. How do I reset my password? Then you have a positive answer, which is how to reset it, and then you have a negative answer, which doesn't answer your question. The idea in training is that you want to teach the model that the question and the positive answer will be represented as vectors that are very close in the embedding space, and the negative answer and the anchor are going to be further apart. That's the goal of the fine-tuning, to take high-quality data and get the real semantic meaning for the text.
Training/Fine-Tuning: Loss Function
How do you do that? I'm putting here a little bit of mathematics, and I'm going to explain each part of it. I think it's beautiful, and this is important that you will see it. InfoNCE, or the long-term in parentheses, loss function is one of the most common ones. If you take a look at different papers from Google or anyone else that is training embedding models, you will see different versions of the same loss function, but this is the basic one. If we go and see the batch, or we have let's say 100 examples of questions and answers, so if we take a look at a log expression, you will see that on the top we have the exponent of s is a cosine similarity between two vectors, the vector of the question and the vector of the positive answer. On the denominator, you're going to see again the similarity of the question and the positives, and the similarity of the question and negatives.
All other documents that are not the positive one to this question are considered negatives, because they are not directly answering the question. When you train an embedding model, the purpose is to bring up the similarity for positives and bring down the similarity for negatives. I added another slide for that just to maybe show it in a geometric way, so that you don't lose the context. Again, we have this log loss of positives versus negatives. If we take a look at the lower part, then you can see that if I have, let's say, a query, how do I reset my password? Then I have a positive question and a bunch of negative questions. Then, before training, you will see that the distance between the positive and negative vectors to the query are maybe, let's say, a little bit similar, and after training, you want to see that the positive answer is closer to the query, and the negatives are further away. I hope you at least enjoyed a little bit from this loss function. It's super beautiful.
Another thing that is interesting about the training is what we call prefix use. What does that mean? Sometimes we have what we call conflicting reward signals. Think about a model that is performing different tasks. Sometimes it is questions and answers. Sometimes it is clustering, as we mentioned before. Sometimes it is other tasks. Then if we take a look at this example, what is the capital of France? I want you to answer what is mostly similar, answer number one or answer number two. I think the answer would be it depends on the task. If we want to do clustering similarity between two sentences, then what is the capital of France, and number one would be more similar. If my task is to pair questions and answers, then what is the capital of France, and number two is more similar. In order to solve that, what is commonly done today when training with fine-tuning is to add prefixes.
As you can see, we have in orange the start clustering, what is the capital of France, and then clustering the answer, and that tells the model, please create vectors for clustering. They're going to get slightly different vectors because the task now is to say, these are two similar sentences. If I provide a different prefix, which is search_query, search_document, so the task is questions and answers. This is where you give the model a signal that we are now talking about a different task. This is one important thing to notice when training.
Use Case at Dell - A Multi-Agent System for Internal Search
I've talked a little bit about the use cases and a little bit generally about the training. Now let's talk about Dell, or what we did at Dell. We have an agentic search at Dell, which means we let R&D teams search within all of Dell's internal sources. For example, Jira, Confluence, GitHub, these are mostly relevant for engineers and product managers, SharePoint, also different databases. I'm going to talk about the architecture, but this is a hierarchical architecture of multiple agents that are making API calls. It also has a component of semantic search, which means we take all the data and ingest it in advance. It has a component of memory management, which is pretty common for agentic search applications. It's also permission aware, which is very important for any enterprise. These are some of the questions that we are getting normally, questions about bug solving, questions about onboarding to a new project, testing, technical configurations, procedural how-to.
We get all sorts of also weird questions, but these are the most common ones. This is a little bit on the architecture of the system itself. We have the orchestrator, or what we call the supervisor, which is the entry point for every question. This is a router that routes the user question to any other of the agents. We have a GitHub agent, which means that it's a model with a set of tools, mainly API tools. We have a Confluence agent that is a model. They all have access, or it's access-based, to the information inside Dell. We have GitLab and GitHub, which is, again, exactly the same. Models with different API tools. We have security agent, which usually makes API calls to OSs like Ubuntu and SUSE, and provide CVE resolutions, and agents that are making database queries. Just to note that each one of these agents are talking only to the supervisor.
We keep them that way in order to keep the context low and the context in place. We found it more effective that way. The supervisors can route the question to one or many agents. They return back an answer. The supervisor decides, do I want to go back to the user with an answer, or go back to the agents and bring another one? We, of course, limit the number of turns, so it won't take like one hour to get back to the user. This is how it works.
This is the general architecture of what we have. We have a web application. We are API first, which means there are other internal applications at Dell that are using this agentic search. It's a skill, and it is an MCP that is used within Windsurf and Claude Code. The backend, other than having this architecture that I explained before, it is using Langfuse for observability. This is an important part, Dell cares really about privacy. All of the data that we are having, it's highly restricted. We are mainly playing with open-source models, which means mostly it's running on-prem. Everything is running on-prem on Dell infrastructure. Recently, we started experimenting with Gemini and Sonnet, but in a very limited way. The whole system is around open source. Embedding, re-rankers, LLMs, and every time there is a new one, we are experimenting, but all of it is on-prem. There is another layer to this application, which is what we call auto data ingestion, or bring your own data there.
That is when someone wants to create their own bot, let's say, you just provide, here is a link to my Confluence or to my Jira, to my GitHub, and then it triggers a pipeline that does a lot of data plumbing, and ingest and chunk all the data, put it in a vector database, and it's ready for you to query. You can create your personal context space. A little bit more about the bring your own data architecture, it's important because this is the part that connects later to our embedding model, which is the main subject. If you have Jira, Confluence, and GitHub, we're taking all of the fields from Confluence, we take all the images and attachments, and so is for Jira. We do semantic chunks with code. We use AST, and we do a lot of cleanups, like these are too many details to talk about.
Then you might ask yourself, ok, so you do all of that job, but the rate of change is very high, so we update it every two days. We go and check with the APIs what were the changes, and then we re-embed all the changes every two days. Everything is saved in pgvector, which is, again, hosted on-prem, which I think is very nice that everything is hosted on-prem at Dell, that it's all private, nothing goes out. Just a little bit about chunking. I'm talking only on Confluence now because the work that we did in training the model, the context was Confluence. We start with an API fetch, or think about Confluence space, if you work with Confluence, you download thousands of pages, then we reformat it into HTML. We filter a lot of noise because there are a lot of emojis and stuff that are not relevant to the model, we turn it into an md file. We detect also tables to make sure that the context of the table is saved even when you chunk. We take all those attachments and then we chunk by paragraphs and use an embedding model and save it in a vector database. This is done for every request that we get and in advance.
Now the question is, ok, so we have a system in place, we have lots of agents and we have also semantic search, now why fine-tune our own embedding? I started the lecture with saying that we saw gaps that the semantic search just didn't solve, and the gaps were mainly about questions on internal products, on abbreviations and acronyms that are specific to Dell, and workflows and processes, everything that is the Dell world or the Dell language, there are a lot of such data at Dell, that led us to think or to hypothesize that this is a reason for failure. Now when you run a RAG system, so there are potentially a lot of problems that could happen. It has a lot of stages and a lot of pieces moving around, so it could be something else. Our hypothesis said, let's try and see if we can improve the result by fine-tuning a model.
Generally speaking, I think that the signals you want to look for if you are planning a domain adaptation are to ask yourself like, is the data of the model out of the shelf that I'm taking on? Now I'm talking about models in the context of open source. We take most of the models from Hugging Face, normally you know what is the training data that they were trained on, you have leaderboards. You ask yourself, is the Dell data even similar to what those models were trained on? It can be that the terminology we use was used when this model was trained originally. These are the signs to look for when you want to train. There is another interesting thing to check. Again, every open-source model comes with a vocabulary. It's a list of tokens that the model has seen. This one was around 30,000. What happens when the model hasn't seen that word, they have a special token called unknown token.
That means the model said, I haven't seen that but I can manage, never mind. I put an unknown token. I wanted to understand how many unknown tokens do we have that the model completely hasn't seen at all? Not that it doesn't understand the semantics, it just didn't see those words. I was surprised to see that these are very general. I put here some examples that I saw, like Base64-encoded strings, or you can see Unicode box-drawing, all of these things that really have no meaning. It makes sense. All of the images, the model didn't recognize, that was surprising. I thought that models are trained on images now. Checkmarks and long camelCase compound words. This was a very small percentage of the data that the model didn't recognize. The reason I checked it is because when you fine-tune a model, I would like the model to semantically understand my data. If most of the tokens that I have in my data do not exist in the model vocabulary, that's a reason to start training from scratch, not fine-tuning. That was a check. The check told me, it's fine. The model doesn't understand images. I don't care. Let's move on. We are continuing with fine-tuning.
Choosing the Base Model
One more thing to consider. How do you choose a base model? Open source now. Again, I work for an enterprise that cares about privacy a lot, so mostly open source running on-prem. The first thing that every company cares about is licensing and commercial usage, especially every large company like Dell. I am not allowed to touch any models the legal team hasn't approved. The second thing that I care about is how open is this model? When I say open, I'm not only talking about the model weights, but did they release the training code? Did they release the data that they trained on? This is very important. Then you look at benchmarks. When you look at benchmarks, I want to take a look at tasks that I care about. I want to train my model to be able to retrieve documents from a vector database. I want to go and take a look at benchmarks that have high scores on that task.
There is also the inference cost and latency. How fast is this model? Does it support multilingual and not only English? Lastly, the context length. How much text can I push in at once? Then we ended up at comparing two, EmbeddingGemma and Nomic Embed, mainly because we were very limited in the licensing part. Just a funny story, before we used those, we used the BGE family. These are Chinese family. Then for some reason, Chinese models were banned from some American companies. Then we had to redo the whole work with models that are allowed. Both of them have great licenses. They are both open, even though I must say that comparing to Google, Nomic Embed by Nomic, they released it all. You are welcome to go and try. They released the training code, the model, the data. Anyone can reproduce the work. It's amazing. In terms of parameters or size, both of them are tiny, so it's great.
They are really fast. Context length, you can see that Google contains only 2K and Nomic Embed contains 8K. Google supports multilingual. If I go to best fit, then we decided, I have a choice now between Confluence, GitHub, and Jira. Now when we took a look at Google, they were very optimized for code search. We chose the EmbeddingGemma for code embedding. For Confluence, we decided we go with Nomic Embed because it has extensive technical documents it was trained on. Also, the context length gives us more flexibility when we want to embed things from Confluence.
Data Prep for Training
Going back to Confluence, I want to talk a little bit about, we decided now to fine-tune, now how do you start. You need to start preparing data, that's the hardest part, harder than just fine-tuning. We started with taking chunks, and I'm going to provide examples in the next slide. The chunking part, we did already in advance, so it was easy just to take the chunks we already handled. Then, step two, once I have one chunk, let's say, I'm taking an LLM to help me generate questions for that chunk. We generated three questions for each chunk, and of course, you can play with the number, that the chunks are supposed to answer those questions. This is how you generate, as you remember, the question and the positive document. Now, I would like to generate the negative documents. How do I do that? I have the questions, so we did a trick, and we took each question, and we went to the vector database, and we say, ok, let's take a model that wasn't trained, and retrieve documents from our vector database, but just, let's cap it so that the similarity when we retrieve is larger than 30%, but less than 80%.
We keep it in a range where the answer probably is not the most exact answer, but are not very far away. It's what we call hard negatives. They are answers that are not exactly answering what you ask, but they're not very far away, and we want to distinguish between those. We took the top 20, once you have 20 for the training, we kept 7 out of them. The number of negatives per training is just a parameter, and you can decide what to do. Then, you create triplets out of this process. How do you create triplets? That was a description of the process, so it's important you see one example in front of you, so a passage. We have to install Windsurf on Ubuntu WSL, just install. This is a chunk that we have. Now, I need to generate three questions out of it with an LLM.
As you can see, I generated three questions that are in purple, and the answers in green are exactly this identical chunk. Now, I went to the database and I retrieved other chunks that are going to be the negative answers. In this process, I've created to myself three samples. Each sample contains one question, one answer, and one document that is positive documents, and then seven negative documents.
I wanted to take a look at the data to see and check two things. On the top, I wanted to check the number of tokens for each part. I wanted to see what is the distribution of tokens for the questions, and you see it's roughly between zero to 50. This is a sample. Then I wanted to see what is the token distribution for the positive answers, which are roughly up to 1,500. Then I wanted to see what is the distribution of the negative answer, which are the same, up to 1,000, but we add a little bit more. This is important because the model is limited by context, so you want to make sure that you don't have very large context. Second thing is the cosine similarity distribution. As you see below, I wanted to compare the distribution of the question and the positives, and the question of the negatives.
What would you expect it to be? In a perfect world, I would expect that the distribution of question and the positive document would be very high, and take it to the right, the green one should be on the right. The distribution of similarities between negatives and the question would be to the left, very low similarities. As you can see here, it's a start where they are pretty similar. My goal, or what I will check after I'm going to train, is if I manage to create that separation, meaning the similarities of positives are going to be on the right side, and similarities of negatives are going to be on the left side. One more thing about fine-tuning with Auto Research. Some of you have trained models in the past. You know that, at least in the past, it was babysitting the models. You have a lot of parameters to play with in the model, learning rate, batch size, whatever it is.
Every time, you do a round, you wait a few hours, and then you start with different parameters. I think a month ago, Andrej Karpathy released what they called Auto Research, and he said, I just created an md file. I told the model, it's an LLM training an LLM. That's what it is. I gave my Claude Code, I think it was Opus 4.6. I told it, here is a training loop, here is the configuration file. You are only allowed to play with the training code and the parameters and the configuration, nothing else. Don't stop until the human stops you. Just make experiments. Each experiment should last 10 minutes, and then check the loss. If the loss goes down, keep those parameters. Loss goes up, remove those parameters, and move on. I just let it run overnight, and it really did save me a lot of time, because I came up, I looked at the experiment he made. I must say that there were some stupid stuff he did, but I chose one of the experiments that I liked, and I set up the learning rate, and the batch size, and everything, to what just the model told me. It was a nice experiment, and I think it is saving time.
I wanted to tell you a little bit about the setup for training. First of all is, I ran on four H100 GPUs. After all, I work at Dell, they have a lot of infrastructure. The number of negatives is 7. I used batch size of 128, and remember, the training data was Confluence spaces of almost all Dell. I counted the tokens, it was around 9 billion tokens in total. Then I wanted just for us to talk, or have a pick on distributed training. Let's take a look at the first part. If I have four GPUs, and I say I have 128 batch size, what does it mean in terms of documents? It means that I have 128 queries, or questions, and then I have, for each one of them, one positive answer, seven negative answers. I ended up with 1,024 additional documents on each GPU. Each GPU is getting one model, and 1,024 documents plus 128 queries.
We go to stage two. We start with the forward path. We put in the text, and we get vectors. What is interesting with this forward path is that, first, it is done in batches. It is done in batches of 32 in order to minimize memory consumption, but also, it is done in a way, we don't save any gradients, or the computational graph, let's call it. If you use PyTorch, so when saving a computational graph, it means you save the whole million parameters model activations, and it takes a lot of memory. When you don't save it, reduces the memory. What do you end up with after you do the forward path? You end up with vector. You started with text, now you have vector. Each vector is a dimension of 768. If we have 128 questions, so only for those, you end up with a matrix of 128 over the dimension of the vector, 768.
This is only for the queries. What else do we have? We have all the documents. We have 1,024 documents that are converted now to vectors in the size dimension of 768. What happened next? You have the all-gather. Each GPU now is collecting all the information from other GPUs. Now each GPU holds 4,096 vectors in a dimension of 768. Now we want to compute the loss. Remember the loss that we presented in the past where we want to compute similarities between the questions and positive answers and negative answers. This is where it is done. What is interesting here is that each GPU is seeing one question, one positive answer, and all the rest are going to be the negatives. You are getting now 4,095 negatives to compare against one positive. Why is it good? Because this is a harder task when the model is training. If you manage to train the model well, this is going to be a high-quality model because the task was differentiating between one question and 4,095 negative answers. Eventually when we do loss backward, there is the GradCache and surrogate trick to reduce memory when you calculate gradients. After we calculate the gradients on each GPU, you average them and then you update the model weights and start all over again.
Evaluation
This was a little bit about the distributed training at a high level. Now I want to go back to my EDA before on similarities. Remember that we said that we have similarities, the green one is the similarities between positives and questions, red is negative and questions. I wanted to say that I want to separate between them. You see the distribution before training and after training. As you can see, after training, you can see better separation, which means that it gives me a good signal or it gives me a signal, ok, the training did something well. Because now I see a separation, I see that the similarities of the questions and positive answers are a little bit more to the right. The question and the negative answer are a little bit more to the left. Yes, it's not perfect, there is still an overlap, but it's better than what it was.
Said, ok, good signal, let's continue. What do we need to check now? Let's talk about the evaluation setup. We have gathered what we call a golden dataset of 300 SME-verified questions, answers, and sources. Sources are like, if I ask you, how do I get Windsurf access? Then you will get an answer, but you will also get the links for Confluence that provide this answer. What I wanted to check is the recall @k, meaning, basically the question is, when I retrieve now, do I have the right sources? Did I retrieve the right URLs or not? When I say recall @1 is when I retrieve from the vector database, then it's top 1. Recall @10, it's top 10, organized by similarity. What we discovered is that, yes, we managed to fetch more correct sources when using the new models. I checked, let's say, top one or top five, but in reality, when you do a search system, you don't take top three or top five.
You take like more top 20. This is just for comparison to understand, ok, did I manage to get more or did I not? It seems like I did manage, at least in 12%, to get more resources right. Then, what is more interesting is eventually we are talking about a system that will provide eventually an answer to the user. What I care about is, did we provide the right answer? We did it, again, on the benchmarks that we built, using LLM-as-a-judge. LLM-as-a-judge has different aspects. One of them is question to answer. I want to know, does the text directly address the question? A2A is answer to answer, meaning does the answer match the ground truth? Because I have the ground truth. Here we saw an increase of a little bit more than 4%. It seems like, I would call it a good improvement, yes? Not a great success, but a very good improvement.
We said, ok, let's deploy it. What do you do in order to monitor? You would fine-tune your model. You have now a new model, and you want to say, do I need to retrain? What do I do? The first thing we do is we check the rate of data change. If we are talking about Confluence, we can check within a month, how much did it change? Do we have 1 million new pages? This is already a reason to start retraining. Check for data drift. You can check the distribution of the training data and compare it to your production data. The last thing is we actually have signs from our systems. If people are using our web application, they have the ability to put thumbs up and thumbs down. Also, we check if they click on the actual sources we provide on the website. If they stop clicking, it gives us a bad sign.
Summary
I hope that you will take away the importance of embedding. I think it's a topic that is normally overlooked. People are talking about embedding, but they don't understand how beautiful it is. Also wanted to talk a little bit about when fine-tuning is needed, a peek into the data preparation we did there and how we train, and why is it important to monitor and evaluate.
Questions and Answers
Participant 1: Before and after fine-tuning, did you compare with providing the documents in the context? Without fine-tuning, did you use RAG approach by sending the related document to the model and getting the answers and comparing that with the fine-tuned embeddings?
Rachel Shalom: Yes. We have RAG. We are using RAG, but not only. Like, when the user is asking questions and we let the router decide, do we need RAG or do we need an API call itself? We did test only the RAG, and it's not exactly testing. We saw at the beginning that this RAG is failing. It's failing normally in specific areas when we have documents that are very specific to Dell, like product relationships and acronyms that are at Dell, this is where there were failures that we tested at the beginning. Again, when you have failures at RAG, and there are many, you ask yourself, ok, so it could be a problem of indexing, it could be a problem of the wrong chunking, there could be many things. This was one of the hypotheses, that it might be that the model doesn't understand the context, and we need to retrain.
Participant 2: You mentioned images as one of the data sources. I was wondering, how does the embedding for images happen at Dell? Are the images embedded as raw content, or do you have some kind of an OCR that describes the images as text, and then the embedding happens?
Rachel Shalom: You are asking about like images, or attachments, or whatever. For different components, we did different things. For images, we took a multi-modal model that described the image and converted it into text, and this is how we chunked and then embed. Same thing for tables, I think. We understand the table structure, and the table start and end. Think about, you have now a table with 200 lines, and very complex. Since we know the dimensions of the table, so when you chunk it, then we always put the name of the columns for each chunk, and we always have in the metadata that this is part of the same table. This is for tables. What else? Attachments. Attachments are PDFs, and PPTs, and all others are parsed and chunked as part of the chunking and embedding. After chunks, we embed it.
Participant 3: I have a question on fine-tuning. Why did you decide you have to find seven negatives, and how did you find those? Was it manual? Was it automated?
Rachel Shalom: How did I decide on seven negatives?
Participant 3: Yes, you mentioned that you have a question, you have one positive and up to seven negatives.
Rachel Shalom: The simple question is, I read the Nomic paper, and they used seven. I said, ok, they had a great success, so I'm going to take seven. That's the simple answer. The second answer is, I let Auto Research play also with the number of negatives, and see what happens to the loss. Auto Research reduced it to like zero or one, and then, your loss is amazing. I'm like, "Oh my God." I kept it seven, because I think I really carefully took a look at the paper, and I thought, ok, it makes sense. If we need to add more, we add more. I didn't plan to put less, because I think the more negatives you have, the better the training will be, but even more complex. I would retrain with different numbers in the next experiments. The basic answer is the paper.
Participant 4: Just to clarify, the fine-tuning workflow that you showed us was for an internal workflow at Dell.
Rachel Shalom: For internal data, you mean?
Participant 4: Or like, the embedding model is an internal embedding model.
Rachel Shalom: The embedding model is open source. It's called Nomic Embed. You can download it from Hugging Face. They released it together with the code, even. They have a bunch of beautiful code to train for different tasks, and the training data. I didn't use, obviously, the training data, but it's running on-prem at Dell. I didn't use any API, if that's what you're asking, to train it. Completely on-prem. I downloaded the model to Dell infrastructure and trained it there.
Participant 4: I was just wondering if you've benchmarked it with some other open-source models that are out there?
Rachel Shalom: If I was experimenting with others?
Participant 4: Yes.
Rachel Shalom: EmbeddingGemma, yes?
Participant 4: Yes, just like OpenAI text embeddings, or anything like that?
Rachel Shalom: The reason I didn't do it is because we are not allowed to send data to OpenAI.

articles.title: GTA 6 rompe récords en Japón: vende más de 200.000 copias físicas y PS5 supera a Switch 2
articles.text:
El lanzamiento de GTA 6 en Japón impulsó las ventas de PlayStation 5 hasta superar por primera vez a Nintendo Switch 2, desde que la nueva consola de Nintendo llegó al mercado. El videojuego de Rockstar Games vendió 200.759 copias físicas durante su primera semana en el país asiático y se convirtió en el título más comercializado entre el 16 y el 22 de noviembre de 2026.
Los datos publicados por la revista japonesa Famitsu, y difundidos por el portal Gematsu, muestran el impacto que tuvo el estreno de Grand Theft Auto VI en el mercado japonés. El juego superó ampliamente al segundo puesto de la clasificación, ocupado por The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake, que registró 35.295 unidades vendidas.
El resultado también se reflejó en el mercado de consolas. Durante esa misma semana, PlayStation 5 comercializó 41.472 unidades, mientras que Nintendo Switch 2 alcanzó las 36.817. De esta manera, Sony consiguió liderar las ventas de hardware en Japón, un mercado donde Nintendo suele tener una presencia especialmente fuerte.
GTA 6 supera las 200.000 copias físicas en su estreno japonés
El desempeño comercial de GTA 6 destaca por la diferencia frente a los demás videojuegos de la clasificación. Sus 200.759 copias físicas representan una distancia considerable respecto al segundo lugar, que no llegó a las 36.000 unidades.
Aunque el título también está disponible para Xbox Series X|S, la mayoría de las ventas físicas japonesas corresponden a PlayStation 5. Esto se explica por la limitada presencia de las consolas de Microsoft en ese mercado, donde Sony y Nintendo concentran buena parte de la preferencia de los jugadores.
El segundo puesto fue para The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake, con 35.295 unidades. En tercer lugar quedó Nintendo Switch Sports Resort, un exclusivo de Switch 2 que vendió 10.486 copias.
La lista también incluye otros títulos conocidos, como Rhythm Paradise Groove, con 7.830 unidades, y Tomodachi Life: Una vida de ensueño, que registró 4.570 ventas. Por su parte, Splatoon Raiders alcanzó las 3.077 copias.
El resto del top 10 estuvo integrado por distintas versiones de Momotaro Dentetsu 2, además de Minecraft y Metaphor: ReFantazio para Nintendo Switch 2.
PS5 supera por primera vez a Nintendo Switch 2 en Japón
El impacto de GTA 6 no se limitó a las ventas del videojuego. La llegada del título también coincidió con un cambio en la clasificación semanal de consolas, en la que PlayStation 5 consiguió ocupar el primer lugar.
Según los datos de Famitsu, Sony vendió 41.472 unidades de PS5 durante la semana analizada. Nintendo Switch 2 quedó en segundo puesto con 36.817 consolas comercializadas, una diferencia de 4.655 unidades.
El tercer lugar fue para la primera Nintendo Switch, que registró 4.362 ventas. En tanto, Xbox Series X|S alcanzó 751 unidades, una cifra que vuelve a reflejar la menor participación de Microsoft en el mercado japonés.
Se trata de un resultado relevante porque Switch 2 había mantenido una posición destacada desde su lanzamiento. Sin embargo, la llegada de uno de los videojuegos más esperados de los últimos años modificó temporalmente el comportamiento de compra de los consumidores.
El lanzamiento de GTA 6 también impulsa las ventas de Rockstar
El desempeño en Japón se suma a los resultados comerciales que el videojuego ha conseguido en otros mercados. Según las cifras recogidas en el material de referencia, GTA 6 ya superó los 47 millones de copias vendidas y reunió a 39 millones de jugadores en PlayStation.
El interés también se ha reflejado en las ventas de las ediciones físicas en países como España y Francia, pese a que estas versiones se comercializan sin disco y sin mapa. Este formato mantiene una presentación física para los compradores, aunque el acceso al juego requiere descargarlo.
El éxito japonés confirma la capacidad de convocatoria de la franquicia, incluso en un mercado donde las preferencias suelen favorecer a los videojuegos de producción local y a las consolas de Nintendo.
Por ahora, las cifras corresponden a la semana comprendida entre el 16 y el 22 de noviembre. Será necesario observar los siguientes reportes de Famitsu para determinar si PlayStation 5 logra mantener el liderazgo frente a Switch 2 o si el resultado estuvo principalmente relacionado con el lanzamiento de GTA 6.

articles.title: Gemini Notebook (NotebookLM) lanza una función que ayuda a recordar información sin tanto esfuerzo
articles.text:
Google ha lanzado un cúmulo de funciones para Gemini Notebook que ayudarán a las personas que estudian o necesitan memorizar las cosas. La actualización más reciente añade soporte para imágenes en las tarjetas didácticas (flashcards). Esto ayudará a que los usuarios comprendan mejor los conceptos combinando información textual y gráfica.
De acuerdo con una publicación en su blog, las tarjetas didácticas ya pueden cargar elementos visuales desde las fuentes originales. Este agregado cambia el formato habitual de las flashcards, que se centraba en preguntas y respuestas de texto. Si bien este modelo funciona para practicar la memoria, en ocasiones nos encontramos con temas que son más difíciles de asimilar y es ahí en donde entra la parte visual.
Además de esto, la actualización también añade un cronómetro integrado para las sesiones de estudio. Los usuarios pueden activarlo mientras repasan sus tarjetas y tiene como objetivo medir cuánto tardan en recuperar la información. El cronómetro será de gran utilidad para quienes están por presentar un examen con límite de tiempo, ya que la IA permite simular condiciones similares a las de una evaluación real.
Por último, Gemini Notebook ya permite programar recordatorios para revisar las tarjetas generadas. Esta función está disponible dentro de la aplicación de Gemini Notebook para el móvil, desde la cual ajustarás las alertas para crear una rutina de estudio. Google afirma que estos recordatorios ayudan a mantener las sesiones periódicas de repaso sin depender únicamente de la memoria o disciplina personal.
Gemini Notebook también mejoró las notas y ahora son herramientas interactivas
La actualización llega a unos días de que Google lanzara una función para transformar notas, investigaciones y otras fuentes en webs interactivas. Los usuarios solo tienen que escribir "crear un sitio" dentro del chat de Gemini Notebook y añadir la descripción de lo que quieren construir. A partir de ese prompt, la IA genera una experiencia interactiva que puede abrirse en una pestaña independiente o compartir con otras personas.
Entre los ejemplos de uso que plantea Google se encuentra una tabla periódica interactiva para explicar cada uno de los elementos, una línea de tiempo histórica, paneles interactivos para explorar datos o herramientas para realizar seguimiento de proyectos. La complejidad del proyecto dependerá de las fuentes y de lo específico que seas al escribir el prompt.
Las nuevas funciones de las tarjetas didácticas y las páginas interactivas ya están disponibles para los clientes de Google Workspace, suscriptores de Workspace Individual y los usuarios con cuentas personales de Google. Como ocurre con cada lanzamiento, el despliegue es gradual y podría tardar en aplicarse en algunos países, por lo que tendrás que revisar más tarde si todavía no aparece en tu sesión.
Aunque el boom de NotebookLM cayó un poco cuando cambió de nombre, Google ha mantenido una estrategia de actualización constante. Gemini Notebook ha recibido varias funciones desde mediados de agosto, como la inteligencia experta, la grabadora de audio para capturar clases o notas, los cuadernos de estudio o las presentaciones y videos personalizables.

articles.title: 'Standoffish behavior, deliberate delays, heavy involvement from lawyers, and a constant theme: prioritizing corporate interests over those of their customers': HaveIBeenPwned's Troy Hunt reveals exactly what companies say when told they've been hacked
articles.text:
'Standoffish behavior, deliberate delays, heavy involvement from lawyers, and a constant theme: prioritizing corporate interests over those of their customers': HaveIBeenPwned's Troy Hunt reveals exactly what companies say when told they've been hacked
"Hack off, Troy"
- HaveIBeenPwned’s Troy Hunt has published a summary about why data breach disclosure is hard
- Hunt fed 8.5 years’ worth of email exchanges into Anthropic’s Claude, and used the AI to compose the summary
- Claude also identified seven patterns in the company responses, none of which were initially customer focused
Claude AI has been used to assess a tranche of disclosure communication emails between Troy Hunt and various hacked businesses over an 8.5 year period – and concluded that those organizations need to do better.
Publishing the results on his website HaveIBeenPwned, Hunt explained that using Claude was the “best way to highlight the behaviors” that he has seen repeated over the best part of a decade.
Using Claude to evaluate the exchanges has certainly done that, with the AI offering suggestions as to how businesses affected by data breaches could make communication and disclosure easier.
No way in
Claude’s analysis of Hunt’s emails covers a large amount of repetition, attempts to control narratives, and contact from legal teams.
Sadly, the customers affected by the data breaches are barely considered by the hacked businesses.
Several patterns are identified by Claude, such as an inability to find a way in to contact someone, a denial, and an open-ended investigation that apparently goes nowhere. It also spotted the lawyer-lead response, requests to review wording, and the bizarre response of “disclosure as harm” – essentially, suggesting Hunt sharing the breach is worse than the breach itself (ignoring the fact that the data is being traded on the dark web).
Organizations interested in the results should, says the AI, publish contact details for their security teams, along with a series of steps that are basically asking organizations to be responsible.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Disclosure experiences
Covering so much correspondence for the report, Claude concludes that the organizations need incentives to agree to disclosure and inform their customers. It notes “every day without a public statement is a day without bad headlines…” while for those affected “every one of those days is a day they're exposed without knowing it.”
Referring to the deep dive into his emails by Claude, Hunt remarked: “Hundreds of emails back and forth with companies that had had data breaches, and some very common patterns. I knew the emails contained standoffish behavior, deliberate delays, heavy involvement from lawyers, and a constant theme: prioritizing corporate interests over those of their customers.”
While the results didn’t necessarily surprise him, revisiting so many disclosure warning events did have an effect. “I didn't know just how stark it would be to read such a candid analysis of my own emails, nor how frustrating it would be to relive many of those disclosure experiences.”
Troy Hunt performs one of the greatest services online, and everyone should be extremely grateful for HaveIBeenPwned.

articles.title: AI Search Is Picking Local Businesses. Will It Pick Yours?
articles.text:
Ask ChatGPT to find a physio near Parramatta and it does not hand you ten blue links. It writes a short answer and names a few clinics.
Google now does something similar with AI Overviews at the top of many searches. For a small business, being named in that paragraph is the new front page.
Photo by Sanket Mishra on Unsplash
Alt text: a person holding a cell phone with a chat app on the screen
The work of getting into those answers has a name: AI SEO. Local SEO Specialist is one Australian service that offers it alongside Google Business Profile and directory work for local firms. You can run many of the checks yourself first, though. This guide shows how AI answers pick businesses and what to test this week.
How Many Australians Already Ask AI First?
More than you might think. The auDA Digital Lives of Australians 2026 report found that 61% of consumers had used AI for some purpose, up from 56% in 2025. Among small businesses, the figure rose from 64% to 72%.
The same survey asked what people use it for. The top use was to analyse or summarise content, such as answering questions, cited by 35% of consumer AI users. That is exactly the habit that turns “who fixes air con in Newcastle?” into a chat prompt.
The research polled 2,080 adults and 408 small business owners or managers. Fieldwork ran from 27 February to 5 March 2026.
Other data points the same way. Results from a national survey on Australia’s AI divide put recent generative AI use at 45.6% of Australians. That study drew on more than 5,500 adults surveyed in 2024, including people in remote and regional areas.
What Is Different About an AI Answer?
A classic search page shows many options and lets you choose. An AI answer makes a shortlist for you. Google describes its AI Overviews as “a snapshot of key information” with links to explore more. It says the feature is available in over 120 countries and territories.
| Result type | What the searcher sees | How many businesses appear | 
| Classic organic results | Ten or so web pages | Many, ranked by page | 
| Google map pack | A map and three listings | Usually three | 
| AI Overview | A written summary with source links | Often a handful | 
| Chatbot answer | A conversational reply | Sometimes only one or two | 
The fewer slots there are, the more each one matters. A café that sits fourth in the map pack can vanish from an AI reply entirely.
Where Do AI Tools Get Facts About a Local Business?
AI tools do not visit your shop. They piece together a picture from what is already online. Local SEO Specialist’s own AI SEO page puts it plainly: the AI pulls information from websites, directories, reviews and articles it trusts.
Alt text: Customer pays cashier at a counter in a shop
That means the inputs are things a business owner can see and fix:
- Your website, especially service pages that say what you do and where.
- Your Google Business Profile, including categories, hours and photos.
- Directory listings, which should carry the same name, address and phone number.
- Customer reviews, and the words people use in them.
- Mentions in local news, industry sites and community pages.
Personal AI agents are also arriving fast. Meta’s launch of Muse in Australia is one example of an assistant that may soon book or compare services for users. Those agents will draw on the same public details.
What Should a Small Business Check This Week?
You can audit your AI visibility in an afternoon with a phone and a notepad. Run these steps in order:
- Ask ChatGPT and Google the questions a customer would ask, with your suburb named.
- Note whether your business appears, and copy any wrong hours, prices or services.
- Open your Google Business Profile and confirm the primary category matches your main service.
- Search your business name on three or four directories and compare every detail.
- Read your top service page aloud and check it names the suburbs you actually cover.
- Turn on multi-factor sign-in for the Google account that owns your profile.
Step six matters more than it looks. A hijacked profile can change your phone number in minutes. Multi-factor authentication is part of the Essential Eight for small and medium Australian businesses, a set of baseline cyber controls.
Repeat the prompts once a month. AI answers change as the tools update and as competitors improve their own details.
When Does It Make Sense to Bring In a Specialist?
Some fixes are quick, like updating hours. Others take steady monthly work, such as earning mentions on trusted sites or rebuilding thin service pages. That is where outside help can pay off.
Local SEO Specialist publishes one example. Its Morgan Insurance Brokers case study reports that visits from ChatGPT grew from 194 to 529, comparing July to September 2025 with the same months in 2026. Enquiry actions from ChatGPT rose from 73 to 187 over that period. The site credits clear service pages, consistent business details and mentions on trusted websites.
The service is run by Caleb Johnstone from the Gold Coast, and he caps his client list at 30. His AI SEO packages cover ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews and Google AI Mode. For a business that has run the checklist above and found gaps, that kind of focused help is a reasonable next step.
Treating AI Answers Like a New Shop Window
AI search will not replace Google Maps overnight, but it is already shaping first impressions. The businesses it names tend to have tidy, consistent and well-described details across the web. Start with the six checks, fix what you can, and revisit the prompts each month.
Frequently Asked Questions
Can a Business Control What ChatGPT Says About It?
Not directly. The tool writes its own answer from public sources. A business can only shape it by keeping those sources accurate and detailed.
Do AI Overviews Show Up for Local Searches In Australia?
Google says AI Overviews are available in over 120 countries and territories. Whether one appears depends on the search, so test your own key questions.
How Often Should a Business Check What AI Says About It?
Once a month is a sensible rhythm. Check sooner after you move premises, change hours or add a new service.
Is AI SEO Different From Regular Local SEO?
It builds on the same groundwork, such as accurate listings and strong service pages. The difference is the goal of being mentioned and cited inside AI-written answers.

articles.title: develoPPP Ventures opens call for SA startups, offering $110k in matching funding
articles.text:
develoPPP Ventures has opened applications for its latest South African cohort, which will see selected startups receive EUR100,000 (US$110,000) in non-dilutive funding.
develoPPP Ventures has backed 178 businesses across Africa, including 11 investments in South Africa. The current call is also open in Kenya, Rwanda, Tanzania, Egypt and Nigeria.
The 12th cohort is run by DEG Impulse, a subsidiary of German development finance institution DEG, with VC4A and Jozi Angels as partners. It is funded by Germany’s Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ).
South African startups with proof of concept and early revenues, that can demonstrate a path to operational break-even within three years, and have secured, or are in advanced talks for, funding, are invited to apply.
The funding uses a 1:1 matching model, so startups must raise at least the same amount from other qualifying sources, including private investors. Jozi Angels will connect founders with angel and venture investors to help them meet that requirement.
“Through the develoPPP Ventures programme, we equip growth-stage entrepreneurs in South Africa with catalytic matching capital and bespoke technical support,” said Tasneem Natha, chief operating officer of Jozi Angels.
Applications close on December 31 and can be submitted here.

articles.title: WhatsApp lance sa fonction de messages planifiés
articles.text:
Après plusieurs semaines de tests dans les versions bêta de ses applications, WhatsApp officialise l’arrivée de sa fonction de planification de messages. L’arrivée de cette nouveauté permet à l’application de messagerie d’être enfin à niveau face aux applications de messagerie de Google et d’Apple.
Des messages planifiés déployés progressivement
L’arrivée des messages planifiés dans WhatsApp vient combler un manque de longue date. La fonction faisait d’autant plus partie de celles qui étaient les plus demandées par les utilisateurs. Concrètement, elle vous permet de rédiger en avance votre missive avec la possibilité de planifier son envoi entre 10 minutes et 14 jours plus tard.
La fonction, qui s’active en effectuant un appui long sur le bouton d’envoi du message, peut être utilisée aussi bien dans les conversations individuelles que dans les conversations de groupe. En plus du texte, vous pourrez y inclure des photos et des vidéos comme avec n’importe quel message.
Sécurité oblige, les messages planifiés profitent du même niveau de confidentialité que les autres et sont chiffrés de bout en bout. La bonne nouvelle, c’est que la planification de vos messages n’est pas soumise au fonctionnement de votre smartphone. WhatsApp précise en effet que « Même si votre téléphone est éteint ou à court de batterie, votre message planifié sera envoyé au moment que vous avez choisi. »/
Vous pourrez ensuite gérer les messages planifiés d’une conversation en vous rendant directement dans les informations détaillées de celle-ci. Vous aurez ainsi la possibilité d’annuler l’envoi d’un message planifié ou encore d’en corriger le contenu.
Le déploiement de cette nouvelle fonctionnalité est en cours et se fera, a priori, de manière progressive. WhatsApp a indiqué sur son blog que les messages planifiés « seront déployés dans le monde entier dans les semaines à venir ».

articles.title: La nueva tele sin cables de Hisense con pantalla Hi-QLED y hasta 10 horas de batería

Los televisores han pasado históricamente por un mismo guión: se anclan a la pared o a un mueble del salón y ahí se quedan. Hisense busca romper esa dinámica en España con el lanzamiento del 32S6S, un televisor portátil de su familia lifestyle que integra batería propia y tecnología Hi-QLED para funcionar sin depender en todo momento de una toma de corriente.
El planteamiento parte de una idea sencilla: acercar la pantalla a donde estés (en otra habitación, en la terraza o en el jardín) y permitir incluso sacarla de casa en una escapada o llevarla a una segunda residencia. En Amazon, está disponible por 1.399 euros.

Hasta 10 horas sin enchufe y panel Hi-QLED
El principal argumento del Hisense 32S6S frente a un televisor tradicional es su batería integrada, con una autonomía que promete hasta 10 horas. Esa cifra abre la puerta a ver una película, seguir un partido, jugar o abrir plataformas de streaming sin tener que buscar un enchufe o tirar de alargadores en zonas exteriores.
En el apartado visual recurre a la tecnología Hi-QLED, enfocada a ofrecer mayor precisión cromática y un nivel de brillo superior para mantener una imagen legible tanto en interiores como en espacios más iluminados. Qué aporta este formato y qué conviene tener en cuenta
Más allá del reclamo de movilidad, llevar el televisor de un espacio a otro plantea matices prácticos que vale la pena sopesar antes de verlo como un sustituto directo de una tele fija. La autonomía máxima de hasta 10 horas depende, eso sí, del brillo y del tipo de uso y un equipo portátil de este tipo suele brillar más como segunda pantalla versátil o de apoyo que como televisor principal para un salón grande.

articles.title: IA : Microsoft alerte sur une vague de pannes à venir dans la tech
articles.text:
L'explosion de la puissance de l'IA oblige les systèmes à une mise à jour très rapide. Ce qui, selon le président de Microsoft, va entraîner nécessairement un certain nombre de problèmes.
La puissance de l'intelligence artificielle se fait aujourd'hui surtout sentir dans le secteur de la cybersécurité, avec la capacité exceptionnelle de l'IA à détecter les vulnérabilités dans les systèmes. Il est donc nécessaire de rapidement patcher des systèmes quelques fois assez vieux, et pour Brad Smith, le président de Microsoft, il faudra s'attendre à ce que ça accroisse temporairement le risque de panne !
L'IA va découvrir de très nombreuses vulnérabilités dans les systèmes ces prochains mois
Brad Smith, le président de Microsoft, s'est ces derniers jours exprimé dans un entretien avec CBS News sur la question de la cybersécurité aujourd'hui. Il a ainsi expliqué que l'arrivée de l'IA obligeait à une transformation, sans précédent dans sa vitesse, des systèmes informatiques.
« Partout dans le monde, les acteurs disposant des moyens technologiques nécessaires utilisent ces [IA] pour identifier les failles et les corriger à un rythme sans précédent, afin de devancer les cybercriminels et de les empêcher de s'en servir pour pirater les systèmes » a-t-il expliqué. Mais en voulant prendre de vitesse les cybercriminels, on peut se créer de nouveaux problèmes.
La pression mise sur les systèmes par les correctifs accroît les possibilités de panne
Brad Smith note en effet que ce rythme d'enfer sera appliqué sur des infrastructures qui peuvent être assez souvent anciennes, et que la vitesse à laquelle les correctifs doivent être appliqués empêche de tester dans les meilleurs conditions les modifications apportées au code. Résultat, « on augmente alors le risque que quelque chose tourne mal ». Brad Smith appelle ce phénomène, les « effets d'entraînement liés à l'IA » (« AI ripple effects »).
Reste que, de toute manière, les divisions IT à travers le monde n'ont pas d'autre choix que de rapidement se mettre à jour, malgré les risques évoqués. Microsoft avait en effet déjà expliqué, dans une publication officielle portant sur la cybersécurité en date du 19 novembre, le fait que les cybercrminels découvraient de plus en plus de failles logicielles avant même que les différentes organisations n'aient le temps d'apporter de correctif. Raison pour laquelle sûrement on observe toutes ces grandes cyberattaques actuellement.
Source : Wccftech

articles.title: Victime d’une cyberattaque, l’Agence France-Presse ferme brutalement l’accès à une de ses plateformes : voici ce que l’on sait
articles.text:
« En maintenance », « Under maintenance », « En mantenimiento »… Depuis le 26 novembre 2026, c’est le message qu’affiche AFP Forum, la plateforme sur laquelle les médias abonnés à l’Agence France-Presse consultent et téléchargent ses dépêches, ses photos et ses vidéos. Pour les rédactions françaises et étrangères qui puisent chaque jour dans ce flux, l’outil est devenu inaccessible du jour au lendemain.
L’AFP a confirmé avoir pris elle-même cette décision après une cyberattaque survenue dans la nuit de mercredi à jeudi. Dans un message interne relayé par Le Monde, la direction explique que l’intrusion a été repérée vers 1 h 30, heure de Paris. Ses équipes ont alors immédiatement isolé la plateforme « pour la protéger ». Le site reste fermé par précaution, et aucune date de rétablissement n’a été annoncée.
Les auteurs de l’attaque restent inconnus
« À ce stade, nous ne disposons d’aucune information sur l’identité des auteurs de cette attaque », indique la direction, qui précise qu’une enquête est en cours avec l’appui d’experts extérieurs.
L’agence n’a précisé ni la manière dont les pirates sont entrés, ni s’ils ont pu accéder à des données. Elle ne sait pas non plus qui est derrière l’opération.
En attendant, l’AFP assure avoir proposé des solutions de repli à ses abonnés pour qu’ils continuent de recevoir ses contenus.

articles.title: Atombombe im Erdorbit: Warum eine Zündung Starlink lahmlegen und GPS verschonen würde
articles.text:
Atombombe im All: Warum eine einzige Zündung fast alle erdnahen Satelliten ausschalten würde
Eine einzige Kernwaffenexplosion in 500 Kilometern Höhe könnte heute binnen einer Woche fast sämtliche erdnahen Satelliten außer Betrieb setzen. Zu diesem Ergebnis kommt eine auf Arxiv veröffentlichte Vorabstudie der US-amerikanischen Hochschulen University of Wisconsin-Madison und Princeton University.
Anlass sind Berichte über ein russisches Nuklearsatelliten-Projekt, vor dem der US-Militärgeheimdienst Defense Intelligence Agency aus Washington Ende Oktober warnte. Anders als in der frühen Raumfahrt umkreisen die Erde nach Daten des US-Astrophysikers Jonathan McDowell inzwischen über 17.200 aktive Satelliten.
Was der US-Atomtest Starfish Prime 1962 bei Satelliten anrichtete
Wie eine solche Waffe im All wirkt, zeigte am 9. Juli 1962 der US-Test „Starfish Prime“ in 400 Kilometern Höhe über dem Nordpazifik. Der gezündete Sprengkopf besaß eine Sprengkraft von 1,4 Megatonnen, was 1,4 Millionen Tonnen herkömmlichem Sprengstoff entspricht.
Durch die zurückbleibende Strahlung fiel binnen Monaten ein Drittel der damals rund 24 Satelliten aus – darunter „Telstar 1“, der erst am Folgetag startete. Direkt beim Zünden erloschen auf dem 1.450 Kilometer entfernten Hawaii laut der Defense Threat Reduction Agency aus dem US-Bundesstaat Virginia zudem rund 300 Straßenlaternen.
Wegen dieser schwer kalkulierbaren Folgen verboten die Atommächte Kernwaffentests im All 1963 vertraglich und untersagten 1967 im Weltraumvertrag auch deren Stationierung. Die Messdaten von 1962 dienen bis heute als Grundlage, um Risiken für große Satellitennetze, wie jenes des US-Raumfahrtunternehmens SpaceX zu berechnen.
Warum das Erdmagnetfeld für Starlink und andere Satelliten zur Falle wird
Im luftleeren Weltraum entsteht bei einer Atomexplosion keine Druckwelle wie in der dichteren Atmosphäre auf der Erde. Der anfängliche Röntgen- und Gammastrahlungsblitz trifft nur jene Flugkörper, die sich im Moment der Zündung zufällig in direkter Sichtlinie befinden.
Die eigentliche Zerstörungswirkung stammt von schnellen Elektronen aus dem radioaktiven Zerfall der Bombe, die das Magnetfeld der Erde wie ein Käfig einsperrt. Es bildet sich ein künstlicher Strahlungsgürtel, den Satelliten immer wieder durchqueren, bis ihre Solarzellen und empfindlichen Computerchips im All versagen.
Wie das Team um den Physikstudenten Zachary Petersen und den Assistenzprofessor Sébastien Philippe vorrechnet, entscheidet der Zündort über die Stärke dieses Gürtels. Über dem Indischen Ozean schluckt die obere Atmosphäre die Elektronen schnell, während das schwache Erdmagnetfeld über dem Südatlantik rund 47 Prozent festhält.
Ausfall im niedrigen Erdorbit verschont GPS und Galileo
Bei einer Megatonne Sprengkraft über dem Südatlantik fallen im Modell binnen sieben Tagen rund 98 Prozent der über 13.000 erdnahen Satelliten aus. Das betrifft den niedrigen Erdorbit unterhalb von 2.000 Kilometern Höhe, den Internetdienste wie Starlink sowie Erdbeobachtungs- und Aufklärungssatelliten nutzen.
Navigationssatelliten für GPS oder Galileo kreisen dagegen in über 20.000 Kilometern Höhe und bleiben ebenso verschont wie Wettersatelliten in rund 36.000 Kilometern. Im niedrigen Orbit können ausgefallene Satelliten nicht mehr ausweichen, was laut Modell in zehn Jahren 26 Zusammenstöße und rund 3.900 Trümmerteile erzeugt.
Zwar bremst die dünne Restatmosphäre tiefer fliegende Wracks ähnlich wie bei Sonnenstürmen im Starlink-Orbit allmählich ab und lässt sie verglühen. „Die Wiederherstellung von Diensten im Orbit würde mehr erfordern als den bloßen Ersatz der verlorenen Raumfahrzeuge“, warnen die Autor:innen wegen der verbleibenden Strahlung.
Warum Schutzschilde und Abwehrraketen im All kaum helfen
Handelsübliche Satelliten überstehen zwar gewöhnliche Teilchenstürme der Sonne, sind aber nicht für künstliche Strahlungsgürtel ausgelegt. „Technisch gesehen könnte man Satelliten abschirmen oder härten“, sagt Direktorin Kari Bingen bei der Denkfabrik Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Weil 90 Prozent der Satelliten kommerziell betrieben werden, rechnet sich der hohe Kostenaufwand für schwere Schutzmäntel laut Bingen für private Betreiber:innen kaum. Auch militärisch greifen Abfangraketen oder Laser im Orbit kaum, da ein Nuklearsatellit sofort zünden kann und nur während des Raketenstarts verwundbar ist.
Was BND und Bundeswehr zu Russlands Plänen sagen
Nach Informationen des Bundesnachrichtendienstes in Berlin lagert bei Moskau ein montierter Satellit namens „Sputnik-S“. Das berichtet auch The Guardian unter Verweis auf Sicherheitskreise. Bereits die bloße Stationierung einer Kernwaffe in der Erdumlaufbahn wäre nach Angaben des Berliner Auswärtigen Amtes ein „eklatanter Bruch des Weltraumvertrages“.
Da sich Deutschland gegen neuen Weltraumschrott verpflichtet hat, verzichtet die Bundeswehr auf Trümmer erzeugende Abschusswaffen im All. Stattdessen plant das Bonner Kommando Cyber- und Informationsraum laut Tagesspiegel zwei Bataillone, um Satelliten durch „Stören, Blenden und Hacken“ auszuschalten.
Welche Grenzen die Berechnung zu Atomwaffen im Orbit hat
Bei der Einordnung des berechneten Szenarios gelten deutliche Einschränkungen, weil die Vorabstudie noch keine unabhängige Fachbegutachtung durchlaufen hat. Zudem unterstellt das Modell einheitlich zwei Millimeter Aluminiumschutz und eine Ausfallgrenze von 400 Gray, dem Hundertfachen einer für Menschen tödlichen Strahlendosis.
Kleinere Sprengköpfe richten geringere Schäden an, wie ein Bericht des Forschungsinstituts Rand Corporation aus Santa Monica im US-Bundesstaat Kalifornien belegt. Bei 110 Kilotonnen Sprengkraft, gut einem Zehntel einer Megatonne, wären rund 20 Prozent der erdnahen Satelliten über Monate gefährdet, aber Stromnetze am Boden verschont.
Unabhängig belegt sind die Geheimdienstangaben nicht, zumal Moskau die Vorwürfe laut der US-Stiftung Secure World Foundation zurückweist. Zudem ließe sich eine heimliche Bewaffnung im Orbit laut einer Studie der US-amerikanischen Hochschule Virginia Tech nur mit Prüfsatelliten aus kurzer Distanz nachweisen.
Im Ernstfall würde der künstliche Strahlungsgürtel in alle Richtungen wirken und russische sowie chinesische Satelliten ebenso ausschalten wie westliche Netze. „Nuklearwaffen sind in erster Linie politische Waffen“, ordnete daher der Politikwissenschaftler Frank Sauer von der Universität der Bundeswehr München gegenüber T-Online ein.

articles.title: Capri Global raises $30M in bonds from BlueOrchard Microfinance
articles.text:
Capri Global raises $30M in bonds from BlueOrchard Microfinance
The fundraise will support Capri Global's MSME lending business and expand access to credit for businesses across India.
Capri Global Capital Limited, a retail-focused non-banking financial company (NBFC), has raised $30 million from the BlueOrchard Microfinance Fund, managed by impact investment firm BlueOrchard Finance Ltd.
According to a company statement, this marks Capri Global’s first-ever fundraise from an impact fund. The proceeds will be deployed towards financing activities for micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), as well as supporting the company’s growth opportunities.
The fundraising was carried out through a private placement of senior secured, US dollar-denominated bonds with a tenor of 36 months and a maturity date in November 2029. BlueOrchard was the sole investor in the issuance, and the bonds will be listed on NSE IFSC Limited.
“India’s MSME sector has significant potential to drive economic growth, entrepreneurship and employment. Realising this potential will require a stronger credit ecosystem that can meet the diverse financing needs of businesses at every stage of their growth. Institutional capital and long-term partnerships will be key to this effort. Our partnership with BlueOrchard strengthens our ability to deepen our reach in the MSME segment and support a more inclusive credit landscape,” said Rajesh Sharma, Managing Director, Capri Global Capital.
Capri Global said this fundraise further diversifies its liability profile demonstrating the ability to access a broad range of domestic and international funding sources.
Alongside development and impact-focused investors, the company’s funding sources include domestic banks and financial institutions, domestic bond issuances, co-lending arrangements, direct assignment transactions and international capital market programmes.
“For impact investing to deliver meaningful outcomes, capital must be channelled through institutions with the ability to reach businesses that are critical to local economies. Our investment in Capri Global reflects our approach of partnering with financial institutions to support the flow of capital to this segment, while contributing to broader economic resilience and sustainable growth,” said Normunds Mizis, Chief Credit Officer, BlueOrchard Finance.

articles.title: Científicos recuperan bajo la Antártida un archivo geológico de entre 17 y 19 millones de años tras dos intentos fallidos y atravesar 523 metros de hielo
articles.text:
Bajo el hielo de la Antártida occidental se encuentran sedimentos que son los que nos indican cómo era esta zona antes de que quedara bajo el hielo. Para ello han tenido que trabajar en un campamento que queda a unos 700 km de las bases antárticas más cercanas. En Crary Ice Rise han conseguido sacar un núcleo de 228 m de longitud de barro y roca. Hasta ahora habían fallado en dos intentos.
Tras perforar 523 metros de hielo, han conseguido recuperar materiales de millones de años de antigüedad. Han analizado los microfósiles de los sedimentos y los más antiguos se remontan hasta hace entre 17 y 19 millones de años. Se trata de los últimos 20 m de la perforación sedimentaria. La mayor parte del núcleo está entre los 7 y los 10 millones de años.
Esto forma parte del proyecto internacional SWAIS2C, que trata de conocer la sensibilidad de la capa de hielo de la Antártida occidental ante un calentamiento de 2 grados Celsius. Los responsables del proyecto pretenden conocer qué pasó en esta zona en épocas cálidas del pasado para poder mejorar las predicciones de su respuesta al calentamiento global.
Primero el hielo, después los sedimentos
Para ello, primero han tenido que crear un agujero en el hielo mediante una técnica de perforación con agua caliente. Una vez hecho el agujero, han podido colocar las tuberías para extraer los materiales del subsuelo. En el comunicado de la expedición destacan que han trabajado en rotación durante las 24 horas del día.
Extraído un segmento, lo describen en el campo y toman fotografías. A medida que van perforando, ven las diferencias entre los diferentes estratos. Por un lado, hay materiales que corresponden a depósitos bajo el hielo sobre el terreno y, por otro, se pueden ver otros sedimentos que muestran que eran otras condiciones marinas.
De esta manera se ha obtenido el núcleo sedimentario más largo que se ha recuperado bajo una capa de hielo. Según la Escuela Politécnica Federal de Zúrich (ETH), esto es muy útil porque muestra una sucesión de ambientes que van desde los depósitos bajo el hielo hasta los de un océano abierto o plataforma flotante. De esta manera se puede estudiar la evolución de este mismo lugar.
Qué cuentan los fósiles sobre su edad y entorno
En un primer momento, la expedición estimaba que podía llegar hasta los 23 millones de años. Sin embargo, se han ido corrigiendo estos valores. Esto es gracias a los ensambles de especies de diatomeas. Estas son algas microscópicas que dejan restos que permiten datar los sedimentos.
También se pueden encontrar restos de conchas o de organismos que requieren de luz. De esta manera podemos saber que se dieron momentos de océano abierto en una zona que está ahora bajo cientos de metros de hielo.
Hasta ahora, las predicciones sobre la respuesta del hielo ante el calentamiento se basaban fundamentalmente en datos satelitales y registros geológicos de zonas cercanas (por ejemplo, bajo plataformas flotantes) o bien en el propio mar de Ross y océano Austral. Con este nuevo núcleo tenemos una secuencia directamente en el margen de la capa de hielo.
Reconstruir el retroceso para mejorar las previsiones
Las observaciones satelitales (que es lo que recoge el proyecto) muestran que esta zona de la Antártida occidental viene perdiendo masa a un ritmo que se ha acelerado en las últimas décadas. Si se derritiera totalmente, produciría un aumento medio global del nivel del mar de entre 4 y 5 metros.
Para estudiar los cambios en nuestro planeta, los investigadores emplean modelos. Para ello deben disponer de datos que les permitan validar sus predicciones. Mediante estos sedimentos van a poder comparar qué es lo que los modelos indican que haría el hielo frente a lo que realmente ocurrió en aquellos episodios en los que la temperatura media global superó en más de 2 °C los niveles preindustriales.
Por otro lado, deben seguir afinando las edades de las diferentes capas. También deben reconstruir las temperaturas oceánicas en los períodos de aguas abiertas. Esto les va a permitir saber qué procesos fueron los que desencadenaron el retroceso de la capa de hielo.

EasyEquities locks investors out after cyber attack
Image Source: Tenor
South Africa’s financial companies have had an uncomfortable week. Yesterday, we told you how SA Home Loans, a mortgage lender, suffered a data breach. Now, EasyEquities, the platform that helps South Africans buy shares of South African, US, UK, and Australian companies, has reported a security incident.
As a precaution, the company reportedly locked customers out of their investment accounts.
What happened? On Thursday, EasyEquities restricted logins while specialists investigated a system incident. Customers couldn’t check their portfolios or trade normally. Access through banking apps, including Capitec and Absa, was also disrupted.
Explain like I’m new here: EasyEquities lets people invest in shares, including small pieces of expensive stocks. Being locked out doesn’t mean your money has disappeared. But it can stop you from selling when prices fall or buying when opportunities appear.
State of play: In a Thursday evening update, EasyEquities said all customer funds were accounted for. It’s still investigating whether personal information was accessed. Customers can contact its trading desk to place certain trades, although withdrawals may be delayed.
Between the lines: There’s a familiar name here. In September, EasyEquities and SA Home Loans were affected by a breach at RelyComply, a company that verifies customers’ identities. Both companies have now reported separate incidents involving their own systems. EasyEquities said its latest incident is unrelated to September’s breach or its recent app redesign.
Zoom out: Investment platforms promise convenience and control. Even when your money is safe, being unable to access it tests both promises. Watching the markets move while you’re locked out is nobody’s idea of easy investing.

Visa opens Cameroon office to grow its digital payments business
Visa executives at the opening ceremony on November 23. Image Source: Visa
Visa has opened a representative office in Douala, Cameroon. The payments giant said it wants to work with banks, fintechs, merchants, and government agencies on expanding card acceptance, e-commerce, financial inclusion, and payment security.
Explain like I’m new here: Visa has been distributing prepaid cards in Cameroon since 2012. A representative office signals its conviction in the Central African payments bloc.
Visa’s new Douala office is its fifth in West and Central Africa, joining Lagos, Accra, Abidjan, and Kinshasa. These offices serve 23 countries, giving Visa a stronger local presence in a region where mobile money dominates everyday digital payments.
Look at the opportunity: As of 2024, debit cards had a 7.8% penetration in Cameroon—about 1.29 million adults used cards, according to the World Bank’s Global Findex. The Bank of Central African States (BEAC), Central Africa’s apex bank, said 1.42 million cards were actively used.
However, cards remain a relatively unpopular payment method in Cameroon, with mobile money dominating more than half of usage. At least 1 in every 2 Cameroonian adults used mobile money.
But even with low adoption, cards remain a big part of Visa’s strategy. Importantly, it doesn’t need to replace mobile money. Visa is already a top card service provider in many African markets. Visa’s opportunity f is handling payments mobile money may not be able to touch: international payments.
