articles.title: La teoría de la conspiración del "pucherazo" domina la recta final de la campaña electoral en España
articles.text:
Lo lógico (lo esperable al menos) es que a estas alturas de la campaña estuviésemos hablando de vivienda, migración, política social, infraestructura ferroviaria o, en fin, cualquiera de las cuestiones que han marcado la agenda de las últimas semanas. La realidad, a 72 horas de sacar las urnas, es que gran parte del foco se centra en otra obsesión: el riesgo de pucherazo, una adulteración de los resultados del 29N por parte del Gobierno. Su fantasma lo agita la oposición y gana fuerza en redes, apuntando a la línea de flotación de la democracia.
La pregunta es... ¿Realmente representa una amenaza real?
“Absoluta de desconfianza”. El entrecomillado es de la presidenta madrileña, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, quien hace unos días, durante una entrevista en la COPE, se mostró “preocupada” por la “sensación absoluta de desconfianza” que le genera el 29N. Y no por lo que dicen los sondeos.
La líder popular habló de “circunstancias totalmente anómalas” que afectan al registro de votantes. “Todos habíamos ido siempre a elecciones sabiendo cuál era el censo. Ahora por la ‘ley de nietos’, de abuelos o de primos, por las regularizaciones, no se sabe”, insistió la dirigente.
¿Es la única? Aunque Ayuso encarna la oposición más dura del PP, no es la única líder de la formación que ha sembrado dudas sobre la limpieza del 29N. El propio Alberto Núñez Feijóo afirma estar “preocupado”: “Sánchez y limpieza electoral son dos conceptos bastante contradictorios”, deslizó el domingo en otra entrevista en Onda Cero. Antes ya había acusado al Gobierno de hacer “ingeniería electoral” con la ‘ley de nietos’, que permitió a los descendientes de exiliados del franquismo obtener la nacionalidad española.
El fantasma del “pucherazo” y “fraude electoral” lo agita también Vox, lo que ha llevado al presidente Pedro Sánchez a acusar a ambas formaciones (PP y Vox) de practicar “un trumpismo preventivo”. “Tengo dudas de que reconozcan el resultado electoral si no suman”, confiesa hoy en El País. No deja de ser curioso, dado que la mayoría de los sondeos (salvo el CIS) dibujan un escenario en el que Feijóo y Abascal alcanzarían una mayoría suficiente para gobernar.
El eco en TikTok. El relato del pucherazo no solo se teje en las entrevistas. También avanza en redes. Lo ha confirmado el analista Marcelino Madrigal en un informe divulgado por Newtral y que se basa en el análisis de casi 1.200 vídeos de contenido electoral publicados en TikTok entre el 2 de octubre y 22 de noviembre. ¿Qué muestra su estudio? Tras analizar piezas que usaban hashtags como ‘pucherazo’, ‘29N’ o ‘ley de nietos’, Madrigal llegó a dos conclusiones.
La primera, que el 21% de los vídeos estudiados difunden la idea del fraude electoral. La segunda, que esas piezas se centran sobre todo en nueve obsesiones: el voto por correo, la ‘ley de nietos’, el papel de ciertas instituciones (Gobierno o Junta Electoral Central), el censo, las papeletas y las urnas, la influencia de Indra y el DNI digital durante el recuento de votos, el CIS, el voto de los residentes en el extranjero (CERA) y las comparaciones con Venezuela.
Más allá de las redes. A pesar de que el 29N se ha visto marcado por el accidente de Urda, la dimisión de Óscar Puente y una huelga general, una búsqueda rápida en la hemeroteca demuestra que esos nueve temas han marcado gran parte del debate, alimentando la narrativa del pucherazo. Aunque las acusaciones de “ingeniería electoral” pueden remontarse al menos al verano, de las obsesiones identificadas por Madrigal quizás la que más fuerza ha ganado en las últimas semanas es la que gira en torno a la limpieza del voto por correo.
¿El motivo? En gran medida las dudas sembradas desde parte de la oposición, que incluso ha pedido a sus votantes que depositen el voto en persona. El propio Feijóo llegó a arrojar dudas sobre el presidente de Correos, Pedro Saura, hombre confianza de Pedro Sánchez. “Confío plenamente en los carteros de Correos. Confío plenamente en los empleados públicos de Correos. No confío en los directivos de Correos”.
Del padrón al DNI digital… A las dudas sobre la fiabilidad del voto por correo se han sumado en las últimas semanas otras acusaciones y bulos, como ha identificado Madrigal en TikTok: se ha hablado de empadronamientos “fraudulentos”, del uso de Indra para alterar los resultados de las urnas, de que quienes usen el DNI digital para identificarse el domingo computarán automáticamente como votantes del PSOE o del reparto de tarjetas censales de personas fallecidas, entre un largo etcétera de teorías sobre pucherazos.
…Y de la ley de nietos a las cajas. La más reciente afecta a la participación de los españoles que residen en el extranjero, el voto CERA. Se ha hablado de un menor control de los sufragios, falta de papeletas y sobre todo, en los últimos días, desde que es posible votar en los consulados, del uso de cajas de cartón para recoger documentación electoral. Quizás por esa razón, el sábado las embajadas españolas de algunas ciudades se encontraron con largas colas de votantes que querían entregar sus papeletas en mano.
Ni siquiera eso ha despejado las dudas. El hecho de que algunos consulados utulicen cajas de cartón para recoger la documentación de quienes tienen su derecho a voto suspendido por el Supremo ha despertado la “inquietud” del PP. Las suspicacias se han extendido también a las redes, donde se cuestiona su legalidad, se critica la falta de vigilancia y se especula con una hipotética mezcla de sufragios. Irónicamente, la medida responde a una orden del Supremo.
Desmontando bulos. La realidad es que gran parte de esos relatos sobre el riesgo de pucherazo son difíciles de sostener. Por ejemplo, desde hace días circulan en redes mensajes sobre supuestos “empadronamientos ilegales” de inmigrantes irregulares para alterar los resultados del 29N o el uso fraudulento de tarjetas censales de personas fallecidas. Ambas teorías tienen puntos débiles evidentes.
Para votar no llega con estar censado en un municipio, es necesario tener la nacionalidad española y figurar en el censo electoral del 1 de agosto de 2026, que suma 38,73 millones de personas. Es decir, el empadronamiento es un paso necesario, pero por sí solo no da acceso a las urnas. Además, cualquier persona que quiera depositar su papeleta debe identificarse con un documento oficial válido. De nada sirve presentarse con la tarjeta censal de un fallecido.
¿Y el DNI digital? Sobre si el DNI digital podría o no usarse para favorecer al partido en el Gobierno, es importante tener presente un dato clave. Las acusaciones que circulan en redes sostienen que los lectores de QR computarán como votos socialistas aquellos que se emitan tras presentar el DNI digital. Sin embargo, el dispositivo no registra votos, solo verifica la identidad de quien vota. La Junta Electoral Central ha reconocido a Newtral que se trata de un bulo.
Más de 30 bulos. El análisis de Newtral no se queda ahí. La web ha identificado más de 30 bulos, con afirmaciones falsas, engañosas o descontextualizadas, y ha desmontado algunos mensajes hablando directamente con los implicados. Un ejemplo: hace poco circuló que “decenas de vecinos” habían acudido al Ayuntamiento de Alcorcón para denunciar el registro de inmigrantes ilegales del Magreb en sus domicilios justo antes del 29N. El Consistorio lo ha desmentido.
Por supuesto, eso no significa que todas las informaciones similares sean falsas o estén infundadas. Arganda del Rey sí ha detectado desde marzo 50 empadronados de manera irregular en una docena de domicilios y en mayo la Guardia Civil informó de 600 “certificaciones fraudulentas” de ciudadanos extranjeros en Archena. Hay más casos, pero eso no significa que los empadronamientos irregulares se hagan con fines electorales.
En los últimos años sí se han dado detenciones por fraudes relacionadas con el voto por correos, pero si por algo destacan casos así es por no ser frecuentes.
“Dos pilares”. Que haya calado la narrativa del pucherazo es importante porque, como recuerda Natalia Junquera en El País, las democracias se basan sobre todo en “dos pilares”: la fiabilidad de los procesos electorales y la aceptación de los resultados que dejan las urnas. Para facilitar ambas, España se ha dotado de un engranaje electoral diseñado para evitar manipulaciones y que se usa desde hace décadas.
Una vez finalizada la votación, las papeletas se cuentan en la propia mesa electoral, de forma pública y ante apoderados de los diferentes partidos políticos. El resultado se plasma en varias actas que acaban en poder de la Junta Electoral y los juzgados y se envían por diferentes vías para evitar problemas. Hay escrutinio público y plazos de reclamación.
¿Qué pasa con Correos? Hace unos días, en plena polémica, Correos aseguró que este año “reforzará la seguridad” de los sufragios “mediante un sistema integral de custodia y seguimiento”. “Su custodia permanente en espacios protegidos y videovigilados las 24/7, y la implantación de balizas GPS para monitorizar en tiempo real los transportes entre centros logísticos y las unidades custodiadoras”. La Ley Orgánica de Régimen Electoral (LOREG) prevé además penas de prisión para quienes no respeten todos “los trámites establecidos”.
Tampoco hay pruebas para afirmar que Indra vaya a manipular los resultados, una teoría que circuló a raíz supuestamente de problemas durante un simulacro electoral. El Gobierno ha confirmado a RTVE que el 18 de noviembre se realizó una prueba durante la que se registraron “incidencias técnicas”. En cualquier caso, Indra no recuenta votos, se limita a recoger los datos de las actas.
Imágenes | PSOE (Flickr), Element5 Digital (Unsplash), PP y Vox España (Flickr)

articles.title: Ramiro Aurín, ingeniero de caminos, sobre las autopistas: "Una carretera sin agujeros es una carretera segura y ahora es un auténtico desastre"
articles.text:
Ramiro Aurín, ingeniero de caminos, canales y puertos, cree que la falta de mantenimiento en España no se queda en las vías del tren. En una entrevista en el pódcast A Contraluz asegura que también alcanza a las autopistas y a la gestión de los ríos, y que esto es algo preocupante.
Del peaje a la gratuidad. Sus críticas se centran sobre todo en la AP-7, que fue liberada en la mayoría de tramos para pasar a ser gratuita. Para Aurín esa decisión ha tenido un precio, porque según su análisis el asfalto se está deteriorando a toda velocidad desde que se levantaron las barreras.
El argumento del pago por uso. Según defiende, el peaje garantizaba una calzada en perfecto estado y permitía a conductores y flotas de transporte ganar tiempo con seguridad. Y opina que desde que pasó a ser gratuita ha estado saturada de camiones, provocando unos desperfectos en el asfalto que el dinero público no consigue reparar a un ritmo suficiente. Vamos, que en su opinión la vía se desgasta más deprisa de lo que se arregla, asegurando que que “una carretera sin agujeros es una carretera segura y ahora es un auténtico desastre”. También acusa al Ejecutivo de haber antepuesto el rédito propagandístico de abrir las barreras a garantizar el dinero para su conservación diaria.
Las presas que no llegaron. El daño que ve en las obras hidráulicas contra inundaciones y sequías es todavía mayor. Aurín recuerda que la planificación hidrológica moderna la impulsó Josep Borrell, que a principios de los noventa compareció en el Congreso como ministro de Obras Públicas y Transportes para hablar del Plan Hidrológico Nacional, y que los gobiernos posteriores le dieron continuidad hasta que, a su juicio, las dinámicas de coalición más recientes giraron en contra de contener los cauces.
Un sesgo contra los embalses. Explica que los acuerdos de Gobierno con formaciones como Podemos, que entró en el Ejecutivo con el nombramiento de ministros de enero de 2020, asentaron la idea de que “las infraestructuras eran algo malo” y de que “hacer un embalse era algo malo en sí mismo”. Esa visión acabó frenando, siempre según el ingeniero, presas y diques de defensa ya proyectados en zonas vulnerables.
Para Aurín, las catástrofes que provocan los fenómenos meteorológicos extremos tienen que prevenirse con ingeniería y criterios científicos contrastados, dejando a un lado los discursos dogmáticos y retomando las obras pendientes. La política de aguas, insiste, “hay que afrontarla con tecnología, con valor y con audacia”.
Foto | Enric en Wikimedia

articles.title: Llamó a la policía porque su expareja le quitó el acceso a su cuenta de Xbox y lo dejó sin poder jugar GTA 6
articles.text:
Una pelea por una cuenta de Xbox terminó con una llamada al 911 justo el fin de semana del estreno de Grand Theft Auto VI. La protagonista, identificada como Ciara Benson, contó en TikTok cómo recuperó el control de su perfil de videojuegos después de que su expareja lo usara durante seis años.
El relato arrancó con un video que Benson subió “porque le pareció gracioso”, según sus propias palabras, y que en pocos días acumuló casi un millón de reproducciones. Lo que parecía una broma casera derivó en un episodio con intervención policial real en el estado de Washington, Estados Unidos.
Cómo fue el conflicto por la cuenta de Xbox
Según narró Benson, su expareja, identificado solo como John, accedía desde hacía seis años a su cuenta de Microsoft sin ser el titular. La mujer decidió terminar con esa situación justo un día después de que él comprara GTA VI, el título que Rockstar Games lanzó el 19 de noviembre.
El conflicto por la custodia de una cuenta compartida de Xbox terminó en una denuncia policial después de que la mujer bloqueara a su expareja justo cuando este había comprado GTA VI. Ella eliminó todos los dispositivos vinculados, cambió la contraseña y aseguró que la cuenta nunca fue de él, sino suya desde el inicio.
“Fui a mi cuenta, eliminé todos los dispositivos, cerré sesión en todas partes, cambié mi contraseña, agregué una restricción. Es mía”, relató Benson en su video. La tiktoker vinculó su decisión a una disputa previa por la manutención del hijo que tiene en común con John, de siete años, y remarcó que ella seguía pagando por un servicio que él utilizaba sin aportar económicamente para el menor.
El quiebre se dio en un momento particularmente sensible para cualquier jugador: según contó, al entrar al perfil descubrió que, además del juego recién comprado, había acceso a “novecientos” títulos más que ahora quedaban bajo su control.
Cómo fue la denuncia ante la policía
El episodio escaló cuando John llamó al 911 para denunciar un presunto fraude con tarjeta de crédito. Según relató Benson en un segundo video, recibió un llamado del Departamento de Policía de Seattle (SPD) en el que los agentes le pidieron explicaciones sobre lo ocurrido para completar un informe de incidente.
La mujer explicó a los oficiales que había retirado de la cuenta todos los métodos de pago porque ninguno le pertenecía. Según contó, la policía ya conocía su primer video viral y estaba al tanto de la situación antes de contactarla.
“Me hizo saber que no había evidencia de que se hubiera cometido un delito”, dijo Benson sobre la respuesta del oficial a cargo. Por los antecedentes de violencia doméstica entre ambos, le entregaron igualmente una copia del informe del incidente, por si la necesitaba en futuros procesos de la corte de familia.
El diálogo con la policía terminó con uno de los oficiales cuando le preguntó a Benson cómo le parecía el juego y si su hijo ya había tenido oportunidad de probarlo. Ella aclaró que el niño, de siete años, no juega GTA y que ella misma apenas había avanzado en la historia del título.
Ante la viralización del video, Benseon comentó que John comenzó a recibir amenazas de muerte a raíz de la difusión del caso, por lo que tuvo que advertir a los seguidores. “Sigue siendo el padre de mi hijo y una persona, un ser humano. Podemos hacerlo mejor”, pidió la mujer, en un llamado directo a que cesaran los ataques.
Cómo GTA 6 ha afectado a Call of Duty
GTA 6 golpeó a su competencia apenas salió a la venta. Según estimaciones de Alinea Analytics, Call of Duty HQ perdió un 42% de sus jugadores diarios durante el fin de semana de estreno, al pasar de 7,5 a 4,4 millones. Fortnite cayó 28% y EA Sports FC 27, un 27%, aunque ambos recuperaron parte de su actividad gracias a eventos y promociones.
Call of Duty, en cambio, seguía un 41% por debajo cuatro días después, lo que evidencia cuánto tiempo de juego absorbió el título de Rockstar Games entre públicos distintos a los habituales.

articles.title: Zoho–LinkedIn report: AI is helping Indian SMBs grow, but skills lag behind
articles.text:
Zoho–LinkedIn report: AI is helping Indian SMBs grow, but skills lag behind
Indian SMBs with in-house AI talent grew their teams 5.2 percentage points faster in H1 2026, more than double the global gap. Yet only 6% have everyday AI skills across their workforce, a new Zoho and LinkedIn report finds.
Picture a typical Indian small-business founder. They run sales, approve leave requests and chase late payments. Their contacts are the company's biggest asset, and their WhatsApp is where most deals get done.
That model builds plenty of businesses, but it also caps how big they can get. The New Rules of Growth: How India's SMBs Are Building to Scale, a new joint report from Zoho and LinkedIn, looks at what happens when that cap arrives. Its answer: growing SMBs are moving work out of the founder's head and into systems, skills and teams.
The study covers July 2024 to June 2026. It combines LinkedIn network data from more than 1.4 billion members, including over 193 million in India, with usage data from more than 78,000 organisations on Zoho Workplace, Zoho People and Bigin by Zoho CRM. It defines an SMB as an India-headquartered business with 11 to 200 employees. The stakes are high: according to the Economic Survey 2025-26, SMBs contribute about 31% of India's GDP and nearly 49% of its exports.
The AI dividend is real
Rather than shrinking their workforce, SMBs that invest in AI talent are hiring faster. In the first half of 2026, Indian SMBs with in-house AI talent grew headcount 5.2 percentage points faster than other SMBs. That is more than double the 2.1-point gap among SMBs globally.
The lift isn't limited to software. Technology leads at 8.9 points, but construction (7.7), wholesale (7.3) and financial services (6.9) are close behind. The link is also strongest in smaller firms: among mid-market companies, the gap shrinks to 0.9 points.
"Those investing in AI talent are showing that AI and jobs can grow together," said Kumaresh Pattabiraman, India Country Manager at LinkedIn. The report adds a caveat: the data shows associations, not cause and effect.
The skills gap
The headline number has a weak spot. SMBs are better at building AI than at using it. LinkedIn data shows 16.3% have AI engineering skills in-house, but only 6.1% have everyday AI literacy across their workforce. Among large enterprises, the figures are more than 34% and 18%.
For most small businesses, everyday literacy matters more. A retailer or manufacturer doesn't need to build AI, but its people need to know how to use it. Pattabiraman's next step: make AI "a skill for every employee, not a specialist skill for a few."
Cautious by design
Part of the reason for the slow rollout is caution. AI-assisted search on Zoho Workplace has roughly doubled, and early adopters are using Bring-Your-Own-Key (BYOK) setups. These connect an AI model of the firm's choice using its own access key, so AI use stays within the contracts and data policies it already manages.
SMBs want the productivity of generative AI, but they are wary of sending sensitive data to outside providers. Use of password management tools has also risen about 35%.
Size matters too. Only 8.6% of micro-firms on Zoho People use AI in their HR tools, compared with 29.6% of larger SMBs. "Despite all the attention on AI, adoption still follows operational maturity," said Praval Singh, VP of Marketing and CX at Zoho.
When the founder is the sales team
More than 80,000 India-headquartered SMB founders on LinkedIn average over 1,300 connections each. Yet only about one in three SMBs has a formal sales leader at Director, VP or CXO level. In most firms, the founder is both head of sales and the face of the brand.
AI is helping lean teams go further. In the 12 months to June 2026, SMB sellers who used AI did roughly 40% more sales activity than those who didn't, and reached nearly twice as many decision-makers. They also grew their networks faster: in the year after adopting AI, their monthly new connections rose 40%, against 31% for similar sellers who didn't.
Meanwhile, routine sales work is moving into software, from the first chat to the final payment. Bigin by Zoho CRM data shows:
- Workflow automation rose about 42%, routing new leads and flagging stalled deals automatically.
- Payment link usage grew about 56%, helping customers pay as soon as a deal is agreed.
- WhatsApp messages sent through the CRM rose almost sixfold, as deals move to mobile and to the channels buyers already use.
Earning trust in public
Buyers now size up a business long before they talk to it, and more SMBs are making sure they can be found.
Monthly active SMB advertisers on LinkedIn grew about 13% year on year, and click-through rates rose roughly 81%. The most engaging 10% of advertisers keep campaigns running 26% longer and use 83% more ad creatives than the bottom 10%. About one in six SMB advertisers now mention AI in their ads, mostly as "AI-powered" or "AI-driven" rather than "AI-native."
The 50-employee wall
In HR, the tipping point comes at about 50 employees. Below it, attendance lives on a spreadsheet and leave is approved in a WhatsApp group. Beyond it, informal processes start to fail. Among Zoho People customers, 68% of larger SMBs use several advanced HR features, against just 9% of micro-firms. About 16% of SMBs on the platform use its AI assistant to handle routine HR queries.
Founders want tools that fit how they already work. Custom workflows (about 35%) and custom modules (27%) are the most used advanced features, well ahead of ready-made ones such as performance management (14%).
Hiring wider, and further away
Skills-based hiring widens the search. Employers in India that hire for skills rather than job titles or degrees can reach 11 times more candidates, and 22 times more for AI roles.
SMBs are also hiring across borders. Their share of hires made outside India rose from about 22% to nearly 27% between 2025 and 2026, led by the US, UAE, UK and Nigeria.
What it adds up to
The report doesn't describe a sweeping transformation. It describes steady, practical progress. Indian SMBs are adopting technology one function at a time and building systems around the people who already make the business work. For founders, the lessons are clear:
- Start with one workflow, such as sales follow-ups or routine HR questions.
- Put guardrails in place first, within your existing permissions and data policies.
- Build systems before you reach 50 employees, not after things start to break.
- Teach AI to everyone, not just a few specialists.
As Singh put it, the priority is "building the skills to use it well, so they can scale without losing agility." The founder's network still opens the first doors. What this report shows is what it takes to keep growing after that.

articles.title: Cloudflare now lets websites add search for AI agents with a single toggle. Site owners foot the query bill.
articles.text:
Cloudflare now lets websites add search for AI agents with a single toggle. Site owners foot the query bill.
Cloudflare has announced a new feature that makes it easier for AI agents to find and retrieve relevant information from websites, helping site owners make their content directly searchable by agents at the flick of a switch.
However, doing so could come at a cost to website owners, who are responsible for the associated search infrastructure charges.
Search for Agents, as it’s called, builds on other initiatives from Cloudflare designed to make the web more accessible to AI systems. Last month, the company officially launched AI Search, a managed service that enables developers to index their own data and integrate search functionality into applications and agents. And this serves as the underlying search infrastructure for Search for Agents.
Back in February, Cloudflare also launched Markdown for Agents, which automatically converts HTML pages into a lightweight, text-based format that AI agents can consume more efficiently — part of a broader evolution of the web to accommodate both human and machine visitors.
Search for Agents takes this further by giving websites their own agent-discoverable search API, allowing agents to query a site’s content directly without having to navigate individual pages to find the information they need.
The agent retrieval problem
Back in September, developer documentation platform Mintlify highlighted a problem with llms.txt, a file that serves AI agents with a map of a website’s content. Larger documentation sites were hitting Mintlify’s 100,000-character limit for these files, resulting in some pages being omitted. The company addressed this by introducing a hierarchy of smaller index files, allowing agents to discover all available pages without having to load the entire index.
The issue was particularly pertinent for Mintlify, which reported in April that AI coding agents accounted for 45.3% of requests across documentation sites powered by its platform, almost on a par with traditional browser traffic.
Cloudflare, for its part, also reported last year that AI crawling triggered by users’ queries had increased more than twentyfold through 2025.
Even with improvements such as those introduced by Mintlify, agents still have to navigate a website’s content index to find the information they need. Search for Agents seeks to bypass that process by allowing agents to query the website directly.
In a blog post published on Wednesday, the company detailed how website operators can enable the feature, currently in beta, via the Quick Actions section of their domain’s Cloudflare dashboard or programmatically through an API.
Once activated, Cloudflare provisions a dedicated AI Search instance and begins crawling and indexing the website’s content. Website operators can subsequently manage that instance from their AI Search dashboard, adjusting settings such as caching and enabling reranking to improve the relevance of search results.
Cloudflare also inserts instructions into the metadata of each page, telling visiting agents where the search API resides and how to use it. For websites that have enabled Markdown for Agents, these instructions are also included in the Markdown document’s YAML front matter.
Agents can then send keywords or natural-language questions to the website’s /.well-known/search endpoint, receiving relevant excerpts from the site’s content in Markdown. The agent can use this to formulate its own response to the user’s question.
Who pays for agent search?
Search for Agents is available across all Cloudflare plans, including its free tier. However, with AI Search billing set to begin on December 1, there are cost considerations for website owners looking to make their content more accessible to AI agents.
Each account receives a monthly allowance of 5 million ingestion tokens, 10 GB-months of storage, and 1,000 queries each for semantic and full-text search. Beyond those allowances, Cloudflare charges $0.75 per million ingestion tokens, $2 per GB-month of storage, $0.75 per 1,000 semantic, vector or hybrid queries, and $0.10 per 1,000 full-text queries.
Moreover, there are limits on how much content Cloudflare can crawl to populate the search index. Customers on the Workers Free plan are limited to 500 pages per day, while paying customers face no daily crawl limit. Both are subject to a 100,000-page limit per discovery crawl.
This raises an interesting question in the context of Cloudflare’s broader efforts to help website owners monetize AI traffic. Last July, the company introduced pay-per-crawl, enabling website owners to charge AI companies for fetching individual pages. The company expanded on that initiative this July with a push toward pay-per-use, whereby publishers would be compensated when their content appears in AI-generated answers. It’s part of a broader effort, as The New Stack reported at the time, to build the economic layer of the AI web.
Then in September, Cloudflare launched its Monetization Gateway in closed beta, enabling domain owners to charge AI agents for accessing websites, APIs, MCP tools and datasets using the x402 payment protocol.
Against that backdrop, the economics of Search for Agents are particularly striking. Having spent much of the past 18 months developing ways for website owners to generate revenue from AI traffic, Cloudflare is now asking those same website owners to shoulder the cost of making their content more readily accessible to AI agents.
“Our data shows that agents have now surpassed humans using the Internet and are an important audience for any website owner.”
So what incentive do website owners have to absorb these costs? According to Celso Martinho, VP of engineering at Cloudflare, it comes down to the growing importance of AI agents as an audience in their own right.
“Our data shows that agents have now surpassed humans using the Internet and are an important audience for any website owner,” Martinho tells The New Stack.
For context, Cloudflare reported back in June that bots, which include AI agents, accounted for 57% of HTML page requests across its network. Martinho also points to existing tools such as Cloudflare’s AI Crawl Control and the x402 payment protocol, which website operators can use to manage and monetize access to their content.
Moreover, plans are afoot to extend Cloudflare’s Monetization Gateway to cover the new search endpoints, which would enable website owners to charge agents directly for search queries.
“We are working on adding first-class support for Search for Agents and other agentic content APIs to Monetization Gateway,” Martinho says, though no timeline was provided.
For now, those search costs fall to website owners.
A common language for agent search?
While companies can, of course, build and expose their own search APIs, Search for Agents essentially gives Cloudflare customers an off-the-shelf solution. According to Martinho, existing agents with web browsing capabilities should be able to discover and use these endpoints without developers having to build dedicated integrations.
Cloudflare has tested the approach extensively across its own blog and developer documentation sites, Martinho says, “demonstrating that using a search API is more efficient for agents than crawling individual pages to find answers.”
“Using a search API is more efficient for agents than crawling individual pages to find answers.”
There have been broader efforts across the industry to standardize how AI agents interact with the world around them. Last December, the Linux Foundation announced the formation of the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), of which Cloudflare is a founding member, bringing projects such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP), AGENTS.md and Goose under a common umbrella.
For now, though, Cloudflare is pursuing its own approach to search endpoint discovery.
“Agents do a pretty good job at adjusting to different instructions and web protocols,” Martinho says, adding that Cloudflare’s research into agent behavior through initiatives such as Radar’s AI Insights and its Agent Readiness project informed its choice of technologies for Search for Agents.
Cloudflare’s approach draws on established web conventions such as well-known URIs and HTTP GET, alongside the newer HTTP QUERY method, an Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) proposed standard co-authored by Cloudflare engineer James Snell.
However, Martinho acknowledges the merits of a broader industry effort in this area.
“Interoperability absolutely matters,” Martinho says. “A common approach to discovering search endpoints across providers would also make sense.”

articles.title: Your Google Meet calls are about to get a little clearer
articles.text:
If you spend a lot of time on Google Meet, you might soon notice that everyone’s video looks a little better. Why? Google is finally upgrading users to higher-res video.
According to an update on the Google Workspace blog, the search giant revealed that it would expand 1080p video sending to Meet on the web for all users. Previously, Full HD video was limited to select paying users, and 1080p receiving was already available to all.
Now, everyone with a computer sporting a 1080p camera and sufficient compute and bandwidth will automatically have 1080p video sending. However, Workspace administrators can set different video quality defaults, so some people might not see the higher resolution depending on their workspace settings. Video settings can be adjusted by heading to Settings > Video.
Google also noted that Meet automatically scales resolution according to the size of the video tiles. In other words, when more people are in the meeting and the video tiles are smaller, it will reduce the resolution accordingly so it doesn’t burn unnecessary CPU or bandwidth.
It’s also worth noting that 1080p video is limited to those using Chromium-based browsers like Google’s own Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Brave, Vivaldi, or others. Non-Chromium browsers like Safari or Firefox won’t have 1080p video.
The search giant didn’t clarify in the blog post if there would be changes to Meet on mobile devices. Currently, smartphones can receive 1080p video, but can only transmit 720p video. Hopefully, with this change on the web, the Meet apps on Android and iOS will be next.
Google started rolling out the change on Nov. 11, but noted it could take as long as 15 days for the change to show up for users.
Source: Google Via: Android Police

articles.title: OpenAI corrige une erreur et réduit votre quota Codex avec GPT-6.2
articles.text:
Vous arriverez au bout de votre quota Codex 40 % plus vite avec GPT-6.2 Astra et 25 % plus vite avec Sol que la semaine dernière, après la correction d'une erreur de facturation par OpenAI. Pour se faire pardonner, la start-up de Sam Altman offre une réinitialisation de quota supplémentaire aux abonnés Go, Plus, Pro et Business.
Au lancement de GPT-6.2 Astra et Sol, le 17 novembre, OpenAI promettait que Sol vous laisserait accomplir davantage de tâches avec votre abonnement payant. Mais depuis cette sortie, OpenAI décomptait trop peu l'utilisation des deux modèles chez la plupart des abonnés, à la suite d'une erreur de facturation reconnue par Thibault Sottiaux, responsable de Codex, l'agent de programmation de la start-up. Un abonné Pro raconte, sur le forum des développeurs d'OpenAI, avoir dépensé avec Astra près de 20 points de son quota hebdomadaire ce jeudi, contre une dizaine mercredi.
OpenAI décomptait trop peu GPT-6.2 dans Codex depuis son lancement
« Nous avons commis une erreur de facturation au lancement de GPT-6.2 », admet Thibault Sottiaux. OpenAI avait d'abord prévenu ses abonnés par un courriel intitulé « An update to Codex usage ». D'après un abonné, qui a recopié ce message sur le forum, OpenAI annonçait que certaines requêtes d'Astra et de Sol, mode Ultrafast compris, entameraient votre quota plus vite. Dans un second e-mail, la start-up donnait enfin les pourcentages et parlait d'une erreur de facturation.
Le prix des abonnements et des crédits achetés est inchangé, et le créateur de ChatGPT promet de ne rien vous facturer pour votre utilisation passée. OpenAI a laissé tel quel le décompte des autres modèles, dont GPT-6 Astra et GPT-6.1 Sol. Et selon Thibault Sottiaux, GPT-6.2 Astra et Sol devraient toujours vous donner plus d'utilisation que GPT-6 Astra et GPT-6.1 Sol.
Sur le forum, plusieurs abonnés voient dans cette correction une hausse de prix déguisée. « Shrinkflation ! », lance l'un d'eux. Un autre reproche à OpenAI un calcul trop opaque pour savoir s'il s'agit d'un bug corrigé ou d'un changement de tarif. Pour lui, payer autant pour moins de service revient à payer plus cher, et il demande depuis quand l'erreur courait et si OpenAI a un jour publié les taux prévus.
OpenAI vous offre une réinitialisation de quota à garder pour plus tard
« Nous sommes désolés d'avoir mal géré cela », a écrit sur X Vaibhav Srivastav, chargé de l'expérience des développeurs chez OpenAI. Il assure que la réinitialisation promise est active pour tous les abonnés Go, Plus, Pro et Business.
Vous pouvez garder cette réinitialisation sur votre compte jusqu'à son expiration, et la déclencher quand vous le voulez. D'après la page d'aide d'OpenAI, une réinitialisation complète remet à zéro vos deux compteurs Codex, celui de la fenêtre de cinq heures et celui de la semaine. Il s'agit d'un bonus ponctuel, et votre forfait garde ensuite ses limites habituelles. Le seul problème, c'est qu'on ignore encore la date d'expiration de ce bonus, d'après l'abonné du forum.
OpenAI a multiplié ces remises à zéro depuis l'été, avec notamment une réinitialisation immédiate des compteurs en juillet. Et dès décembre, ChatGPT, Work et Codex partageront un seul quota, calculé en tokens pour les abonnés Plus, Pro et Business. Seule la discussion rapide Instant chat sera décomptée à part.

articles.title: Les profils criminels de GTA 6 font jaser, et Rockstar le savait
articles.text:
GTA 6 introduit un système de réputation, baptisé « profil criminel », qui évolue en fonction de votre manière de jouer. Cinq profils sont possibles pour Jason et Lucia : Professionnel, Endurci, Violent, Psycho et Irrécupérable. Jason et Lucia démarrent tous deux au niveau Endurci. Plus vous êtes violent, plus vous glissez vers Violent puis Psycho. Attention, rester trop longtemps Psycho fait basculer dans Irrécupérable, un statut irréversible.
La réputation régit plusieurs choses importantes, de la manière dont les PNJ de GTA 6 réagissent à votre contact, à la manière de gagner de la concentration. Surtout, la fin que vous obtiendrez dépend du statut de Jason, de celui de Lucia ainsi que de leur niveau de relation. Cette réputation dissuade de s’adonner totalement à la violence gratuite, sous peine d’atteindre un point de non-retour. Depuis la sortie du jeu, le 19 novembre sur PS5 et Xbox Series X|S, le système divise les joueurs. Une partie apprécie la dimension jeu de rôle, d’autres n’acceptent pas de voir leurs carnages à Vice City jugés.
Pourquoi Rockstar a mis un système de réputation punitif dans GTA 6
Ce système de réputation de GTA 6, qui est une évolution du système d’honneur de Red Dead Redemption 2, peut être considéré comme punitif, puisqu’il encourage à jouer plus « proprement » et à rester sur le droit chemin. Pour ne pas atteindre Irrécupérable, il faut privilégier les neutralisations non létales (en visant les points jaunes quand on active la concentration en appuyant sur les deux sticks), éviter de tirer le premier et ne pas tuer gratuitement (même les animaux).
Dans une interview accordée avant la sortie du jeu à Video Games Chronicle et publiée ce jeudi 26 novembre, Rob Nelson, producteur de GTA 6 et codirecteur du studio Rockstar North, explique que l’équipe savait qu’une partie des joueurs rejetterait cette nouveauté. « Je pense que cela ouvre un nouvel éventail de choix et de décisions pour le joueur. Vous pouvez toujours faire tout ce que vous vouliez faire auparavant, mais vous avez désormais d’autres options », confie-t-il.
Avec ce système, comme avec la prise en compte de l’empathie, Rockstar veut pousser les joueuses et les joueurs à jouer autrement dans GTA 6. Un choix dicté par l’intrigue et les personnages. Rob Nelson argumente : « Dans GTA 5, on commençait par un braquage de banque à North Yankton, on tuait d’entrée de jeu une quarantaine de flics, et on posait immédiatement les bases de ce que sont ces personnages. Nous en étions conscients. Lucia retire les balles du chargeur au début du jeu. Elle entre [dans le bâtiment], et ce n’est pas comme si l’on pouvait tuer un tas de gens. Nous voulions donc les faire démarrer avec un peu moins de passif. Ils essaient de s’en sortir en menant cette vie semi-légale. »

articles.title: The FCC approves SpaceX's plan for up to a million data-center satellites
articles.text:
What just happened? The vision of millions of data-center satellites orbiting Earth has seemed like a far-off concept, but the FCC has just given SpaceX approval to launch up to one million of these structures into Earth orbit, and the company says the first could be launched as early as 2028 Chairman Brendan Carr said the satellites will use solar power to extend America's lead in AI, or "Super Intelligence," as US executive agencies must now call it in most official communications.
SpaceX filed its application back in January, giving the FCC a little under ten months to sign off on the first constellation of its kind in the US. The Starmind satellites will process data in low Earth orbit and use lasers to communicate with one another and with Starlink satellites. Radio links will serve as a backup.
The FCC statement makes the bold claim that the system will "bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilisation – one that can harness the full power of the sun." Proposed in 1964 by astrophysicist Nikolai Kardashev, a Kardashev Type II civilisation is a hypothetical advanced society capable of capturing and using the entire energy output of its host star.
 – Brendan Carr (@BrendanCarrFCC) November 25, 2026
Musk kept his response to Carr's announcement on X short but sweet. "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world," the SpaceX CEO wrote.
We got a look at what SpaceX plans to put up there back in June, when Musk showed off the first-generation AI1 satellite. With its wings fully deployed, the thing measures almost 230 feet across, making it wider than a Boeing 747-8. SpaceX says it can deliver 120 kilowatts of sustained power to its computing hardware, peaking at 150 kW. For comparison, a single Nvidia GB300 rack is rated at 140 kW.
Getting the first satellite into orbit should be the easy part, at least by SpaceX's standards. Under the FCC licence, the company has until November 25, 2033, to get a single satellite up and running, though SpaceX told investors it could start deploying them as early as 2028. The deadlines get considerably more demanding from there. SpaceX needs 100,000 operational by November 2035, half a million by November 2038, and the full million by November 2040.
Unsurprisingly, astronomers aren't quite as enthusiastic about the prospect as Musk. The American Astronomical Society, which asked the FCC to reject the application, warned that satellites this large would appear brighter and remain visible for longer, making it harder for ground-based telescopes to observe the night sky.
There's also the question of what happens to all that hardware when it stops working. SpaceX wants the option of sending retired satellites into orbit around the sun. The FCC says it needs more detail before it will sign off on that idea. SpaceX must also submit a final debris plan before deploying any Starmind satellites that will operate above 600 kilometers (373 miles).
"Any serious attempt at this is going to further pollute the night sky and runs a serious risk of a cascading chain reaction of space junk collisions, which would be a disaster for all of humanity," astrophysicist and author Adam Becker told CNBC. "Musk and Carr are either profoundly stupid themselves, or hoping the rest of us are too stupid to notice this is nonsense."
SpaceX is far from alone in its plans for deploying data-centers in space. Google's Project Suncatcher sent its first prototype into orbit aboard a SpaceX rocket in October. Google switched on the satellite's Tensor Processing Unit, sent it a prompt, and got a haiku back. For a bigger test, Google has booked a ride with one of Musk's rivals. Blue Origin's New Glenn is scheduled to carry several Google computing satellites into orbit in early 2029.
Jeff Bezos' company has orbital data center ambitions of its own, having asked the FCC for permission to deploy up to 51,600 satellites under the name Project Sunrise.
Then there's Washington startup Starcloud, which sent an Nvidia H100 GPU into space last year. The company used it to run one of Google's Gemma models and train a small language model on the complete works of Shakespeare. Its plans for a second satellite include something a little less literary: Starcloud wants to see if it can mine Bitcoin in orbit.

articles.title: 100,000 Potentially Impacted by Colorado Data Breach
articles.text:
The Colorado Governor’s Office of Information Technology (OIT) has disclosed a data breach impacting data that residents uploaded to the myColorado application.
Colorado’s official mobile application, myColorado is used for digital identification, state services, and document storage. It has approximately 2.1 million users.
OIT took the application offline last week, after identifying unauthorized access to platform data, and immediately initiated incident response and an investigation into the incident.
One week after the outage began, OIT said it discovered the incident after the attackers triggered the automated threat detection systems deployed within its Amazon Web Services (AWS) environment.
The investigation has determined that the attackers accessed documents stored within the ‘myCards and Documents’ section of the application, which includes user-uploaded data, such as PDF files and photos of government IDs, vehicle registrations, and insurance cards.
According to Colorado, approximately 100,000 individuals might have been affected, but no payment information was accessed.
“Staff are working around the clock to match the inappropriately accessed documents to individual users. As that matching continues, OIT will further refine estimates on the number of people whose data was involved,” Colorado said.
The myColorado application remains offline and OIT has not announced a restoration date. The state expects to start sending direct notifications to the affected individuals on November 27.
“Our main goal is to protect the security of users. Additionally, we are prioritizing direct notification of users involved in the incident and getting the app up and running as soon as possible, with security enhancements in place,” said state CIO and OIT executive director Sarah Tuneberg.

articles.title: Mock Service Worker Releases v3.0 with ESM-Only Build, Socket-Based Interception and GraphQL Subs
articles.text:
Mock Service Worker, the API mocking library maintained by Artem Zakharchenko, has released version 3.0, nearly three years after the Fetch-based v2.0 rewrite. The release ships as ESM-only, completes the library's GraphQL story with subscription support, and introduces a socket-based interception algorithm in Node.js that Zakharchenko describes as going as deep into the runtime as JavaScript will allow without recompiling Node.
The headline breaking change is that MSW is now distributed natively as ECMAScript Modules only, with support for Node.js v18 and v20 dropped in favour of v22, v24, and v26. TypeScript 5.9 is now the minimum supported version. Several transitive dependencies have been removed, including graphql (now a proper optional peer), path-to-regexp, picocolors, and statuses. The result is a library tarball that drops from 416KB to 234KB, with type definitions shrinking by half, from 190KB to 90KB.
Alongside ESM, v3.0 introduces granular entrypoints that replace the single msw import with designated paths for each protocol:
import { http } from 'msw/http'
import { graphql } from 'msw/graphql'
import { sse } from 'msw/sse'
import { ws } from 'msw/ws'
GraphQL subscription support, a long-standing community request on the project's tracker, lands in this release. Building on the WebSocket interception shipped previously, subscription handlers can now be defined against a graphql.link() and publish events on demand, closing the gap between MSW's HTTP, WebSocket, and GraphQL coverage.
An experimental defineNetwork API is introduced as the eventual replacement for setupServer and setupWorker. The new primitive splits interception into sources (where traffic comes from) and handlers (how it is answered), allowing teams to replay HAR files, combine custom interceptors, or hand control of request timing to a test runner. The first ecosystem package to expose it directly is @msw/cloudflare, which wraps the API for Workers environments.
The most technically significant change sits in the underlying Interceptors library. Zakharchenko writes that after seven attempts at the problem, the team has moved network interception in Node.js down to the TCP and TLS wraps, the JavaScript bindings for Node's C-level network code. Moving any lower, he notes, would require recompiling Node.js itself. The new architecture supports arbitrary socket-based protocols, with SMTP cited as an early example. Nock already relies on the Interceptors library for its Node.js support.
A GitHub discussion reports failing tests after upgrading, traced to MSW now intercepting the browser-issued OPTIONS preflight requests that previous versions quietly ignored. Separately, a developer in discussion #2771 challenged the earlier decision to deprioritise Jest and JSDOM, arguing that a runner with 46 million weekly downloads warrants a formal breaking-change note rather than a quiet docs change.
In the Node-only space, MSW continues to compete with Nock, fetch-mock, and undici's built-in MockAgent, though as a recent comparison notes, none of those cover both browser and server with a single handler definition.
Teams on v2 should consult the official 2.x to 3.x migration guide before upgrading. Full release notes are available on GitHub.
Mock Service Worker is an open-source, MIT-licensed JavaScript library for mocking network traffic using Service Workers in the browser and runtime-level interception in Node.js. It is used widely for frontend and full-stack testing, and now covers HTTP, WebSocket, Server-Sent Events, and GraphQL including subscriptions.

articles.title: Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution
articles.text:
Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution
- Date:
  November 16, 2026
- Source:
  University of Innsbruck
- Summary:
  Scientists have developed a new way to determine whether quantum simulations can be trusted, solving a growing problem as quantum computers become too powerful for conventional machines to check. Demonstrated on a 51-qubit system, the technique measures uncertainty and provides verifiable error margins that could help unlock the full potential of quantum computing.
- Share:
As quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them? Scientists have now developed a promising new method that could help overcome this challenge by measuring the accuracy of quantum simulations and identifying how much uncertainty their predictions contain.
The technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results. Researchers successfully demonstrated the approach using a quantum simulator with up to 51 qubits in Innsbruck, Austria.
Quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all. However, this progress creates a verification problem. When a simulation is small enough, scientists can compare its results with calculations performed on a conventional computer. As quantum systems grow beyond those limits, that direct comparison becomes impractical, making alternative ways to assess their reliability essential.
A New Way to Measure Quantum Computing Accuracy
The breakthrough comes from an international research team led by Tristan Kraft at the Technical University of Munich and Peter Zoller at the University of Innsbruck and the Institute for Quantum Optics and Quantum Information of the Austrian Academy of Sciences, working alongside Barbara Kraus of the Technical University of Munich. The researchers developed a method for experimentally determining how a quantum simulator operates and translating uncertainties in its behavior into measurable limits on the accuracy of its results.
Quantum simulators are specialized physical systems designed to reproduce the behavior of other quantum systems. They are especially useful for investigating situations involving large numbers of interacting particles, where the calculations required can quickly overwhelm even powerful conventional computers.
But quantum experiments are never entirely free from errors. "But no real experiment is perfect," says Tristan Kraft. "Interactions may turn out differently than expected, the system is influenced by its environment, and measurements are also subject to uncertainties."
Rather than assuming a quantum simulator behaves exactly as intended, the new approach examines experimental data to determine what is actually happening inside the system. This allows researchers to identify important interactions and account for disturbances such as fluctuations and noise.
"From this data, we determine the relevant interactions as well as key influences from fluctuations and noise. We then calculate how the uncertainties in this model affect the simulation results," explains Tristan Kraft. "The quantum simulator thus provides not just a single value, but a result with error margins that quantify its accuracy."
Successfully Tested on a 51 Qubit Quantum Simulator
To evaluate the method, the researchers began with a relatively small quantum system containing ten trapped ions. Because conventional computers can still calculate the behavior of a system of this size, the team could test its reconstructed models and calculated error limits against independent measurements.
After this initial validation, the researchers expanded their experiments to a chain of 51 trapped ions. The larger demonstration, carried out by a team led by Manoj Joshi and Christian Roos using an ion trap quantum simulator, showed that the technique could also work with substantially more complex quantum systems.
This represents an important step toward establishing how trustworthy quantum simulation results are, particularly as quantum devices advance into territory where direct verification with traditional computing methods becomes increasingly difficult.
Extending the Breakthrough to More Complex Quantum Systems
The next challenge is to bring the technique to two-dimensional quantum simulators. These systems can model more complicated interactions among particles, making them valuable for exploring quantum physics. At the same time, their growing complexity makes their results particularly difficult to confirm using conventional calculations.
"This is particularly important because classical calculations for such systems become significantly more difficult as the number of particles increases," explains quantum computing pioneer Peter Zoller. "This also makes independent verification of the results increasingly complex, making the question of experimentally determined error limits all the more important."
The researchers are now adapting their method for the newest generation of two-dimensional quantum simulators, which offer improved precision and can investigate systems containing larger numbers of particles.
Looking further ahead, the approach could help scientists establish a more meaningful way to measure quantum advantage, the ability of quantum systems to outperform conventional computers. Instead of comparing machines based only on their processing speed or the size of the problems they can handle, researchers could also examine how accurately each system produces its answers.
"After all, when a classical computer and a quantum simulator tackle the same problem, it's not just a matter of which one delivers a result faster. What's also crucial is which one can solve the problem with a smaller, verifiable margin of error," says Peter Zoller.
This shift could change how progress in quantum computing is evaluated. Future breakthroughs may be judged not simply by how many particles a simulator can model or how quickly it performs calculations, but by its ability to solve increasingly difficult problems with demonstrably reliable results.
The findings were published in Physical Review X. The research received support from the Austrian Science Fund (FWF), the German Ministry of Research, Technology and Space, the European Union, BMW, and other funding organizations.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Innsbruck. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Tristan Kraft, Manoj K. Joshi, William T. Lam, Tobias Olsacher, Florian Kranzl, Johannes Franke, Lata Kh Joshi, Rainer Blatt, Augusto Smerzi, Daniel Stilck França, Benoît Vermersch, Barbara Kraus, Christian F. Roos, Peter Zoller. Bounded-Error Quantum Simulation via Hamiltonian and Lindbladian Learning. Physical Review X, 2026; 16 (3) DOI: 10.1103/s96t-n8tx

articles.title: Kenya drops FlexPay criminal case in $240,000 Naivas dispute
articles.text:
Kenyan prosecutors have dropped criminal charges against four executives of fintech firm FlexPay over theft of KES 31.2 million ($240,000) claimed by supermarket chain Naivas, directing the police to close the investigation and advising the retailer to pursue the money through the civil courts.
The Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP), in a letter dated November 6 seen by TechCabal, reversed its earlier decision to charge the four after a review of evidence submitted by the Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) found the dispute civil in nature.
The decision brings to an end months of criminal investigations that saw two FlexPay executives arrested in September following the collapse of a five-year partnership between the fintech and Kenya’s largest supermarket chain, through which the two companies had processed more than KES 3 billion ($23.1 million) in customer transactions, according to court documents.
“The Director of Public Prosecutions, upon further independent and thorough review of the evidence contained in the inquiry file, has established that the dispute is civil in nature,” the ODPP said in the letter addressed to the Nairobi Regional Criminal Investigation Officer.
“Consequently, the Director of Public Prosecutions directs that the complainant, Naivas Limited, be advised to seek civil redress and the investigation file be closed with no further police action.”
Police as debt collectors
The letter followed separate representations made by lawyers from Ayieko Kangethe & Co Advocates and Guandaru Thuita & Company Advocates on September 2 and September 9, respectively, challenging the decision to institute criminal proceedings.
FlexPay directors Dennis Karanu Mwangi and Richard Machomba, chief growth officer and former director Martin Kariuki Maina, and shareholder Johnson Gituma Mwangi had faced possible prosecution for stealing by an agent after Naivas lodged a police complaint.
The four, alongside Flexitech Group Limited, the company that operates FlexPay, filed a case at the High Court in September, accusing the supermarket chain of using the police to recover a disputed commercial debt.
Four days after the DPP directed the closure of the investigation, High Court judge Roseline Aburili issued orders barring the police and prosecutors from arresting, detaining or charging the four over the dispute pending the determination of their constitutional petition.
“The prosecution must be seen to be in the public interest and not intended to aid a complainant to recover a civil debt,” Justice Aburili said in her November 10 ruling.
“Public interest is not merely served by securing convictions at all costs; it is primarily anchored on the integrity of the administration of justice. The public must have confidence that the criminal process is even-handed.”
The prosecutors’ decision is a setback for Naivas, which had maintained that FlexPay collected money on its behalf and failed to remit it, amounting to theft rather than a breach of a commercial agreement.
Competing claims
According to court documents seen by TechCabal, Naivas and FlexPay entered into a seven-year agreement on February 10, 2021, that allowed customers of the supermarket chain to pay for goods in instalments through the fintech’s digital platform.
The agreement, subsequently amended in February 2022 and December 2023, was to run until February 2028.
In an affidavit filed on October 7, Naivas told the court that FlexPay retained a 5% commission on customer payments and was required to remit the remaining 95% to the retailer by the next business day.
Naivas said the arrangement worked for five years until early 2026, when FlexPay allegedly stopped remitting the money collected from shoppers.
The retailer claimed that the fintech had written letters acknowledging the outstanding amounts and requesting more time to pay. It subsequently reported the matter to the police.
FlexPay disputed the nature of the arrangement, maintaining that it was a corporate customer of Naivas and not an agent of the supermarket chain.
The fintech told the court that Naivas had opened a corporate credit account in its name, through which it bought goods on credit and periodically settled the outstanding balances, establishing a creditor-debtor relationship between the two companies.
FlexPay also claimed that Naivas owed it at least KES 24 million ($185,000) in unreimbursed customer loyalty points and that it had incurred losses exceeding KES 300 million ($2.3 million) through alleged price manipulation by employees of the supermarket chain.
The fintech further claimed that KES 3.07 million ($23,600) it paid Naivas during the dispute had not been credited to its account. Neither the DPP’s decision nor the High Court ruling determined the validity of the financial claims either company made.
The DPP’s decision to close the inquiry file, three months after its initial correspondence with investigators on August 11, now leaves Naivas the option of pursuing its claim through civil proceedings against its former technology partner.

articles.title: Apple no tira la toalla con el iPad plegable, pero no te hagas muchas ilusiones
articles.text:
Los rumores de que Apple trabaja en un iPad plegable no son nuevos. Las especulaciones en torno a este dispositivo son tan antiguas como las del recientemente lanzado iPhone Duo, pero todo apunta a que, a pesar de varios desafíos técnicos y de diseño, los de Cupertino siguen firmes con su desarrollo.
Así lo sostuvo Mark Gurman en la más reciente edición de su pódcast. El periodista de Bloomberg, el insider más confiable en lo que respecta al mundo Apple, indicó que los californianos siguen preparando un iPad plegable. El mismo tendrá la pantalla más grande jamás vista en el catálogo de tablets de la manzana, con un panel flexible de entre 19 y 20 pulgadas.
Gurman ha mencionado que el iPad plegable se está desarrollando bajo el nombre clave Project J312. El susodicho afirma que el diseño del dispositivo se parece al de un iPhone Duo, pero gigante y sin una pantalla exterior. Todavía no hay detalles sobre otras características técnicas; por ejemplo, qué chip podría impulsarlo.
Lo que sí sería un hecho es que el presunto iPad plegable estaría muy lejos de ser asequible. De acuerdo con el periodista, el dispositivo se lanzaría con un precio de entre 3.000 y 5.000 dólares. Así que si te interesa la idea de cargar un dispositivo de este tipo en tu mochila, vas a tener que desembolsar a lo grande.
El iPad plegable todavía está en marcha, pero afronta varios problemas
Los comentarios de Mark Gurman apuntan a que, si bien el iPad plegable continúa en desarrollo, ha enfrentado varios problemas. Esto se condice con un reporte previo del periodista, quien en octubre del año pasado reveló que Apple habría postergado su lanzamiento hasta 2029.
Los de Cupertino habrían apuntado a estrenarlo en 2027, pero luego lo retrasaron hasta 2028 y, más tarde, hasta 2029. Por entonces comentó que uno de los grandes inconvenientes de los ingenieros de la manzana era cómo reducir el peso del aparato. El prototipo de iPad plegable supuestamente pesaba 1,6 kilos, casi un kilo más que el iPad Pro más pesado de la actualidad.
Gurman también plantea que Apple aún no se decide sobre el software del presunto iPad plegable. Desde la compañía no estarían del todo seguros respecto de dotarlo de iPadOS, o si dan el salto que tanto reclaman los usuarios y le instalan macOS. Al parecer, tampoco se descarta desarrollar un software totalmente nuevo para el factor de forma.
Sea como sea, el iPad plegable todavía está lejos de llegar al mercado. Si bien el proyecto estaría entre las prioridades de John Ternus, Apple todavía podría descartarlo y enfocar sus recursos en una iniciativa diferente.

articles.title: Netflix’s coziest show has made a very quiet return
articles.text:
The bigger Netflix gets, the easier it is to miss stuff. This is true of all digital platforms, of course, but it’s especially true of Netflix of late, as the streaming service’s lineup now also includes a growing library of reality shows, live-programming, and even games. It makes it easy for some of the best shows to zoom right past you, unnoticed — which almost happened to me with Midnight Diner.
Netflix’s coziest show has made a very quiet return
A new season of Midnight Diner: Tokyo Stories is streaming now, though it’s easy to miss.
If you haven’t seen it, Midnight Diner is probably the most comforting thing available on Netflix. The show follows the patrons of a cozy little restaurant tucked away in the backstreets of Shinjuku, which is only open during the unusual hours of midnight to 7:00AM. This, in turn, attracts a unique blend of customers, who help each other out under the watchful eye of the shop’s owner (Kaoru Kobayashi), known only as “master.” The show aired for three seasons on Japanese TV, before being picked up by Netflix for a handful more under the subtitle Tokyo Stories.
What’s especially notable about the show’s return is the huge gap: season 2 of the Netflix iteration streamed in 2019, and it took seven years for it to come back. The break was so long that season 3’s first episode, which premiered in October, is about the restaurant’s struggles during the pandemic. There are a bunch of cute scenes of the diner’s regulars sneaking outside to check if the restaurant is open yet, and wondering if it will ever be able to. If nothing else, the break was a chance for the reliable master to finally take a vacation.
But once Midnight Diner’s new season gets going, it’s right back to everything that made it beloved. Each episode uses a different dish as a way of exploring a particular story. An overworked manga artist imagines the life he missed out on over plates of spicy konjac, while a pair of old friends reconnect while munching on pork cutlet sandwiches. What’s remarkable about the show is the way it balances being a charming, comforting watch with exploring truly difficult and heartbreaking topics. It’s the combination of sweetness and sadness that makes it work so well. It’s as likely to make you laugh as it is to make you cry.
And unlike most Netflix series, the whole season isn’t streaming all at once. Instead, new episodes come out every Tuesday; so far six of a planned 10 episodes are available. It’s a welcome way to spend an evening, as the show’s slow pace and warm sense of humanity can feel like all-too rare traits in the current streaming landscape.
But the main reason I’m even writing about Midnight Diner’s return is that it has been so easy to miss. There’s been next to no promotion for it — all I could find was a trailer on Netflix’s Japanese YouTube channel — and I only happened upon it accidentally after the initial premiere while browsing aimlessly through Netflix’s new releases. This, despite being someone who has watched and rewatched the previous seasons multiple times. You’d think I’d get a notification or something. Netflix has always been full of hidden gems, but now that it’s busier than ever, those gems are all the more hidden.

articles.title: The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel
articles.text:
The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel
Avi Davidson is the first at-home user of an experimental prosthetic hand that lets him feel his wife’s hand in his own.
Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. Since then, he’s cycled through a few prosthetics. But his latest is different—it’s wired up to nerves in the upper part of his forearm and allows him to feel pressure. For the first time in years, he can use his left limb to handle delicate objects like grapes, eggs, and a loved one’s hand.
Davidson, who is taking part in a clinical trial run by the University of Utah, is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted in his arm. But he’s the first to take it home and use it independently.
The hand is part of the bionic LUKE arm, named after Luke Skywalker of Star Wars, who was fitted with a lifelike prosthetic arm after his own was light-sabered off. The arm was developed in the 2000s, initially trialed in 2014, and approved by the FDA that same year. The trial that Davidson is enrolled in isn’t so focused on the arm itself but on a new way to connect it to a person’s nervous system. The connection allows users to control movements and receive feedback about how much pressure they’re applying.
Researchers hope that Davidson’s experiences will help them answer some long-standing questions about the technology, including how useful it really is in day-to-day life. They want to know when the device is helpful and where it might fail. They also want to learn how it might affect Davidson’s well-being as well as his brain and nervous system.
The loss of a limb
In 2009, when he was 16, Davidson climbed a telephone pole to get the best shot of a sunset. “I climbed about 35 feet up,” he recalls. But he lost his footing as he tried to descend. He grabbed for a wire, which ended up electrocuting him, before he fell to the ground.
The accident resulted in second- and third-degree burns over 37% of his body, says Davidson, “and I broke my back in approximately 50 separate locations.” He also broke eight ribs, and his spinal cord was severed. He’s pretty sure he broke his left wrist, too. But around 10 days later, his left hand—his dominant hand, and the one he’d grabbed the wire with—had started to develop gangrene. It was amputated.
Davidson was ultimately in a coma for around a month. “Once I woke up, they explained to me: You’re paralyzed, you’re never going to walk again, and also, we took your left hand,” he recalls. “A bit of an inconvenience at 16, to say the least.”
Davidson, now 33 and a trauma therapist, went on to have physical therapy and adjusted to life in his changed body. He’s tried a range of prosthetic hands. The first one, which he received a year and a half after his injury, was a basic hook that allowed him to pick things up. It wasn’t fancy, but it gave him “a psychological feeling of returning to being whole,” he says.
The hands he’s tried since have been more advanced—some have allowed him to control individual fingers with muscle movements, for example. Some have been covered by his medical insurance, which allows for replacements around every five years, he says. Others he’s had to buy himself. He bought his third prosthetic hand, for example, from eBay. “It’s funny to think I bought a secondhand second hand,” he says.
New connections
A chance encounter with a scientist at a supermarket introduced Davidson to the research team at the University of Utah, which specialized in researching devices that plug into the body. Since 2013, the team had been running a trial of a system that could connect with the nerves of a residual limb, allowing an amputee to control a bionic one. Davidson turned out to be an ideal candidate, says Jake George, director of the university’s neurorobotics lab.
Davidson, who was keen to take part, first had to undergo what George describes as “pretty extensive” physical and psychological evaluations. Not only did he have to be well enough for surgery, but the team also scanned his brain to make sure that he still had a mental representation of his left hand—suggesting he’d be able to move a bionic one. They also ran tests to check that the nerves in his arm were working.
A therapist evaluated Davidson’s motivations for taking part in the trial. “Our patients aren’t being compensated, they don’t get to keep the device, and they go through two surgeries—the surgery to get it in and the surgery to take it out,” says George. “Avi’s doing this because he wants to help others.”
In late January of this year, Davidson flew from Florida to Utah to undergo his first surgery. It was a fairly complicated procedure involving engineers as well as a full surgical team. “We [researchers] stand in the back of the room and basically answer the question when the surgeon asks, ‘Where do I put the damn thing?’” says George. The surgeon exposed three nerves in Davidson’s arm and implanted an electrode array containing 100 needles in each one.
Nerves are floppy, so pushing electrodes into them doesn’t do much, says George. Instead, the team connected the electrodes to the nerves using what he describes as a “compressed-air gun.” “You shoot the grid of needles into the nerve at a very, very high velocity,” he says.
The team also inserted 24 electrodes into the muscles around the nerves. Wires for each of the nerve arrays and for pairs of muscle electrodes were left protruding from Davidson’s skin. After the surgery, he was offered some time to recover. “By day two, I’m like ‘No, let’s get me on the machines,’” he says.
That next step involved training a computer system to essentially translate the electrical activity in Davidson’s nerves into signals for bionic hand and wrist movements.
To get it up and running, the team had to train the device in two directions. The first involved converting nerve activity into hand, wrist, and finger movements. The researchers did this by listening in on the signals collected from the hundreds of electrical connection points in Davidson’s arm while he thought about various movements. That part was easy, says George: “It takes a matter of about five minutes.”
The second direction—linking the electrodes to sensations felt by the prosthetic—is much more time-consuming. Team members would stimulate each of the electrode connection points in turn, asking Davidson if he felt anything. They’d then turn up the signal at each of those points to see the effect. “It’s like a three-day process,” says George.
Becoming bionic
Davidson’s wires have since been connected and simplified, says George, who describes the process as “more or less like plugging in an HDMI cord or a USB-C cord.” When he wants to use his prosthetic, Davidson must first put it on, connect it to the wires, and then initiate it using a small computer.
He’s also had to undergo extensive physical therapy to learn how to control the hand. After all, it’s nothing like the prostheses he’s used in the past. “It’s almost like learning a different language with this kind of technology,” says Leanne Seckinger, an occupational therapist at the University of Utah Health System, who works with Davidson.
At first, she and Davidson worked on learning to hold and stabilize objects. They focused on Davidson’s personal goals—he wanted to be able to cook at home, so the pair worked on strategies to hold and manipulate utensils, prepare and chop ingredients, and carry plates and bowls. “He was able to crack an egg,” says Seckinger. “He made an omelet.”
Davidson has been using the hand at home since July 10, and he has noticed improvements. At first it took him a few minutes to write his name; now he can manage it in seconds. “The things I’m able to do with it now are tremendous, comparatively to where I was at initially,” he says.
Today, he says, he wears the hand around six days a week. He changes the batteries once or twice during the day and takes it off overnight. It’s heavy, weighing in at around five pounds, he says.
The hand can be useful, but it has also proved surprising. Sometimes, Davidson feels pain in it. This could be what’s known as “phantom pain”—a symptom experienced by some people who have lost a limb.
Curiously, he also says he experiences wrist strain. Davidson says he’s been getting a stiffness in his prosthetic wrist similar to what he experiences when he’s been typing for a long time with his flesh-and-blood right hand. He’s also realized that he can relieve the tension by pulling the bionic fingers back to stretch out his prosthetic wrist. “It’s weird,” he says.
The phenomenon “makes no sense physiologically,” says Chris Duncan, a rehabilitation doctor and chief medical officer at BIOS, a neurotechnology company that is supporting the trial. Stretching a typical hand pulls on tendons that extend down the forearm. There aren’t any tendons in a bionic arm—Davidson’s “stretches” are just moving actuators, says Duncan. He doesn’t know why it’s helpful but suspects it might have something to do with how the hand is represented in his mind. “What Avi’s experiencing is kind of like uncharted territory, honestly,” he says.
The research team is currently planning a bigger study and hopes to get the two-way sensation device approved by the FDA so that it can be covered by health insurance. “They need to understand that this is a useful new technological paradigm that will bring value to patients,” says Duncan. Team members also hope the technology will allow users to operate other devices, such as remote controls and wheelchairs.
Davidson will have his implants and the hand for a couple more months at least. But the trial was designed to run for “at least” one year, and that year will be up by the end of January 2027. “I’m not quite sure what happens after that,” he says.
George hopes the trial could be extended, but that will depend on funding. “From our perspective, we’d like to go as long as we can,” he says. “We don’t want to leave Avi without support.”
Davidson isn’t too worried about what comes next, though. “I went into this knowing that this was not something that I get to keep,” he says. “I am not going to benefit from this … I wanted to be a part of this in the context of being able to help push the technology forward.”
